name: Bhauma-Kara Dynasty
description: The Bhauma-Kara Dynasty governed the historical territory of Toshala along the coastal plains of modern Odisha from the late eighth century. Emerging following the eclipse of the Shailodbhavas, the realm initially promoted Mahayana Buddhism before embracing Shaivism and Vaishnavism under subsequent monarchs. Notably distinguished by the sovereign succession of at least seven queens regnant, the dynasty maintained an influential riverine administrative seat at Guhadevapataka until succumbing to Somavamshi and Bhanja expansion in the tenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Guhadevapataka; Common languages: Sanskrit and Odra Prakrit; Religion: Buddhism, Shaivism and Vaishnavism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Maharajadhiraja; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 736; Succeeded by: Somavamshi dynasty and Bhanja dynasty

name: Imperial Abbey of Hersfeld
label: holy roman empire
description: The Imperial Abbey of Hersfeld was an influential Benedictine monastic principality enjoying imperial immediacy within the Holy Roman Empire. Established near the junction of the Fulda and Haune rivers under the patronage of Charlemagne, the abbey commanded vast estates across Hesse and Thuringia. It retained its sovereign territorial privileges for centuries, directing regional ecclesiastic administration and economic life until political pressures from neighbouring landgraves culminated in its secularisation and annexation by Hesse-Kassel. \n\n Status: Imperial abbey; Capital: Hersfeld Abbey; Common languages: Latin and Old High German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Ecclesiastical principality; Ruler title: Prince-Abbot; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 775; Disestablished: 1648; Succeeded by: Landgraviate of Hesse-Kassel

name: Prince-Bishopric of Strasbourg
label: holy roman empire
description: The Prince-Bishopric of Strasbourg was an ecclesiastical state of the Holy Roman Empire that exercised temporal dominion across parts of Lower Alsace and the Upper Rhine valley. Governed by prince-bishops from episcopal residences in Strasbourg and Saverne, the principality frequently negotiated delicate balances of authority with the increasingly autonomous imperial city of Strasbourg. Although French conquests during the seventeenth century detached its cis-Rhenish territories, its trans-Rhenish domains endured until secularisation in 1803 transferred them to Baden. \n\n Status: Prince-bishopric; Capital: Strasbourg; Common languages: Alsatian, German and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Ecclesiastical principality; Ruler title: Prince-Bishop; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 982; Disestablished: 1803; Succeeded by: Kingdom of France and Margraviate of Baden

name: Kingdom of Abkhazia
description: The Kingdom of Abkhazia arose as a major western Caucasian realm during the late eighth century after Prince Leon threw off Byzantine suzerainty with Khazar assistance. Encompassing territories from the Black Sea shoreline across ancient Lazica, the monarchy transferred its royal seat inland from coastal Anacopia to Kutaisi. Its rulers patronised Georgian liturgical and cultural institutions, laying the foundation for dynastic union in 1008 when King Bagrat III inherited the realm to create the Kingdom of Georgia. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Anacopia and Kutaisi; Common languages: Georgian and Greek; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 778; Disestablished: 1008; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Georgia

name: Rustamid Imamate
description: The Rustamid Imamate was an Ibadi theocracy centred in north-central Algeria, founded by the Persian-descended religious scholar Abd al-Rahman ibn Rustam. Establishing their fortified capital at Tahert, the Rustamid imams forged a prosperous commercial crossroads that welcomed diverse Muslim communities and directed lucrative trans-Saharan trading caravans. Their dominion extended eastwards towards the Nafusa Mountains of Libya until religious and military onslaughts by the burgeoning Fatimid Caliphate brought about their collapse in 909. \n\n Status: Sovereign imamate; Capital: Tahert; Official languages: Arabic; Common languages: Arabic, Berber and Persian; Religion: Ibadi Islam; Government: Theocratic elective imamate; Ruler title: Imam; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 777; Disestablished: 909; Succeeded by: Fatimid Caliphate

name: Dingnan Circuit
description: The Dingnan Circuit, alternatively designated Xiasui, functioned as a de facto autonomous military prefecture in the northern Ordos loop, centred around Xiazhou in modern Shaanxi. Bestowed upon the Tangut Tuoba chieftains by the Tang court for aiding in quelling the Huang Chao rebellion, the circuit preserved regional self-governance under the hereditary Li clan across subsequent dynasties. Resisting repeated attempts at centralisation by Later Tang and Song monarchs, this durable enclave formed the direct precursor to the Western Xia Empire. \n\n Status: Autonomous military circuit; Administrative seat: Xiazhou; Common languages: Tangut and Middle Chinese; Religion: Buddhism; Government: Hereditary military governorship; Ruler title: Jiedushi; Historical era: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms; Established: 787; Succeeded by: Western Xia

name: Idrisid Dynasty
description: The Idrisid Dynasty was an early Islamic realm established in the western Maghreb by Idris ibn Abdallah, an Alid prince seeking refuge following the Battle of Fakhkh. Anchoring his initial authority among the Berber confederacies of Volubilis, the dynasty soon constructed the flourishing metropolis of Fes as its primary capital. The Idrisids directed the early spread of urban Islamic culture and Arabised scholarship across Morocco until tenth-century civil partitions and mounting rivalries between the Fatimids and Umayyads undermined their sovereignty. \n\n Status: Sovereign emirate; Capital: Fes; Official languages: Arabic; Common languages: Arabic and Berber; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 788; Disestablished: 974; Succeeded by: Zenata confederations and Caliphate of Cordoba

name: Principality of Hamamshen
description: The Principality of Hamamshen was a semi-isolated Armenian mountainous domain founded around the Black Sea ranges of northeastern Anatolia by Prince Hamam Amatuni. Fleeing Abbasid persecution and devastation in the Armenian highlands, the Amatuni nobility established an enduring haven that nurtured distinct regional traditions and the Homshetsi dialect. Guarded by the rugged Pontic Alps, the principality successfully maintained its local Christian autonomy for centuries until the expanding Ottoman Empire annexed its fortresses during the late fifteenth century. \n\n Status: Autonomous principality; Capital: Hamamshen; Common languages: Armenian; Religion: Armenian Apostolic Church; Government: Principality; Ruler title: Prince; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 790; Disestablished: 1486; Succeeded by: Ottoman Empire

name: Justanids
description: The Justanids were an indigenous Iranian dynasty that controlled the rugged Daylamite highlands of Gilan from their fortified stronghold at Rudbar. Originally adhering to Zoroastrianism, the monarchs adopted Zaydi Shi'ism during the early ninth century, transforming their mountainous redoubt into a sanctuary for persecuted Alid dissidents fleeing the Abbasid Caliphate. Renowned for their fierce military independence and elite infantry, the Justanids retained substantial local autonomy throughout the Iranian Intermezzo until regional supremacy passed to the Nizari Ismailis of Alamut. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Rudbar; Common languages: Daylami and Persian; Religion: Zoroastrianism and Zaydi Islam; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 791; Disestablished: 1044; Succeeded by: Nizari Ismaili state

name: Imperial Abbey of Murbach
label: holy roman empire
description: The Imperial Abbey of Murbach was a prestigious Benedictine monastic estate situated in southern Alsace at the base of the Grand Ballon in the Vosges. Founded during the eighth century by Count Eberhard and organised under Saint Pirmin, the abbey received extensive imperial immunities and territorial grants from Carolingian and Ottonian rulers. Operating as a sovereign ecclesiastical lord within the Holy Roman Empire, Murbach administered numerous towns and agricultural estates until seventeenth-century conflicts and revolutionary upheaval dismantled its historic privileges. \n\n Status: Imperial abbey; Capital: Murbach; Common languages: Alsatian, Latin and German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Ecclesiastical principality; Ruler title: Prince-Abbot; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 727; Disestablished: 1789; Succeeded by: Kingdom of France

name: Marca Hispanica
description: The Marca Hispanica was a defensive frontier zone established by Charlemagne along the eastern Pyrenean borderlands to safeguard Frankish Gaul against the Umayyad Emirate of Cordoba. Administered through a confederacy of fortified counties subject to Carolingian royal oversight, the march was anchored by the strategically vital maritime fortress of Barcelona following its capture in 801. Over the course of the ninth and tenth centuries, diminishing imperial control enabled local comital dynasties to convert their border garrisons into self-governing feudal principalities. \n\n Status: Imperial march; Capital: Barcelona; Common languages: Latin, Old Catalan and Old Occitan; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Military border protectorate; Ruler title: Margrave; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 795; Disestablished: 951; Preceded by: Emirate of Cordoba; Succeeded by: County of Barcelona

name: Obotrite Confederation
description: The Obotrite Confederation was a powerful league of Polabian Slavic tribes established across modern Mecklenburg and eastern Holstein. Maintaining major strongholds at Veligrad and Liubice, the Obotrites allied with Charlemagne during the Saxon Wars, securing temporary dominion over Nordalbingian lands after defeating the Saxons at Bornhoved in 798. The confederacy vigorously defended its pagan religious heritage and regional independence against neighbouring Scandinavian and Saxon incursions until prolonged Ottonian eastward expansion gradually subordinated its princes to imperial feudal vassalage. \n\n Status: Tribal confederation; Capital: Liubice; Common languages: Polabian and Old Saxon; Religion: Slavic paganism; Government: Tribal principality; Ruler title: Prince; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 796; Disestablished: 962; Succeeded by: Billung March and Principality of Mecklenburg

name: Avar Khaganate
description: The Avar Khaganate during this final era operated as a humbled tributary realm under Frankish suzerainty following Charlemagne's decisive capture of the nomadic royal ring in 796. Confined largely to the Pannonian plains east of the Danube, the surviving Avar nobility accepted Christian baptism and Frankish imperial oversight, governing from administrative centres around Sirmium. Crushed between relentless Slavic revolts and Frankish border colonisation, this remnant nomadic confederacy rapidly disintegrated before vanishing entirely from European annals during the 830s. \n\n Status: Client khaganate; Capital: Sirmium; Common languages: Avar Turkic and Late Common Slavic; Religion: Chalcedonian Christianity and Tengrism; Government: Nomadic confederation under vassalage; Ruler title: Khagan; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 797; Disestablished: 830; Preceded by: Avar Khaganate; Succeeded by: Carolingian Empire and Principality of Lower Pannonia

name: Frankish Empire
description: The Frankish Empire emerged as the dominant Western European power when Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne as Roman emperor at Old Saint Peter's Basilica on Christmas Day in 800. Governed from the imperial palace at Aachen, the Carolingian realm united modern France, Germany, the Low Countries and northern Italy under a centralised Christian administrative apparatus. Internal dynastic rivalries following the death of Louis the Pious triggered civil conflict, ultimately leading to the momentous partition of the empire under the Treaty of Verdun in 843. \n\n Status: Imperial monarchy; Capital: Aachen; Official languages: Medieval Latin; Common languages: Old High German, Old French and Romance dialects; Religion: Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 25 December 800; Disestablished: 1 September 843; Succeeded by: West Francia, Middle Francia and East Francia

name: Aghlabids
description: The Aghlabids were an Arab Muslim dynasty established by Ibrahim ibn al-Aghlab, ruling Ifriqiya and the central Mediterranean from their political seat at Kairouan. While maintaining nominal allegiance to the Abbasid caliphs in Baghdad, the emirate operated with practical independence, transforming its palace complexes at al-Abbasiyya and Raqqada into thriving cultural capitals. Aghlabid naval forces famously spearheaded the prolonged Islamic conquest of Byzantine Sicily, commanding maritime trade until military defeat at the hands of the Ismaili Fatimids dissolved the dynasty in 909. \n\n Status: Autonomous emirate; Capital: Kairouan; Official languages: Arabic; Common languages: Arabic and Berber; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Hereditary emirate; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 800; Disestablished: 909; Succeeded by: Fatimid Caliphate

name: Chera-Perumal Kingdom
description: The Chera-Perumal Kingdom was a medieval South Indian polity that governed the fertile coastal tracts of modern Kerala from its royal headquarters at Mahodayapuram, near present-day Kodungallur. Claiming lineage from the early Cheras, the monarchy presided over a flourishing maritime economy stimulated by extensive Indian Ocean spice commerce through bustling emporia such as Kollam. Sustained by an influential network of Nambudiri Brahmin agricultural settlements and local warrior councils, the kingdom flourished autonomously until prolonged tenth-century military friction with the Cholas transformed regional governance. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Kodungallur; Common languages: Old Malayalam and Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Cheraman Perumal; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 800; Disestablished: 951; Succeeded by: Later Chera principalities

name: Faroe Islands
label: norse/viking polities
description: The Faroe Islands formed an autonomous Norse maritime commonwealth established in the North Atlantic following Scandinavian migration in the early ninth century. Governed through the open-air popular assembly known as the Logting meeting at Tinganes in Torshavn, the insular society was organised around independent clan homesteads, fishing, fowling and sheep farming. Following communal conversion to Christianity around the turn of the eleventh century, internal chieftains gradually succumbed to overseas royal pressure, resulting in the archipelago's formal submission to the Norwegian Crown in 1036. \n\n Status: Autonomous commonwealth; Capital: Torshavn; Common languages: Old Norse; Religion: Norse paganism and Roman Catholicism; Government: Parliamentary tribal republic; Legislature: Logting; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 801; Disestablished: 1036; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Norway

name: Hsenwi State
label: shan states
description: Hsenwi State, also remembered in chronicles as Theinni, was one of the most prominent Tai Shan principalities established in the rugged highlands of northeastern Myanmar. Centred upon the broad valley of the Nam Tu River from its capital at Hsenwi town, the realm commanded lucrative trans-Himalayan trade routes linking Upper Burma with Yunnan. Ruled by a hereditary Saopha, the state maintained diplomatic independence through alliances and strategic tributary gestures until King Bayinnaung of the Toungoo Empire conquered the Shan realms in 1558. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Hsenwi; Common languages: Shan and Tai Nua; Religion: Theravada Buddhism and animism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Saopha; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 801; Disestablished: 1558; Succeeded by: Toungoo Empire

name: Kalinagos
description: The Kalinagos, historically designated by Europeans as the Island Caribs, constituted an autonomous maritime indigenous society across the Lesser Antilles, spanning islands from Dominica to Saint Vincent. Organised into decentralised village settlements under elected war leaders and village councils, they maintained a skilled seafaring culture dependent on seafaring canoe voyages, coastal fishing and shifting horticulture. Fiercely protecting their archipelagic territory, the Kalinagos mounted formidable resistance against Spanish, French and English colonial encroachments until demographic collapse and military pacification curtailed their autonomy by the early eighteenth century. \n\n Status: Decentralised tribal confederation; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Kalinago and Carib pidgin; Religion: Traditional animism; Government: Tribal council of chiefs; Ruler title: Ouboutou; Historical era: Postclassical to Early Modern; Established: 801; Disestablished: 1701

name: Kingdom of Hariphunchai
label: mon kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of Hariphunchai was a prominent Mon mandala polity centred in the fertile Ping River basin of northern Thailand, with its capital at modern Lamphun. Tracing its legendary foundation to the Dvaravati princess Camadevi, the realm flourished as a vital northern redoubt of Mon literacy, Theravada Buddhist scholarship and distinctive brick temple architecture. The kingdom maintained extensive diplomatic and religious networks across mainland Southeast Asia for centuries until King Mangrai of Lan Na besieged and captured Lamphun in 1292, incorporating its territories into his expanding Tai state. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Hariphunchai; Common languages: Old Mon and Pali; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Mandala monarchy; Ruler title: Monarch; Historical era: Post-classical; Established: 629; Disestablished: 1292; Succeeded by: Lan Na

name: Kingdom of Lhuentse
description: The Kingdom of Lhuentse was an independent mountain realm established in the deeply incised valleys of the Kurtoe region in northeastern Bhutan. Emerging amidst the political fragmentation of the eastern Himalayas, the polity was governed by hereditary local nobility who fortified strategic crags and directed riverine agricultural valleys. Maintaining ancestral Buddhist traditions and distinct textile arts in isolation from outside powers, Lhuentse retained its autonomy until the religious unifier Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal integrated the territory into the central theocratic state of Bhutan in 1641. \n\n Status: Petty kingdom; Capital: Lhuentse Dzong; Common languages: Dzongkha and Chocha Ngacha; Religion: Tibetan Buddhism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 801; Disestablished: 1641; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Bhutan

name: Kingdom of Trashigang
description: The Kingdom of Trashigang was an autonomous eastern Himalayan principality situated high above the confluence of the Drangme Chhu and Gamri rivers in eastern Bhutan. Governed by regional chieftains who ruled over scattered clan communities and terraced mountain settlements, the kingdom controlled vital trading paths running south toward Assam. Operating independently for centuries amidst neighbouring highland polities, Trashigang's sovereign status came to an end when the consolidating forces of Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal absorbed the valley into a unified Bhutanese realm in 1641. \n\n Status: Petty kingdom; Capital: Trashigang Dzong; Common languages: Tshangla and Dzongkha; Religion: Tibetan Buddhism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 801; Disestablished: 1641; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Bhutan

name: Kingdom of Trongsa
description: The Kingdom of Trongsa occupied a commanding strategic position overlooking the deep gorge of the Mangde Chhu river in central Bhutan. Dominating the principal mountain passes connecting the eastern and western districts of the country, local lords extracted tolls and exercised sovereign authority over surrounding agrarian hamlets. The independent polity sustained distinct feudal institutions until the centralising military campaigns of Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal annexed the district in 1641, laying the groundwork for Trongsa's future role as a powerful provincial fortress under the Drukpa hierarchy. \n\n Status: Petty kingdom; Capital: Trongsa Dzong; Common languages: Dzongkha and Mangde; Religion: Tibetan Buddhism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 801; Disestablished: 1641; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Bhutan

name: Kingdom of Zhemgang
description: The Kingdom of Zhemgang was an autonomous highland state established across the heavily forested ridges and gorges of the historical Kheng region in south-central Bhutan. Governed by hereditary chieftains from ancestral ridge-top strongholds, the polity maintained a self-sufficient rural economy based on terrace farming, bamboo crafts and barter trade with the southern plains. Like its neighbouring mountain principalities, Zhemgang preserved its territorial sovereignty until the comprehensive seventeenth-century consolidation campaigns of Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal integrated its valleys into the unified Bhutanese state in 1641. \n\n Status: Petty kingdom; Capital: Zhemgang Dzong; Common languages: Khengkha and Dzongkha; Religion: Tibetan Buddhism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 801; Disestablished: 1641; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Bhutan

name: Somavamshi Dynasty
description: The Somavamshi Dynasty, also known as the Kesharis, was an illustrious royal lineage that ruled extensive territories across modern Odisha and eastern India from the ninth century. Migrating eastward from Dakshina Kosala, the dynasty conquered Kalinga and Utkala, displacing the Bhauma-Karas and establishing administrative capitals at Yayatinagara and Abhinava-Yayatinagara. Their reigns inaugurated a golden age of classic Odishan temple architecture, patronising monumental Shaivite sanctuaries at Bhubaneswar until Eastern Ganga armies under Anantavarman Chodaganga conquered their realm in the early twelfth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Yayatinagara; Official languages: Sanskrit; Common languages: Sanskrit and Odra Prakrit; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Maharajadhiraja; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 800; Disestablished: 1110; Succeeded by: Eastern Ganga dynasty

name: Sultanate of Kilwa
label: polities of the swahili coast
description: The Sultanate of Kilwa was the most affluent maritime mercantile empire on the medieval Swahili Coast, headquartered on the offshore island of Kilwa Kisiwani in southern Tanzania. Originating as a coastal trading settlement before being transformed under the Shirazi dynastic lineage, the sultanate commanded Indian Ocean commerce by monopolising the lucrative gold export networks of Sofala. At its zenith, Kilwa presided over coral-stone palaces, extensive harbour installations and mints striking local coinage until Portuguese naval incursions in 1505 disrupted its maritime hegemony. \n\n Status: Sovereign sultanate; Capital: Kilwa Kisiwani; Common languages: Swahili, Arabic and Persian; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Sultanate; Ruler title: Sultan; Currency: Kilwa dinar; Historical era: Shirazi era; Established: 957; Disestablished: 1506; Succeeded by: Portuguese Empire

name: Takrur Kingdom
description: The Takrur Kingdom was an ancient West African state established along the lower Senegal River valley, with its principal urban centre located near modern Podor. Benefiting from early agricultural productivity and active involvement in trans-Saharan trade routes exchanging gold and desert salt, the realm flourished as a powerful contemporary of the Ghana Empire. Under King War Jabi during the early eleventh century, Takrur became one of the first Sub-Saharan polities to adopt Islam officially, maintaining commercial vitality until expanding Jolof and Malian forces absorbed its domains. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Takrur; Common languages: Serer, Fula and Arabic; Religion: Islam and traditional animism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 801; Disestablished: 1286; Succeeded by: Jolof Empire and Mali Empire

name: Tanjungpura Kingdom
description: The Tanjungpura Kingdom was an ancient coastal Malay polity established along the southwestern shoreline of Borneo, corresponding to the modern Ketapang Regency of West Kalimantan. Commanding strategic maritime trade lanes across the Java Sea from shifting royal capitals including Sukadana and Negeri Baru, the kingdom maintained extensive mercantile links with Javanese and Sumatran empires. Known in ancient records as Bakulapura, Tanjungpura navigated shifting tributary relationships with Singasari and Majapahit while preserving substantial regional sovereignty over coastal estuaries and inland forest extraction. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Sukadana; Common languages: Malay; Religion: Animism and Hinduism-Buddhism; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Postclassical; Established: 800; Disestablished: 1401; Succeeded by: Sukadana Sultanate

name: Tatar Confederation
description: The Tatar Confederation was a formidable league of nomadic Mongolic pastoralist clans inhabiting the fertile steppe surrounding Lake Hulun and Lake Buir in northeastern Mongolia. Operating without a permanent urban capital, the confederacy relied on mobile seasonal encampments, cavalry warfare and tribal councils to govern its vast pasturelands. Frequently contending against neighbouring nomadic leagues and balancing tributary relations with northern Chinese courts, the Tatars remained powerful steppe contenders until Temujin decisively defeated their armies in 1202, incorporating their clans into the Mongol Empire. \n\n Status: Nomadic confederation; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Mongolic; Religion: Tengrism; Government: Elective nomadic monarchy; Legislature: Kurultai; Ruler title: Chieftain; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 801; Disestablished: 1202; Succeeded by: Khamag Mongol

name: State of the Shirvanshahs
label: caucasian khanates
description: The State of the Shirvanshahs was an enduring monarchy established across the eastern Caucasus along the Caspian coastline of present-day Azerbaijan. Originating under Arab governors from the Banu Shayban who gradually Persianised, the dynasty attained complete independence under Haytham ibn Khalid in 861 and ruled from their ancient stronghold of Shamakhi. The Shirvanshahs fostered a brilliant cultural renaissance, subsidising eminent Persian poets and erecting formidable fortifications before mounting expansion by Safavid Iran under Shah Tahmasp I brought the kingdom to an end in 1538. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Shamakhi; Official languages: Persian; Common languages: Persian and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Shirvanshah; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 861; Disestablished: 1538; Succeeded by: Safavid Empire

name: Principality of Nitra
description: The Principality of Nitra was an early West Slavic domain established around the river valleys of southwestern Slovakia, with its political and religious centre at Nitra. Under the leadership of Prince Pribina, the realm emerged from the post-Avar period as an autonomous polity where the first recorded Christian church among West Slavs was consecrated around 828. Territorial competition with neighbouring Moravian princes swiftly intensified, culminating in Pribina's expulsion by Mojmir I around 833 and the unification of Nitra into the expanding Great Moravian state. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Nitra; Common languages: Late Common Slavic; Religion: Slavic paganism and Latin Christianity; Government: Principality; Ruler title: Prince; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 806; Disestablished: 834; Preceded by: Samo's Empire; Succeeded by: Great Moravia

name: Saracen Corsica
label: small arab emirates in europe
description: Saracen Corsica denotes a temporary military foothold established by Muslim naval expeditionary forces on the island of Corsica during the early ninth century. Operating without a permanent administrative capital, North African and Andalusian raiders occupied fortified coastal anchorages to raid the Tyrrhenian seaways and interrupt Mediterranean commerce. Frankish naval counteroffensives organised under Carolingian commanders swiftly contested their presence, culminating in naval engagements that expelled the garrison and restored Christian imperial authority over the island by 812. \n\n Status: Military naval outpost; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Arabic and Romance; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Military encampment; Ruler title: Naval commander; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 811; Disestablished: 812; Succeeded by: March of Corsica

name: Narentine State
description: The Narentine State, known in Byzantine annals as Pagania, was a fiercely independent South Slavic tribal principality centred along the Neretva River and the Dalmatian littoral around Makarska. Resolute in their adherence to Slavic paganism long after neighbouring peoples converted, the Narentines developed formidable naval raiding fleets that dominated the Adriatic Sea. Their corsairs regularly defeated Venetian fleets and extracted maritime tributes until systematic naval campaigns launched by the Republic of Venice under Doge Pietro II Orseolo broke their power around the turn of the eleventh century. \n\n Status: Tribal principality; Capital: Makarska; Common languages: South Slavic; Religion: Slavic paganism; Government: Chiefdom; Ruler title: Prince; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 813; Disestablished: 1001; Succeeded by: Republic of Venice

name: Kingdom of Pamplona
description: The Kingdom of Pamplona was a Basque monarchy established in the western Pyrenees around the city of Pamplona, laying the territorial foundation for the later Kingdom of Navarre. Arising in 824 under Inigo Arista through an alliance with the local Muslim Banu Qasi dynasty to resist Frankish Carolingian incursions, the realm secured control over essential mountain passes. Pamplona gradually expanded across Navarre and the Upper Ebro, countering both Cordoban emirs and northern lords until dynastic partitions under King Sancho the Great reorganised the realm in 1035. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Pamplona; Common languages: Basque, Old Spanish and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 824; Disestablished: 1035; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Navarre and Kingdom of Aragon

name: Agder
label: norwegian petty kingdoms
description: Agder was a Norse petty kingdom situated across the southernmost coastal rim of Norway, with an influential royal chieftain seat established at Spangereid. Controlling vital sea routes connecting the Skagerrak with the North Sea, the local monarchs grew wealthy through coastal commerce, fishing and overseas Viking voyages. The kingdom preserved its distinct assembly traditions and dynastic independence through the early ninth century until dynastic marriages and the centralising conquests of Harald Fairhair subsumed the territory into the newly unified Kingdom of Norway. \n\n Status: Petty kingdom; Capital: Spangereid; Common languages: Old Norse; Religion: Norse paganism; Government: Petty monarchy; Ruler title: Petty King; Historical era: Viking Age; Established: 821; Disestablished: 901; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Norway

name: Alvheim
label: norwegian petty kingdoms
description: Alvheim was an early medieval Norse petty realm located along the maritime borderlands of the Oslofjord, encompassing territories corresponding to the historical province of Bohuslan between the Glomma and Gota rivers. Governed by independent chieftains, the kingdom was celebrated in Norse sagas for its strategic maritime position and bitter rivalries with neighbouring Vestfold rulers. The autonomy of Alvheim was brought to a decisive conclusion during the late ninth century when King Harald Fairhair campaigned across eastern Norway, annexing the region directly into his fledgling crown. \n\n Status: Petty kingdom; Capital: Alvheim; Common languages: Old Norse; Religion: Norse paganism; Government: Petty monarchy; Ruler title: Petty King; Historical era: Viking Age; Established: 821; Disestablished: 873; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Norway

name: Halogaland
label: norwegian petty kingdoms
description: Halogaland was the northernmost Norse realm of the early Viking Age, extending across the rugged Arctic coastlines and fjords from Namdalen northwards toward Tromso and the Lofoten archipelago. Governed by powerful chieftains and jarls, the kingdom derived vast wealth from walrus ivory, marine mammal oil, fur exports and tribute collected from the indigenous Sami populations. Halogaland maintained an autonomous maritime existence until King Harald Fairhair secured the allegiance of its northern jarls during the late ninth century, integrating their estates into the unified Norwegian realm. \n\n Status: Petty kingdom; Capital: Tromso; Common languages: Old Norse and Sami; Religion: Norse paganism; Government: Petty monarchy; Ruler title: Jarl; Historical era: Viking Age; Established: 821; Disestablished: 873; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Norway

name: Hordaland
label: norwegian petty kingdoms
description: Hordaland was an autonomous coastal petty kingdom in western Norway centred around the deep fjords and islands adjacent to present-day Bergen. Governed by proud sea-kings based at royal estates such as Alrekstad, the realm exercised substantial naval influence across the North Sea trade lanes. Hordaland formed the core of regional resistance against the eastward expansion of the Vestfold dynasty, culminating in the historic Battle of Hafrsfjord, where the defeat and death of King Eirik led to the kingdom's incorporation into the unified Norwegian realm. \n\n Status: Petty kingdom; Capital: Bergen; Common languages: Old Norse; Religion: Norse paganism; Government: Petty monarchy; Ruler title: Petty King; Historical era: Viking Age; Established: 821; Disestablished: 901; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Norway

name: Kingdom of Aragon
description: The Kingdom of Aragon originated as a hardy Pyrenean domain along the Aragon river valley before emerging as a sovereign kingdom under Ramiro I in 1035. Establishing its initial royal seat at Jaca and later at captured Zaragoza, the realm spearheaded major southward expansions against Islamic taifa states during the Reconquista. Following its twelfth-century dynastic union with the County of Barcelona to create the Crown of Aragon, the kingdom preserved its autonomous Corts and distinctive legal privileges until the accession of Ferdinand II in 1479 united the crowns of Aragon and Castile. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Zaragoza and Jaca; Common languages: Aragonese, Latin and Catalan; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: King; Legislature: Cortes of Aragon; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 1035; Disestablished: 1479; Succeeded by: Crown of Aragon and Catholic Monarchy of Spain

name: Rogaland
label: norwegian petty kingdoms
description: Rogaland was an influential maritime petty kingdom situated in southwestern Norway, commanding the strategic shipping corridor of the Karmsund from its ancestral royal stronghold at Avaldsnes. The realm prospered through extensive maritime shipping, fishing and early Viking expeditions across the British Isles. As the site of the decisive naval Battle of Hafrsfjord around 872, Rogaland witnessed the defeat of its local monarch King Sulke by Harald Fairhair, who converted Avaldsnes into his principal royal residence and absorbed the district into the unified crown of Norway. \n\n Status: Petty kingdom; Capital: Avaldsnes; Common languages: Old Norse; Religion: Norse paganism; Government: Petty monarchy; Ruler title: Petty King; Historical era: Viking Age; Established: 821; Disestablished: 901; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Norway

name: Sogn
label: norwegian petty kingdoms
description: Sogn was an independent Norse petty kingdom situated in western Norway, encompassing the rugged shores and sheltered inlets of the vast Sognefjord. Anchored administratively around the ancient settlement of Sogndal, the realm was governed by local sea-kings who drew sustenance from fjord agriculture, timber harvesting and coastal seafaring. Following the dynastic marriage of Princess Ragnhild to Halfdan the Black of Vestfold, her son Harald Fairhair inherited the territory upon his grandfather's demise, peacefully absorbing Sogn into the expanding domains that formed the unified Norwegian monarchy. \n\n Status: Petty kingdom; Capital: Sogndal; Common languages: Old Norse; Religion: Norse paganism; Government: Petty monarchy; Ruler title: Petty King; Historical era: Viking Age; Established: 821; Disestablished: 861; Succeeded by: Vestfold and Kingdom of Norway

name: Vestfold
label: norwegian petty kingdoms
description: Vestfold was a pre-eminent Norse kingdom situated along the western shoreline of the Oslofjord, anchored by the ancient royal and commercial centre of Tonsberg. Ruled by the legendary Yngling dynasty, including chieftains Gudrod the Hunter and Halfdan the Black, the realm profited from productive agricultural lowlands, extensive seafaring networks and rich burial mounds. Vestfold served as the crucial territorial base for Harald Fairhair, whose systematic military campaigns across the late ninth century consolidated Norway's fractured petty kingdoms into a single sovereign realm. \n\n Status: Petty kingdom; Capital: Tonsberg; Common languages: Old Norse; Religion: Norse paganism; Government: Petty monarchy; Ruler title: Petty King; Historical era: Viking Age; Established: 821; Disestablished: 873; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Norway

name: Tahirid Dynasty
label: iranian intermezzo
description: The Tahirid Dynasty was an autonomous Persian dehqan regime that governed Greater Khorasan as hereditary viceroys on behalf of the Abbasid Caliphate. Established by the celebrated military general Tahir ibn Husayn following his pivotal support for Caliph al-Ma'mun, the dynasty administered its vast eastern domains from regional capitals at Merv and Nishapur while simultaneously commanding the police forces of Baghdad. Although remaining loyal vassals to the caliphal throne, the Tahirids exercised practical self-governance until the insurgent Saffarid commander Ya'qub ibn al-Layth captured Nishapur in 873. \n\n Status: Caliphal governorate; Capital: Hamadan; Common languages: Early New Persian and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Hereditary emirate; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 821; Disestablished: 873; Preceded by: Abbasid Caliphate; Succeeded by: Saffarid dynasty

name: Garhwal Kingdom
description: The Garhwal Kingdom was an independent Himalayan state established across the rugged mountain ranges of modern Uttarakhand in northern India. Founded by Raja Kanak Pal of the Panwar dynasty, the realm united numerous alpine valleys and fortified garrisons under a centralised monarchy headquartered at Srinagar. Benefiting from control over revered pilgrimage corridors to Badrinath and Kedarnath, the kingdom defended its high-altitude frontiers against northern Tibetan incursions and neighbouring hill rajas for nearly a millennium until the Gorkha invasion of 1803. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Srinagar (Garhwal); Common languages: Garhwali and Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 823; Disestablished: 1804; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Nepal

name: Kingdom of Kent
label: saxon polities in britain
description: The Kingdom of Kent during the mid-ninth century functioned as a dependent Anglo-Saxon sub-kingdom subordinate to Mercian political hegemony. Governed from the historic ecclesiastical and administrative seat of Canterbury, the realm encompassed fertile agricultural lands and vital Channel ferry ports linking Britain to the European continent. While local charters still acknowledged regional rulers, Kent was increasingly buffeted by escalating Viking maritime raids and intense political rivalry between Mercia and Wessex, which ultimately absorbed the territory into the West Saxon crown. \n\n Status: Protectorate; Capital: Canterbury; Official languages: Kentish Old English; Common languages: Old English and Latin; Religion: Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Client monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 826; Disestablished: 872; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Wessex

name: Emirate of Crete
description: The Emirate of Crete was an autonomous Muslim seafaring realm established when Andalusian exiles led by Abu Hafs seized the Mediterranean island from Byzantine administration in the late 820s. Operating under nominal Abbasid suzerainty from their heavily fortified capital at Chandax, the emirs transformed Crete into a formidable naval base that dominated eastern Mediterranean shipping lanes. For over a century, the emirate defied Byzantine counteroffensives through aggressive corsair warfare and prosperous regional commerce until General Nikephoros Phokas recaptured the island in 961. \n\n Status: Nominal vassal emirate; Capital: Chandax; Common languages: Arabic and Greek; Religion: Sunni Islam and Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruler title: Emir; Currency: Gold dinar; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 827; Disestablished: 961; Succeeded by: Byzantine Empire

name: Kingdom of Mercia
label: anglian polities in britain
description: The Kingdom of Mercia during this period operated as a truncated client state and protectorate under the paramountcy of the Kingdom of Wessex. Following the partition of its eastern territories by the Viking invaders of the Danelaw, western Mercian lords ruled from royal seats such as Tamworth in close military cooperation with King Alfred the Great. Commanded by Ealdorman Aethelred and Princess Aethelflaed, the realm constructed fortified burhs to stem Norse incursions before King Edward the Elder permanently incorporated the territory into the fledgling Kingdom of England. \n\n Status: Client kingdom; Capital: Tamworth; Official languages: Mercian Old English; Common languages: Old English; Religion: Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Monarchy under vassalage; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 830; Disestablished: 919; Succeeded by: Kingdom of England

name: Great Moravia
description: Great Moravia was the earliest prominent West Slavic empire to consolidate Central Europe, centred along the fertile valleys of the Morava River with its administrative citadel at Mikulcice. Reaching its geopolitical zenith under Prince Svatopluk I, the realm fostered the birth of Slavic written culture by welcoming the mission of Saints Cyril and Methodius, who instituted the Glagolitic script and Old Church Slavonic liturgy. Weakened by internal succession quarrels after Svatopluk's death, the confederated state collapsed around 907 beneath the destructive onslaught of migrating Hungarian horsemen. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Mikulcice; Common languages: Late Common Slavic and Old Church Slavonic; Religion: Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Prince; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 833; Disestablished: 907; Succeeded by: Duchy of Bohemia and Principality of Hungary

name: Barwani State
description: Barwani State was an ancient Rajput kingdom established along the rugged slopes of the Satpura Range south of the Narmada River in central India. Founded in the ninth century by the Sisodia clan from Mewar, the principality maintained its dynastic seat at Barwani amidst dense teak forests and rocky defiles. The rulers preserved administrative autonomy through shifting allegiances with the Malwa Sultanate and the Mughal Empire, protecting their local trade passes and tribal subjects until Maratha encroachments altered the regional balance of power. \n\n Status: Sovereign princely state; Capital: Barwani; Common languages: Nimadi, Hindi and Bhili; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Rana; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 836; Disestablished: 1802; Succeeded by: Maratha Empire

name: Republic of Amalfi
description: The Republic of Amalfi emerged as an autonomous maritime city-state on the Tyrrhenian coast of southern Italy after separating from the Duchy of Naples in 839. Governed by elected magistrates and later hereditary dukes, the seafaring commonwealth developed extensive trading networks linking southern Italy with Constantinople, Egypt and the Levant. Amalfi pioneered early Mediterranean maritime law through the celebrated Tavole Amalfitane and amassed immense mercantile wealth until aggressive competition from neighbouring powers and eventual Norman conquest curtailed its commercial dominance. \n\n Status: Maritime republic; Capital: Amalfi; Common languages: Latin, Italian Romance and Greek; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Merchant republic; Ruler title: Duke; Currency: Tari; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 839; Disestablished: 1137; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Sicily

name: Duchy of Gaeta
label: byzantine successors in southern italy;maritime republics
description: The Duchy of Gaeta was an autonomous maritime enclave situated on a fortified rocky promontory along the Tyrrhenian coast of central Italy. Initially subject to Byzantine Naples, Gaeta asserted practical independence under the hereditary Docibilis family from the mid-ninth century onward, minting its own currency and fielding powerful merchant fleets. The duchy played a prominent role in coastal defence against Saracen raids, notably participating in the victorious Battle of Ostia in 849, and preserved its municipal privileges until Norman monarchs incorporated it in 1140. \n\n Status: Sovereign duchy; Capital: Gaeta; Common languages: Medieval Latin and Italian Romance; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Duke; Currency: Follaro gaetano; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 839; Disestablished: 1140; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Sicily

name: Duchy of Sorrento
description: The Duchy of Sorrento was a compact maritime principality established on the rugged Sorrentine Peninsula overlooking the Bay of Naples. Gaining de facto independence from Byzantine Naples in the 840s, the city-state allied closely with neighbouring Christian republics to combat Mediterranean piracy, actively contributing warships to the Campania League's victory over Saracen raiders at Ostia in 849. Governed by local dukes, Sorrento maintained agricultural orchards and maritime trade routes until internal dynastic strife exposed the peninsula to Norman annexation in the late eleventh century. \n\n Status: Sovereign duchy; Capital: Sorrento; Common languages: Latin, Neapolitan and Greek; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Elective duchy; Ruler title: Duke; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 840; Disestablished: 1078; Preceded by: Duchy of Naples; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Sicily

name: Principality of Lower Pannonia
description: The Principality of Lower Pannonia was a Slavic client domain established under East Frankish suzerainty across the lowlands surrounding Lake Balaton in modern Hungary. Granted by King Louis the German to Prince Pribina following his flight from Nitra, the realm was governed from the fortified marshland stronghold of Mosaburg. Under Pribina and his successor Kocel, the principality flourished as a major crossroads of Christian evangelisation, providing crucial patronage to Saints Cyril and Methodius until renewed Carolingian-Moravian conflicts and the Magyar migration dismantled its autonomy. \n\n Status: Vassal principality; Capital: Mosaburg; Common languages: Late Common Slavic and Old High German; Religion: Latin Christianity; Government: Client principality; Ruler title: Prince; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 840; Disestablished: 877; Preceded by: Avar Khaganate; Succeeded by: East Francia

name: Emirate of Melitene
description: The Emirate of Melitene was an aggressive Muslim frontier principality centred on the strategic fortress city of Malatya in eastern Anatolia. Governed by the capable and bellicose emir Umar al-Aqta, the state operated as a vital bastion of the Abbasid border defensive march against the Byzantine Empire. Allied with the heterodox Paulicians of Tephrike, Melitene launched repeated deep cavalry incursions into Anatolia until Byzantine imperial forces encircled and routed Umar's army at the Battle of Lalakaon in 863, where the emir was slain. \n\n Status: Frontier emirate; Capital: Malatya; Common languages: Arabic, Greek and Armenian; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Military emirate; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 841; Disestablished: 863; Succeeded by: Byzantine Empire

name: Emirate of Taranto
label: small arab emirates in europe
description: The Emirate of Taranto was an early medieval Muslim enclave established on the Ionian coastline of southern Italy, controlling the strategic fortified port of Taranto. Originating around 840 under a military commander named Saba following the initial Islamic conquests in Sicily, the settlement developed into a fortified naval redoubt that raided across Apulia, Calabria and the Adriatic Sea. Taranto's raiders repeatedly defeated Venetian and Byzantine squadrons until Byzantine imperial forces under general Apostyppes recaptured the fortress in 880, restoring Christian imperial control over southern Italy. \n\n Status: Military emirate; Capital: Taranto; Common languages: Arabic, Greek and Italian Romance; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Military emirate; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 841; Disestablished: 881; Succeeded by: Byzantine Empire

name: Kara-Khanid Khanate
description: The Kara-Khanid Khanate was a powerful Karluk Turkic confederation that ruled extensive territories across Central Asia and the Tarim Basin from capitals at Balasagun and Kashgar. Following their conversion to Islam under Sultan Satuq Bughra Khan during the mid-tenth century, the dynasty synthesised nomadic Turkic traditions with Perso-Islamic urban statecraft. After overthrowing the Samanids in 999 to conquer Transoxiana, the realm consolidated regional trade along the Silk Road until internal dynastic rivalries led to its partition into distinct Western and Eastern Khanates in 1042. \n\n Status: Sovereign khaganate; Capital: Balasagun and Kashgar; Common languages: Khaqani Turkic, Persian and Arabic; Religion: Islam; Government: Dual monarchy; Ruler title: Khagan; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 840; Disestablished: 1042; Succeeded by: Western Kara-Khanid Khanate and Eastern Kara-Khanid Khanate

name: Yenisei Kyrgyz Khaganate
description: The Yenisei Kyrgyz Khaganate attained steppe supremacy across northern Inner Asia following its decisive destruction of the Uyghur Khaganate in 840. Operating from ancestral nomadic heartlands in the upper Yenisei basin without a permanent stone capital, the Kyrgyz exercised military hegemony over the Mongolian plateau through mobile cavalry columns rather than administrative bureaucracy. The khagans maintained traditional Tengrist rites while controlling lucrative Siberian fur routes and northern trading tracks until the rising power of the Khitan Liao dynasty expelled them back to the Siberian forest margins around 925. \n\n Status: Nomadic empire; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Yenisei Kyrgyz and Old Turkic; Religion: Tengrism; Government: Nomadic monarchy; Ruler title: Khagan; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 840; Disestablished: 925; Preceded by: Uyghur Khaganate; Succeeded by: Liao dynasty

name: Kingdom of Ösung
label: tibetan era of fragmentation
description: The Kingdom of Osung emerged during the violent dissolution of the Tibetan Empire following the assassination of King Langdarma in 842. Formed around the royal claimant Osung, who contested central Tibet against his half-brother Yumtan in the civil war of U-Yor, the state initially struggled for mastery over the ancient dynastic palaces of Lhasa. As regional revolts shattered royal prestige, Osung's lineage retreated westward into Ngari, preserving imperial lineage traditions and laying the dynastic groundwork for the later Himalayan kingdoms of Guge and Purang. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Lhasa; Common languages: Classical Tibetan; Religion: Tibetan Buddhism and Bon; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Era of Fragmentation; Established: 843; Disestablished: 926; Preceded by: Tibetan Empire; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Guge

name: Kingdom of Yumtän
label: tibetan era of fragmentation
description: The Kingdom of Yumtan was a splinter realm established in the central Tibetan plateau amidst the chaotic fragmentation of the Tibetan Empire after 842. Proclaimed monarch by aristocratic factions in opposition to Prince Osung, Yumtan commanded garrisons in the core province of U and fortified residences surrounding Lhasa. The kingdom's authority was severely undermined by widespread anti-Buddhist uprisings, peasant revolts and insubordinate frontier warlords, resulting in the rapid disintegration of its administrative machinery into petty clan lordships by the early tenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Lhasa; Common languages: Classical Tibetan; Religion: Tibetan Buddhism and Bon; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Era of Fragmentation; Established: 843; Disestablished: 911; Preceded by: Tibetan Empire; Succeeded by: Central Tibetan warlord clans

name: Kingdom of the East Franks
label: barbarian kingdoms;frankish polities
description: The Kingdom of the East Franks was created by the Treaty of Verdun in 843, allocating the eastern portions of the Carolingian realm to King Louis the German. Encompassing the tribal stem duchies of Saxony, Franconia, Swabia and Bavaria, the monarchy was administered through an itinerant royal court frequenting imperial palaces in Frankfurt and Regensburg. The state successfully rebuffed Magyar incursions and consolidated Germanic territorial identity, evolving steadily across the tenth century until the coronation of King Otto the Great in 962 inaugurated the Holy Roman Empire. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Administrative seat: Mobile court; Common languages: Old High German, Old Saxon and Medieval Latin; Religion: Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 843; Disestablished: 962; Succeeded by: Holy Roman Empire and Kingdom of Germany

name: Kingdom of the West Franks
label: barbarian kingdoms;frankish polities
description: The Kingdom of the West Franks was established under the Treaty of Verdun in 843 when the Carolingian Empire was partitioned, placing its western territories under King Charles the Bald. Governing from palaces at Laon, Compiegne and Paris, the crown struggled continuously against devastating Viking river raids and the decentralising ambitions of powerful regional magnates in Aquitaine and Flanders. Although royal power became increasingly circumscribed to the Île-de-France, the realm maintained institutional continuity until the election of Hugh Capet in 987 founded the Kingdom of France. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Paris and Laon; Official languages: Medieval Latin; Common languages: Old French and Old Occitan; Religion: Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 843; Disestablished: 987; Succeeded by: Kingdom of France

name: Middle Francia
label: barbarian kingdoms;frankish polities
description: Middle Francia was a short-lived Carolingian realm created by the Treaty of Verdun in 843 as the imperial domain of Emperor Lothair I. Stretching as an elongated corridor from Frisia and the Low Countries through the Rhineland and Burgundy down into northern Italy, the kingdom contained the historic imperial capital of Aachen. Despite its rich cultural assets and prestige as the imperial heartland, the polity lacked geographic cohesion and was formally partitioned among Lothair's three sons under the Treaty of Prüm upon his abdication in 855. \n\n Status: Imperial kingdom; Capital: Aachen; Official languages: Medieval Latin; Common languages: Old High German, Old Dutch and Old French; Religion: Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Imperial monarchy; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 843; Disestablished: 855; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Italy, Lotharingia and Kingdom of Provence

name: Kingdom of Qocho
description: The Kingdom of Qocho, also designated the Idiqut state of Gaochang, was established in the Turpan Basin by Uyghur refugees escaping the fall of their steppe khaganate in 840. Governing from winter headquarters at Qocho and summer palaces at Beshbalik, the kingdom synthesised nomadic traditions with sedentary Sogdian, Tocharian and Chinese cultural elements. Embracing Buddhism and Manichaeism alongside flourishing oasis agriculture and Silk Road trade, Qocho maintained intellectual and artistic vitality until accepting tributary status under the Western Liao in the early twelfth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Gaochang; Common languages: Old Uyghur, Middle Chinese and Tocharian; Religion: Buddhism and Manichaeism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Idiqut; Historical era: Postclassical; Established: 843; Disestablished: 1133; Preceded by: Uyghur Khaganate; Succeeded by: Qara Khitai

name: Kingdom of Scotland
label: celtic polities
description: The Kingdom of Scotland emerged during the mid-ninth century through the traditional unification of the Pictish and Gaelic realms of Dal Riata under King Kenneth MacAlpin. Centred ritually upon the Stone of Destiny at Scone and later governed from royal residences in Perth and Edinburgh, the monarchy expanded across the Lowlands and Highlands to encompass northern Great Britain. Resolutely defending its sovereign independence against Anglo-Saxon and Norman English encroachments throughout the Middle Ages, Scotland retained its autonomous crown until the Union of the Crowns in 1603. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Scone and Edinburgh; Common languages: Middle Irish, Scottish Gaelic, Scots and Latin; Religion: Chalcedonian Christianity and Roman Catholicism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 843; Disestablished: 1603; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Great Britain

name: Emirate of Bari
label: small arab emirates in europe
description: The Emirate of Bari was a short-lived Islamic military state established along the Adriatic coast of Apulia, centred on the fortified port city of Bari. Founded around 847 by Berber warriors under the commander Khalfûn, it was the only formal Muslim emirate established on the mainland of the Italian peninsula. Nominally recognising the Abbasid caliph, the emirs conducted devastating raids throughout southern Italy until a combined land and naval siege by Holy Roman Emperor Louis II and Byzantine forces captured the stronghold in 871. \n\n Status: Autonomous emirate; Capital: Bari; Official languages: Arabic; Common languages: Arabic, Italian Romance and Greek; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Military emirate; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 847; Disestablished: 871; Succeeded by: Byzantine Empire

name: Yufirids
description: The Yufirids were an indigenous Arab Himyarite dynasty that governed the rugged highlands of central Yemen from fortified citadels at Shibam Kawkaban and Sanaa. Founded by Yu'fir ibn Abd al-Rahman, the dynasty threw off direct caliphal administration while continuing to acknowledge nominal Abbasid suzerainty. Championing Sunni orthodoxy against the emergent Zaydi Shia imamate in northern Yemen, the Yufirids exercised substantial regional dominion over mountain trade routes until internecine dynastic bloodshed and pressure from rival lowland regimes extinguished their realm in 997. \n\n Status: Autonomous emirate; Capital: Shibam Kawkaban and Sanaa; Common languages: Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Hereditary emirate; Ruler title: Emir; Currency: Dinar; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 847; Disestablished: 997; Succeeded by: Ziyadid dynasty

name: Guiyi Circuit
label: five dynasties and ten kingdoms - other countries  (chinese history)
description: The Guiyi Circuit was a de facto autonomous Chinese regional government established along the eastern Silk Road across the Hexi Corridor, headquartered at Dunhuang in Shazhou. Founded by the local general Zhang Yichao after overthrowing Tibetan imperial garrisons in 848, the circuit nominally declared allegiance to the Tang dynasty while operating as a self-governing frontier principality. Patronising the renowned Mogao Buddhist cave temples and managing delicate diplomatic ties with neighbouring Uyghurs and Sogdians, Guiyi preserved Han Chinese administrative traditions until Western Xia forces conquered the region. \n\n Status: Autonomous military circuit; Capital: Dunhuang; Common languages: Middle Chinese, Old Tibetan and Sogdian; Religion: Buddhism; Government: Hereditary military circuit; Ruler title: Jiedushi; Historical era: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms; Established: 848; Disestablished: 1036; Succeeded by: Western Xia

name: Pagan Kingdom
description: The Pagan Kingdom was the first Burmese empire to unify the fertile Irrawaddy river basin and its peripheral hill tracts, establishing its monumental capital at Pagan. Founded in the mid-ninth century by the Mranma ancestors of the Bamar people, the monarchy rose to imperial stature under King Anawrahta during the eleventh century. The realm became a radiant centre of Theravada Buddhist scholarship, constructing thousands of magnificent brick pagodas across the arid plains until devastating military campaigns by the Mongol Empire precipitated its fragmentation in 1287. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Pagan; Common languages: Old Burmese, Mon and Pyu; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Postclassical; Established: 23 December 849; Disestablished: 1287; Succeeded by: Myinsaing Kingdom and Hanthawaddy Kingdom

name: Chimor
description: Chimor was a powerful pre-Columbian empire that dominated the desert coastline of northern Peru from its sprawling adobe metropolis at Chan Chan in the Moche Valley. Tracing its royal lineage to the mythical founder Taycanamo, the state engineered sophisticated canal networks that transformed arid river valleys into highly productive agricultural oases. The kingdom expanded across a thousand kilometres of Pacific littoral, incorporating adjacent regional cultures until the imperial armies of the Inca Empire under Topa Inca Yupanqui conquered the realm around 1470. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Chan Chan; Official languages: Quingnam; Common languages: Mochica; Religion: Polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Chimor Capac; Historical era: Late Intermediate; Established: 850; Disestablished: 1470; Succeeded by: Inca Empire

name: County of Marsi
description: The County of Marsi was a prominent feudal domain situated in the rugged central Apennines of Abruzzo, encompassing the fertile basin around Lake Fucino. Established by a noble lineage of Frankish origin operating within the orbit of the Duchy of Spoleto, the counts governed from their formidable stronghold at Celano. The dynasty exercised autonomous territorial jurisdiction over mountain passes and agricultural communities for three centuries until the centralising campaigns of King Roger II absorbed their lordships into the Norman Kingdom of Sicily in 1144. \n\n Status: Feudal county; Capital: Celano; Common languages: Medieval Latin and Italian Romance; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Count; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 851; Disestablished: 1144; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Sicily

name: Emirate of Amantea
label: small arab emirates in europe
description: The Emirate of Amantea was an ephemeral Muslim naval principality established on the rocky Tyrrhenian coastline of central Calabria, centred upon the cliff-top settlement of Amantea. Occupied by Arab expeditionary forces around the middle of the ninth century, the fortress served as a fortified launching point for naval sorties against Christian shipping and incursions into the Calabrian interior. Amantea maintained its defiant independence until Byzantine armies commanded by General Nikephoros Phokas the Elder launched a comprehensive offensive in 886, restoring imperial Byzantine rule across Calabria. \n\n Status: Military naval emirate; Capital: Amantea; Common languages: Arabic, Greek and Calabrian Romance; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Military emirate; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 851; Disestablished: 886; Succeeded by: Byzantine Empire

name: Gao Empire
description: The Gao Empire was an early Songhai state established along the eastern bend of the Niger River in eastern Mali, with its commercial and political capital at Gao. Ruled by the ancient Za dynasty, the kingdom flourished as a vital southern terminus for trans-Saharan camel caravans trading Saharan salt for sub-Saharan gold and agricultural produce. Adopting Islam during the eleventh century, the rulers governed a prosperous riverine society that laid the political, cultural and institutional foundations for the later imperial rise of the Songhai Empire. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Gao; Common languages: Songhai; Religion: Islam and traditional animism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Za; Historical era: Postclassical; Established: 850; Disestablished: 1201; Succeeded by: Mali Empire and Songhai Empire

name: Hindu Shahi
description: The Hindu Shahi dynasty was a formidable northern monarchy that governed the Kabul Valley, Gandhara and the Punjab during the early medieval period. Originating after the Brahmin minister Kallar displaced the Turk Shahis, the dynasty moved its principal royal capital from Kabul eastwards to the Indus fortress of Udabhandapura, modern Hund, in response to Saffarid expansion. The Shahis tenaciously defended northern India against repeated incursions by the Ghaznavid Empire until Sultan Mahmud of Ghazni decisively broke their military resistance in the early eleventh century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Hund; Common languages: Sanskrit and Prakrit; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Maharajadhiraja; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 822; Disestablished: 1026; Preceded by: Turk Shahi; Succeeded by: Ghaznavid Empire

name: Kingdom of Malindi
label: polities of the swahili coast
description: The Kingdom of Malindi was an ancient Swahili maritime city-state situated along the Indian Ocean coast of modern Kenya, north of Mombasa on the Galana River estuary. Thriving as a bustling commercial port, the kingdom engaged in extensive maritime trade with Arabia, Persia, India and Ming China, exporting high-grade ivory, timber and agricultural commodities. The merchant oligarchy maintained fierce regional rivalry against neighbouring Mombasa, which ultimately led Malindi to form a fateful naval alliance with Portuguese navigators upon the arrival of Vasco da Gama in 1498. \n\n Status: Sovereign city-state; Capital: Malindi; Common languages: Swahili and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 851; Disestablished: 1501; Succeeded by: Portuguese Empire

name: Uxmal
label: mesoamerican polities
description: Uxmal was a pre-eminent Maya city-state that flourished in the Puuc hills of the northwestern Yucatan Peninsula during the Late and Terminal Classic periods. Governed by divine kings such as Chan Chak K'ak'nal Ajaw, the urban centre commanded regional trade and constructed magnificent stone complexes, including the Pyramid of the Magician and the Governor's Palace. Characterised by sophisticated rainwater cistern engineering and exquisite mosaic stone friezes dedicated to the rain god Chaac, Uxmal dominated regional Maya politics until political collapse led to its gradual abandonment around 1100. \n\n Status: Sovereign city-state; Capital: Uxmal; Common languages: Yucatec Maya; Religion: Maya polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Ajaw; Historical era: Terminal Classic Mesoamerica; Established: 850; Disestablished: 1100; Succeeded by: Chichen Itza

name: Kingdom of Brittany
label: celtic polities of brittany;celtic polities
description: The Kingdom of Brittany was a sovereign Celtic monarchy founded after King Erispoe defeated the West Frankish monarch Charles the Bald at the Battle of Jengland in August 851. Establishing administrative centres at Rennes and Nantes, the Breton monarchs expanded their borders across the Cotentin and Avranchin while patronising native monastic institutions and legal codes. Following the reign of King Alan the Great, severe Norse invasions devastated the country and interrupted the monarchy in 919 until Alan Twistedbeard expelled the raiders in 939, re-establishing the realm as a duchy. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Rennes; Common languages: Breton, Latin and Gallo; Religion: Catholicism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 22 August 851; Disestablished: 939; Preceded by: Cornouaille and Domnonee; Succeeded by: Duchy of Brittany

name: Principality of Salerno
label: lombard polities
description: The Principality of Salerno was a major Lombard sovereign state in southern Italy, created in 851 following a protracted civil war that partitioned the Principality of Benevento. Governed by Prince Siconulf and his successors from the coastal stronghold of Salerno, the realm commanded extensive agricultural lowlands and prosperous Tyrrhenian maritime ports. Renowned for its cosmopolitan culture and the founding of the Schola Medica Salernitana, the principality successfully navigated rivalries between Carolingians and Byzantines until the Norman commander Robert Guiscard conquered the city in 1077. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Salerno; Official languages: Latin; Common languages: Latin and Lombardic; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Prince; Currency: Monetazione di Salerno; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 851; Disestablished: 1077; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Sicily

name: Kingdom of Dublin
label: irish medieval kingdoms;norse/viking polities
description: The Kingdom of Dublin, known to its founders as Dyflin, was the earliest and most resilient Norse kingdom established on the island of Ireland. Founded along the River Liffey in the 850s by the Viking sea-kings Amlaib Conung and Ivar the Boneless, the settlement grew into a wealthy urban trading hub and slave market dominating the Irish Sea. Governed by the Ui Imair dynasty, the kingdom fought continuous campaigns against Irish provincial high kings until Anglo-Norman crusaders under Richard de Clare seized the city in 1171. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Dublin; Common languages: Old Norse and Middle Irish; Religion: Norse paganism and Roman Catholicism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Currency: Silver penny; Historical era: Viking Age; Established: 853; Disestablished: 1171; Succeeded by: Lordship of Ireland

name: Kingdom of Italy
label: barbarian kingdoms;frankish polities
description: The Kingdom of Italy during this era was the imperial domain of Emperor Louis II, established as a distinct Carolingian monarchy under the Treaty of Prum in September 855. Centred upon the ancient Lombard royal capital at Pavia, the kingdom encompassed northern and central Italy while pursuing active military pacification of the southern provinces. Louis II dedicated his reign to defending the peninsula from Saracen incursions, culminating in the celebrated liberation of Bari in 871, before his death in 875 without male issue triggered renewed dynastic partition disputes. \n\n Status: Imperial kingdom; Capital: Pavia; Official languages: Medieval Latin; Common languages: Medieval Latin, Italian Romance and Lombardic; Religion: Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Emperor and King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 855; Disestablished: 875; Preceded by: Middle Francia; Succeeded by: Frankish Empire

name: Kingdom of Lotharingia
label: barbarian kingdoms;frankish polities
description: The Kingdom of Lotharingia was created under the Treaty of Prum in 855 as the northern realm of Middle Francia, allocated to King Lothair II. Encompassing the historic Austrasian homelands across the Low Countries, Alsace and the Rhineland from its administrative seat at Metz, the realm possessed immense dynastic prestige. Lothair II's reign was dominated by bitter marital disputes with Queen Teutberga and endless intrigues by his royal uncles, leading directly to the partition of Lotharingia between East and West Francia under the Treaty of Meerssen in 870. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Metz; Official languages: Medieval Latin; Common languages: Old Frankish, Old Dutch and Old High German; Religion: Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 855; Disestablished: 870; Preceded by: Middle Francia; Succeeded by: East Francia and West Francia

name: Kingdom of Provence
label: barbarian kingdoms;frankish polities
description: The Kingdom of Provence, also known as the Kingdom of Lower Burgundy, was formed in September 855 following the Treaty of Prum for Charles of Provence, the youngest son of Emperor Lothair I. Governed from the historic administrative city of Vienne with the counsel of Count Gerard, the kingdom encompassed the Rhone valley, Cisjuran Burgundy and the Mediterranean shores of Provence. Due to Charles's frail health and premature death in 863 without an heir, the southern realm was partitioned between his surviving brothers, Emperor Louis II and King Lothair II. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Vienne; Official languages: Medieval Latin; Common languages: Old Occitan, Old Franco-Provencal and Vulgar Latin; Religion: Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 855; Disestablished: 863; Preceded by: Middle Francia; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Italy and Lotharingia

name: Utpala Dynasty
description: The Utpala Dynasty was an illustrious medieval monarchy that ruled over Kashmir and adjacent Himalayan tracts from its capital at Avantipur. Founded in 855 by King Avantivarman after replacing the Karkotas, the dynasty oversaw a celebrated era of agricultural prosperity and cultural achievement, highlighted by innovative irrigation canalisation directed by the engineer Suyya. Renowned for constructing monumental stone temples dedicated to Vishnu and Shiva, the realm retained administrative independence through the tenth century, ending when the legendary Queen Didda arranged the peaceful succession of the Lohara dynasty. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Avantipur; Official languages: Sanskrit; Common languages: Sanskrit and Kashmiri; Religion: Vaishnavism and Shaivism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Monarch; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 855; Disestablished: 1003; Preceded by: Karkota Empire; Succeeded by: Lohara dynasty

name: Principality of Salerno, Duchy of Naples and Republic of Amalfi (Military Occupation)
description: The joint military occupation administered by the Principality of Salerno, the Duchy of Naples and the Republic of Amalfi functioned as a coordinated emergency deployment in southern Italy during the summer of 859. Formed to counter aggressive Saracen coastal raiding and stabilise disputed border territories along the northern Campanian frontier, the alliance temporarily garrisoned strategic strongpoints under unified consular and ducal command. Headquartered operationally at Salerno, this defensive security zone maintained regional order until local border pacts and renewed municipal autonomy superseded the coalition's joint martial jurisdiction. \n\n Status: Military occupation zone; Administrative seat: Salerno; Common languages: Latin and Italian Romance; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Joint military administration; Ruler title: Allied military commanders; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 1 June 859; Disestablished: 1 July 859; Preceded by: Principality of Benevento; Succeeded by: Principality of Salerno

name: Emirate of Manzikert
description: The Emirate of Manzikert was an influential Muslim border state established by the Arab Kaysite dynasty around Lake Van in the Armenian highlands, with its capital at Manzikert. Rising to prominence following the decline of direct Abbasid caliphal governorship in Arminiya, the Kaysite emirs ruled an ethnically mixed population of Muslims and Armenian Christians. The emirate balanced cautious tributary diplomacy between the Byzantine Empire and the burgeoning Bagratid Kingdom of Armenia until Byzantine eastward military expansion dismantled the Muslim dynasty in the mid-tenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign emirate; Capital: Manzikert; Common languages: Arabic and Armenian; Religion: Sunni Islam and Armenian Apostolic Christianity; Government: Hereditary emirate; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 860; Disestablished: 964; Preceded by: Arminiya; Succeeded by: Bagratid Kingdom of Armenia

name: Pecheneg Khanates
description: The Pecheneg Khanates constituted a powerful confederation of nomadic Turkic horse-archer tribes that held sway across the vast Pontic-Caspian steppe from the Don River to the Danube. Operating without permanent stone cities, the Pechenegs maintained mobile wagon encampments and were divided into eight autonomous tribal hordes governed by elected chieftains.
