Commanding vital overland river crossings north of the Black Sea, they exerted formidable military pressure through frequent raids against Kievan Rus' and the Byzantine Empire until devastating defeats in the eleventh century broke their confederacy. \n\n Status: Nomadic tribal confederation; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Pecheneg Turkic; Religion: Tengrism, Islam and Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Nomadic elective chiefdom; Ruler title: Khan; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 861; Disestablished: 1054; Succeeded by: Cuman-Kipchak Confederation

name: Dulafid Dynasty
description: The Dulafid Dynasty was an autonomous Arab ruling family that held sway over the central Iranian province of Jibal from their fortified capital at Karaj Abi Dulaf. Originally serving as loyal governors for the Abbasid caliphs, the Dulafids asserted practical territorial sovereignty in the wake of imperial instability following the Anarchy at Samarra in 861. Balancing complex rivalries between neighbouring Daylamites, Saffarids and caliphal armies, the dynasty governed key highland trade arteries until Caliph al-Mu'tadid led a successful military campaign that reincorporated Jibal into direct Abbasid rule. \n\n Status: Sovereign emirate; Capital: Karaj Abi Dulaf; Common languages: Classical Arabic and Persian; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Hereditary emirate; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 862; Disestablished: 898; Preceded by: Abbasid Caliphate; Succeeded by: Abbasid Caliphate

name: Habbari Dynasty
description: The Habbari Dynasty was an autonomous Arab regime that governed Greater Sindh from its fortified riverine metropolis at Mansura on the Indus. Established when Umar bin Abdul Aziz al-Habbari asserted local dominance in the 850s, the emirate maintained nominal spiritual allegiance to the Abbasid caliphs while exercising practical domestic sovereignty. The Habbaris fostered an affluent mercantile crossroads combining Arab and Indic commercial networks until Sultan Mahmud of Ghazni invaded the lower Indus in 1026, sacking Mansura and extinguishing the dynasty. \n\n Status: Autonomous emirate; Capital: Mansura; Common languages: Arabic and Sindhi; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Hereditary emirate; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 854; Disestablished: 1026; Preceded by: Caliphal province of Sind; Succeeded by: Ghaznavid Empire and Soomro dynasty

name: Saffarid Dynasty
label: iranian intermezzo
description: The Saffarid Dynasty was an indigenous Persianate monarchy founded by the charismatic military adventurer Ya'qub ibn al-Layth al-Saffar, originating from the arid borderlands of Sistan. Establishing their royal capital at Zaranj, the Saffarids expanded rapidly across eastern Iran and Central Asia, overthrowing the Tahirids in Khorasan and advancing to the gates of Baghdad. Although marking the resurgence of native Persian dynastic governance during the Iranian Intermezzo, their imperial ascendancy was checked by the Samanids at the Battle of Balkh in 900. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Zaranj; Common languages: Persian and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 861; Disestablished: 1002; Preceded by: Tahirid dynasty; Succeeded by: Samanid Empire

name: Kievan Rus'
label: norse/viking polities
description: Kievan Rus' was a powerful medieval East Slavic federation established along the crucial riverine trade arteries linking Scandinavia with the Byzantine Empire. Uniting the regional tribes under the Varangian Rurik dynasty following Prince Oleg's capture of Kyiv in 882, the realm expanded to encompass vast territories from the Baltic to the Black Sea. Under Grand Prince Vladimir the Great, the state adopted Byzantine Christianity in 988, inaugurating a golden age of legal codification and monumental stone architecture before dynastic partitions fragmented the realm. \n\n Status: Sovereign grand principality; Capital: Kyiv; Common languages: Old East Slavic, Old Church Slavonic and Old Norse; Religion: Slavic paganism and Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Grand Prince; Currency: Grivna; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 882; Disestablished: 1133; Succeeded by: Principality of Kiev

name: Principality of Capua
label: lombard polities
description: The Principality of Capua was an autonomous Lombard realm situated in the fertile Campanian plains of southern Italy, centred upon the fortified city of Capua on the Volturno River. Originating as a rebellious gastaldate within the Principality of Salerno, the domain achieved practical independence under the energetic leadership of the Landulfid dynasty. Capua dominated the surrounding Terra di Lavoro and spearheaded regional campaigns against Saracen settlements, culminating in dynastic union with Benevento under Prince Atenulf I before eventual absorption into the Norman Kingdom of Sicily. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Capua; Common languages: Medieval Latin and Lombardic; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Prince; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 861; Disestablished: 1156; Preceded by: Principality of Salerno; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Sicily

name: Alid Emirate
description: The Alid Emirate, often designated the Zaydi realm of Tabaristan, was a theocratic principality founded along the southern Caspian littoral between the rugged Alborz Mountains and the sea. Established in 864 by the Alid missionary Hasan ibn Zayd, the state provided a permanent bastion for Zaydi Shi'ism and protected indigenous Daylami and Gilani populations against Abbasid taxation. Although briefly suppressed by the Samanids in 900, the emirate was restored under al-Utrush before internal succession conflicts ended its sovereign independence in 928. \n\n Status: Theocratic emirate; Capital: Amol; Common languages: Mazandarani, Persian and Arabic; Religion: Zaydi Shia Islam; Government: Theocratic monarchy; Ruler title: Emir; Currency: Dirham; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 864; Disestablished: 928; Preceded by: Abbasid Caliphate; Succeeded by: Samanid Empire and Ziyarid dynasty

name: Kingdom of Bavaria
label: barbarian kingdoms;frankish polities
description: The Kingdom of Bavaria during this Carolingian era was the sovereign realm ruled by Carloman, the eldest son of King Louis the German. Administered from the ancient Roman and ducal stronghold of Regensburg, the kingdom controlled the Danube basin and directed defensive marches across Carantania and Pannonia. Carloman maintained an assertive eastern frontier policy against Great Moravia and briefly annexed the Italian crown in 877 before ill health forced him to surrender his Bavarian domains to his brother Louis the Younger in 880. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Regensburg; Official languages: Medieval Latin; Common languages: Old High German and Bavarian; Religion: Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 865; Disestablished: 880; Preceded by: East Francia; Succeeded by: Kingdom of the East Franks

name: Danelaw
label: norse/viking polities
description: The Danelaw was the extensive domain of eastern and northern England where Scandinavian customs and legal codes held sway following the invasions of the Great Heathen Army from 865 onward. Formalised through treaties between King Alfred the Great of Wessex and the Danish leader Guthrum, the realm encompassed the Kingdom of York and the confederated Five Boroughs of the East Midlands. Operating under Norse military aristocracies, the territory maintained thriving commercial links with Scandinavia until the West Saxon reconquest culminated in the expulsion of Eric Bloodaxe in 954. \n\n Status: Autonomous Scandinavian domain; Capital: York; Common languages: Old Norse and Old English; Religion: Norse paganism and Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Military aristocracy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Viking Age; Established: 865; Disestablished: 954; Succeeded by: Kingdom of England

name: Ganzhou Uyghur Kingdom
description: The Ganzhou Uyghur Kingdom, also known as the Hexi Uyghur state, was an independent realm established along the Hexi Corridor in modern Gansu by the royal Yaglakar clan. Governing from their oasis capital at Ganzhou, modern Zhangye, the Uyghurs transitioned from Manichaeism to become devout patrons of Buddhist monasteries and cave temples. Commanding the crucial overland commercial gateway between northern China and Central Asia, the kingdom maintained tributary ties with Chinese dynasties until the expanding Tangut armies of Western Xia conquered Ganzhou in 1028. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Zhangye; Common languages: Old Uyghur and Middle Chinese; Religion: Manichaeism and Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Idiqut; Historical era: Postclassical; Established: 867; Disestablished: 1028; Preceded by: Uyghur Khaganate; Succeeded by: Western Xia

name: Jinghai Circuit
description: The Jinghai Circuit was a strategic frontier military circuit established across northern Vietnam by the Tang dynasty after General Gao Pian expelled invading Nanzhao armies in 866. Governed from the fortified administrative citadel of Dai La, modern Hanoi, the province replaced the former Protectorate General of Annan as an imperial buffer command. Although officially subordinate to the Chinese imperial court, the circuit operated with growing administrative detachment as central Tang authority collapsed, paving the way for native Vietnamese clans to assume de facto hereditary governance. \n\n Status: Imperial military circuit; Administrative seat: Hanoi; Official languages: Middle Chinese; Common languages: Middle Chinese and Old Vietnamese; Religion: Buddhism, Taoism and Vietnamese folk religion; Government: Military governorship; Ruler title: Jiedushi; Historical era: Postclassical; Established: 866; Disestablished: 908; Preceded by: Annan Protectorate; Succeeded by: Khuc family autonomy

name: Ziyadid Dynasty
description: The Ziyadid Dynasty was an influential Arab Muslim monarchy that ruled the coastal lowlands of the Tihama in western Yemen from their newly constructed capital at Zabid. Dispatched by Abbasid Caliph al-Ma'mun to subdue regional unrest, the dynasty quickly consolidated autonomous dominion over the southern Red Sea maritime trade routes from Aden northward. Sponsoring Islamic jurisprudence and architectural foundations in Zabid, the Sunni monarchs successfully countered highland tribal revolts until internal palace intrigues and slave insurrections transferred power to the Najahid dynasty in the early eleventh century. \n\n Status: Autonomous emirate; Capital: Zabid; Common languages: Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Hereditary emirate; Ruler title: Emir; Currency: Dinar; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 819; Disestablished: 1023; Preceded by: Abbasid Caliphate; Succeeded by: Najahid dynasty

name: Kingdom of Northumbria
label: saxon polities in britain
description: The Kingdom of Northumbria during this troubled phase functioned as a fragmented client realm subordinate to the Norse conquerors of the Danelaw. Following the catastrophic defeat and execution of rival kings Aella and Osberht at York in March 867, Viking commanders installed puppet Anglo-Saxon rulers to extract tribute and oversee civil administration. While Danish warlords ruled directly from the thriving commercial centre of Jorvik, indigenous client lords governing from Bamburgh maintained tenuous regional control until Anglo-Saxon and Scottish forces annexed the remaining marches. \n\n Status: Client kingdom; Capital: Jorvik; Common languages: Old English and Old Norse; Religion: Chalcedonian Christianity and Norse paganism; Government: Puppet monarchy under vassalage; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Viking Age; Established: 21 March 867; Disestablished: 928; Preceded by: Kingdom of Northumbria; Succeeded by: Danelaw and Kingdom of England

name: Tulunids
description: The Tulunids were the first autonomous Muslim dynasty to rule Egypt and Syria independently of the Abbasid Caliphate, founded by the Turkic military officer Ahmad ibn Tulun in 868. Establishing an opulent capital at al-Qatai near modern Cairo, the dynasty constructed monumental public works, including the iconic Ibn Tulun Mosque, and accumulated vast agricultural wealth from the Nile Delta. Tulunid armies extended their authority across Palestine, Syria and the Hejaz until the caliphal court dispatched an imperial army that sacked al-Qatai and restored direct Abbasid rule in 905. \n\n Status: Autonomous emirate; Capital: Al-Qatai; Common languages: Arabic and Coptic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Hereditary emirate; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 868; Disestablished: 905

name: Duchy of Bohemia
description: The Duchy of Bohemia emerged as an autonomous Slavic principality under the Premyslid dynasty, operating as a feudal vassal of East Francia from 871 onward. Shifting allegiance from disintegrating Great Moravia to the East Frankish king Arnulf, the Bohemian dukes established their seat of government at Prague Castle and promoted Western Latin Christianity. Despite dynastic turbulence and pagan resistance, celebrated figures like Duke Wenceslaus I consolidated municipal institutions and defensive borders, integrating the Czech lands deeply into the political architecture of the German imperial sphere. \n\n Status: Vassal duchy; Capital: Prague; Common languages: Old Czech and Medieval Latin; Religion: Latin Christianity; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Duke; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 870; Disestablished: 963; Preceded by: Great Moravia; Succeeded by: Holy Roman Empire

name: Paulician Principality
description: The Paulician Principality was an autonomous militant haven established by heterodox Christian dissidents in eastern Anatolia, centred upon the impregnable mountain citadel of Tephrike, modern Divrigi. Founded by the renegade Byzantine officer Karbeas following anti-Paulician persecutions, the principality forged strategic military alliances with neighbouring Muslim frontier emirs. Under Karbeas and his fiery successor Chrysocheir, Paulician raiding armies plundered deep into Byzantine Asia Minor until Emperor Basil I mounted a decisive counteroffensive, crushing the sectarian forces at Bathys Ryax and razing Tephrike in 878. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Divrigi; Common languages: Armenian, Greek and Syriac; Religion: Paulician Christianity; Government: Military theocracy; Ruler title: Archon; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 872; Disestablished: 879; Succeeded by: Byzantine Empire

name: Kingdom of Norway
description: The Kingdom of Norway was founded during the late ninth century when King Harald Fairhair subjugated rival coastal jarls at the naval Battle of Hafrsfjord, uniting the Norse petty realms into a single sovereign crown. Governing from royal manors such as Avaldsnes and later ecclesiastical centres at Nidaros and Bergen, the Fairhair dynasty established royal administrative control over maritime trade and tax collection. This unified monarchy laid the enduring foundation for Norwegian nationhood, expanding transatlantic Norse navigation and resisting Danish hegemony across subsequent centuries. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Avaldsnes and Nidaros; Common languages: Old Norse; Religion: Norse paganism and Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Viking Age; Established: 872; Disestablished: 971; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Denmark

name: Great Qi
description: Great Qi was an insurgent rebel dynasty established across central China by the peasant army commander Huang Chao during the climactic agrarian rebellions of the late Tang period. Originating among displaced salt merchants and famine-stricken peasants, the insurgent forces swept across southern and central China before capturing the imperial capitals of Luoyang and Changan in 880, where Huang Chao proclaimed himself emperor. Lacking a coherent administrative apparatus to govern conquered territories, the regime was swiftly isolated and dismantled by loyalist Tang commanders and Shatuo Turkic cavalry in 884. \n\n Status: Insurgent state; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Middle Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion, Buddhism and Taoism; Government: Revolutionary monarchy; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Late Tang dynasty; Established: 875; Disestablished: 1 September 884; Succeeded by: Tang dynasty

name: Kingdom of Alemannia
label: barbarian kingdoms;frankish polities
description: The Kingdom of Alemannia was an autonomous East Frankish realm created on 28 August 876 following the dynastic partition of King Louis the German's territories among his three sons. Allocated to the youngest brother, Charles the Fat, the state comprised Swabia, Raetia and southern Alsace, with administrative assemblies frequently held around Lake Constance. Charles leveraged his southern territory as a springboard into northern Italy, acquiring the Italian crown in 879 and imperial coronation in 881 before the demise of his brothers allowed him to reunite East Francia in 882. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Constance; Official languages: Medieval Latin; Common languages: Old High German and Alemannic; Religion: Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 28 August 876; Disestablished: 20 January 882; Preceded by: East Francia; Succeeded by: Frankish Empire

name: Kingdom of the East Franks
label: barbarian kingdoms;frankish polities
description: The Kingdom of the East Franks during this five-year partition encompassed the northern and central stem duchies of Saxony, Franconia and Thuringia under the rule of King Louis the Younger. Following the death of Louis the German in August 876, Louis defended his inheritance by decisively repelling a West Frankish invasion at the Battle of Andernach. After securing western Lotharingia through the Treaty of Ribemont in 880 and inheriting Bavaria, Louis governed an expansive Germanic domain until his premature death without heirs in 882 reunited the crown under Charles the Fat. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Magdeburg; Official languages: Medieval Latin; Common languages: Old Saxon, Old High German and Old Frankish; Religion: Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 28 August 876; Disestablished: 20 January 882; Preceded by: East Francia; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Alemannia

name: Chiefdom of Bozhou
label: four great native chiefdoms in guizhou
description: The Chiefdom of Bozhou was a long-lived hereditary Tusi state established across the karst highlands of northern Guizhou, centred upon modern Zunyi. Founded in 876 by General Yang Duan after liberating the prefecture from Nanzhao invaders, the chiefdom received imperial confirmation from the Tang court and maintained unbroken rule under the Yang dynasty for over seven centuries. Ranking among the four great native domains of Guizhou, Bozhou defended its mountain passes and mineral wealth until the ill-fated rebellion of Yang Yinglong provoked a massive Ming military campaign that abolished the chiefdom in 1600. \n\n Status: Autonomous native chiefdom; Capital: Bozhou; Common languages: Nasu, Chinese and Gelao; Religion: Chinese folk religion and Buddhism; Government: Hereditary chieftancy; Ruler title: Tusi Chieftain; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 876; Disestablished: 1600; Succeeded by: Ming dynasty

name: Kingdom of Provence
label: barbarian kingdoms;frankish polities
description: The Kingdom of Provence, also known as the Kingdom of Lower Burgundy, was proclaimed at the Council of Mantaille on 15 October 879 when Count Boso of Vienne was elected monarch. Marking the first election of a non-Carolingian noble to kingship in post-Verdun Europe, the state extended across the Rhone valley, Provence and Cisjuran Burgundy from its capital at Vienne. Resisting determined military sieges by allied Carolingian monarchs, the realm maintained independent sovereignty under Boso and his son Louis the Blind until dynastic negotiations merged it into the united Kingdom of Burgundy in 933. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Vienne; Official languages: Medieval Latin; Common languages: Old Occitan, Franco-Provencal and Vulgar Latin; Religion: Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 15 October 879; Disestablished: 934; Preceded by: West Francia; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Arles

name: County of Barcelona
label: catalan counties
description: The County of Barcelona was the leading Catalan feudal domain established in northeastern Iberia, originating within the Carolingian defensive marches of the Pyrenean frontier. Under the visionary stewardship of Count Wilfred the Hairy in the 880s, the comital office became hereditary, progressively shedding Carolingian administrative vassalage to operate as an independent sovereign realm. From its fortified coastal capital of Barcelona, the county coordinated regional defence against Andalusian raids and consolidated neighbouring counties, ultimately forming the nucleus of the Principality of Catalonia through dynastic union with Aragon in 1162. \n\n Status: Sovereign county; Capital: Barcelona; Common languages: Old Catalan, Latin and Old Occitan; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Count; Legislature: Comital Court; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 880; Disestablished: 1162; Succeeded by: Crown of Aragon and Principality of Catalonia

name: County of Cerdanya
label: catalan counties
description: The County of Cerdanya was an autonomous Catalan mountain principality established in the upper valley of the Segre River high in the eastern Pyrenees. Originally organised as a Frankish frontier march, the county achieved hereditary independence under Count Wilfred the Hairy and his heirs, who administered strategic alpine defiles and seasonal pasturelands from Puigcerda. Sustaining active monastic foundations and resisting both Moorish incursions and aristocratic encroachments, Cerdanya maintained vibrant feudal self-governance until dynastic marriages and lack of direct heirs transferred the territory to the Counts of Barcelona. \n\n Status: Feudal county; Capital: Puigcerda; Common languages: Old Catalan and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Count of Cerdanya; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 880; Disestablished: 1059; Succeeded by: County of Barcelona

name: County of Pallars
label: catalan counties
description: The County of Pallars was an independent Pyrenean feudal realm centred along the upper river basin of the Noguera Pallaresa in north-central Catalonia. Gaining autonomy from the Frankish counts of Toulouse in 872 under Count Raymond I, the domain maintained its comital court at Sort amidst high alpine valleys and isolated mountain passes. The counts established dynastic alliances with neighbouring Navarre and Aragon, protecting their secluded agrarian communities from external conquest until eleventh-century dynastic partitions divided the territory into the separate counties of Pallars Sobira and Pallars Jussa. \n\n Status: Feudal county; Capital: Sort; Common languages: Old Catalan, Latin and Basque; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Count of Pallars; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 880; Disestablished: 1194; Succeeded by: County of Pallars Sobira and County of Pallars Jussa

name: County of Ribagorza
label: catalan counties
description: The County of Ribagorza was an autonomous medieval border state situated along the southern valleys of the central Pyrenees, encompassing the basins of the Esera and Isabena rivers. Established as an independent comital domain under Raymond I after breaking away from the Frankish counts of Toulouse, the county was governed from its fortified seat at Benabarre. name: County of Roussillon
label: catalan counties
description: The County of Roussillon was a historic Catalan principality established on the coastal plains and foothills of the eastern Pyrenees, anchored by its capital at Perpignan. Emerging from the Carolingian defensive marches of Septimania, the realm attained hereditary comital independence during the late ninth century under the descendants of Sunifred I. Navigating complex diplomatic balances between the Counts of Barcelona and the lords of southern France, Roussillon guarded maritime routes between the Iberian Peninsula and Gaul until the childless Count Girart II bequeathed his county to the Crown of Aragon in 1172. \n\n Status: Feudal county; Capital: Perpignan; Common languages: Old Catalan, Latin and Old Occitan; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Count of Roussillon; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 880; Disestablished: 1172; Succeeded by: Crown of Aragon

name: County of Urgell
label: catalan counties
description: The County of Urgell was an autonomous Pyrenean principality situated in northwestern Catalonia, centred along the fertile valley of the Upper Segre River around La Seu d'Urgell. Transformed into a hereditary dynasty under Count Wilfred the Hairy and his son Sunifred II in the late ninth century, the county served as a crucial bastion of Christian resistance against Muslim Taifa frontiers. Working in close administrative harmony with the influential Bishopric of Urgell, the comital line expanded southwards into the Lleida plain until dynastic rebellions culminated in its crown annexation in 1413. \n\n Status: Feudal county; Capital: La Seu d'Urgell; Common languages: Old Catalan and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Count of Urgell; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 880; Disestablished: 949; Succeeded by: Principality of Catalonia and Crown of Aragon

name: Duchy of Croatia
description: The Duchy of Croatia was an independent South Slavic realm established across the Dalmatian littoral and inland mountain basins, governed from itinerant royal residences at Knin, Nin and Klis. Following Duke Branimir's diplomatic alignment with the Holy See, Pope John VIII formally recognised Croatian territorial sovereignty in 879. The Trpimirovic dynasty developed a formidable navy in the Adriatic Sea, asserting dominion over coastal cities and extracting maritime tribute from the Republic of Venice until Duke Tomislav was crowned the first King of Croatia around 925. \n\n Status: Sovereign duchy; Capital: Knin; Common languages: Old Croatian and Latin; Religion: Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Duchy; Ruler title: Duke; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 879; Disestablished: 925; Preceded by: Byzantine Empire; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Croatia

name: Kingdom of the West Franks
label: barbarian kingdoms;frankish polities
description: The Kingdom of the West Franks during this brief division represented the northern portion of the divided realm, ruled by King Louis III following the partition pact of Amiens in March 880. Administering Neustria and the northern Frankish marchlands from his court at Compiegne, Louis III distinguished himself through decisive military leadership against Scandinavian invaders, immortalised by his crushing victory over Norse forces at the Battle of Saucourt in 881. His energetic reign abruptly concluded with his accidental death in August 882, upon which his southern co-ruler Carloman II reunited the West Frankish crown. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Compiegne; Official languages: Medieval Latin; Common languages: Old French and Old Frankish; Religion: Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 11 March 880; Disestablished: 5 August 882; Preceded by: West Francia; Succeeded by: Kingdom of the West Franks

name: Kingdom of the West Franks
label: barbarian kingdoms;frankish polities
description: The Kingdom of the West Franks during this concurrent partition encompassed the southern territories of Aquitaine and northern Burgundy under the sovereignty of King Carloman II. Governed from regional administrative centres near Vienne, the young monarch faced complex feudal challenges, including internal magnate resistance and the secession of Duke Boso in Provence. Cooperating closely with his brother Louis III to subdue regional rebellions and secure the southern frontiers, Carloman inherited the entire West Frankish monarchy following Louis's untimely death in August 882. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Vienne; Official languages: Medieval Latin; Common languages: Old Occitan and Old French; Religion: Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 11 March 880; Disestablished: 5 August 882; Preceded by: West Francia; Succeeded by: Kingdom of the West Franks

description: The Kingdom of the West Franks during early 881 witnessed a coordinated royal condominium administered jointly by the brothers King Louis III and King Carloman II. Operating from royal headquarters at Compiegne, the joint sovereigns pooled their military forces to wage an aggressive campaign against Duke Boso of Provence, who had illicitly claimed royal titles across the Rhone valley. After recapturing Macon and surrounding border cantons, the brother kings established joint administrative jurisdiction over the recovered frontier territories until ongoing Provençal resistance and external Viking raids compelled a strategic realignment. \n\n Status: Sovereign joint monarchy; Capital: Compiegne; Official languages: Medieval Latin; Common languages: Old French and Old Occitan; Religion: Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Dual feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Co-Kings; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 881; Disestablished: 881; Preceded by: Kingdom of Provence; Succeeded by: Kingdom of the West Franks

name: Emirate of Agropoli
label: small arab emirates in europe
description: The Emirate of Agropoli was a fortified Muslim coastal redoubt established on a high rocky promontory overlooking the Tyrrhenian Sea in the Cilento region of southern Italy. Seized by Saracen seafaring warriors in the 880s, the garrison commanded sea passages south of the Gulf of Salerno and launched frequent incursions into the inland valleys of Campania and Lucania. name: Traetto
label: small arab emirates in europe
description: Traetto was a fortified Muslim military colony established near the mouth of the Garigliano River beside modern Minturno in southern Lazio. Settled in the 880s following complex diplomatic maneuvers with local Campanian dukes, the base grew into an entrenched pirate fortress that terrorised central Italy for over thirty years. The Arab raiders plundered venerated abbeys such as Monte Cassino and Farfa and threatened Rome itself until Pope John X marshalled the Christian League, which decisively besieged and annihilated the garrison at the Battle of Garigliano in 915. \n\n Status: Fortified military colony; Capital: Traetto; Common languages: Arabic and Italian Romance; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Military garrison; Ruler title: Commander; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 884; Disestablished: 1 September 915; Succeeded by: Papal States and Duchy of Gaeta

name: Kingdom of Armenia
description: The Kingdom of Armenia during the Bagratid era was a sovereign Christian monarchy restored across the Armenian highlands by King Ashot I after two centuries of Arab caliphal domination. Courted simultaneously by Abbasid caliphs and Byzantine emperors, the Bagratuni dynasty established a flourishing realm that transferred its royal capital successively through Bagaran, Shirakavan and Kars before settling at the magnificent walled city of Ani. Renowned for innovative stone ecclesiastical architecture and vibrant trade networks, the kingdom maintained sovereignty until Byzantine annexations extinguished the royal line at Ani in 1045. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Ani; Common languages: Armenian; Religion: Armenian Apostolic Church; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Currency: Byzantine hyperpyron; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 885; Disestablished: 1045; Preceded by: Arminiya; Succeeded by: Byzantine Empire

name: Kingdom of the East Franks
label: barbarian kingdoms;frankish polities
description: The Kingdom of the East Franks under Arnulf of Carinthia was established in November 887 after the East Frankish magnates deposed the ineffective Emperor Charles the Fat. Governing from imperial residences at Regensburg and Frankfurt, King Arnulf demonstrated energetic military leadership, decisively routing Scandinavian Viking armies at the Battle of Leuven in 891. Enforcing his authority over Lotharingia and Moravia, Arnulf conducted successful military expeditions into Italy and was crowned Roman Emperor in Rome in 896, maintaining imperial prestige until his death in 899 ushered in the child-reign of Louis the Child. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Administrative seat: Regensburg; Official languages: Medieval Latin; Common languages: Old High German and Old Saxon; Religion: Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King and Emperor; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 17 November 887; Disestablished: 8 December 899; Preceded by: Frankish Empire; Succeeded by: Kingdom of the East Franks

name: Kingdom of Burgundy
label: barbarian kingdoms;frankish polities
description: The Kingdom of Burgundy, established as Upper Burgundy following the death of Emperor Charles the Fat in January 888, was founded when Duke Rudolph I was crowned monarch at Saint-Maurice. Centred upon Lake Geneva, the Jura Mountains and the Swiss plateau, the realm commanded vital alpine passes linking northern Europe with the Italian peninsula. name: Kingdom of Italy
label: barbarian kingdoms;frankish polities
description: The Kingdom of Italy during these periods was governed by Berengar of Friuli, who was elected king by northern Italian magnates at Pavia in January 888 following the collapse of Charles the Fat's empire. Challenged by rival claimants throughout his reign, Berengar struggled to preserve administrative cohesion across Lombardy against invading Magyar horsemen and ambitious regional marquises. name: County of Toulouse
description: The County of Toulouse was a powerful feudal domain in southern France that nominally recognised the suzerainty of the West Frankish crown while functioning with absolute territorial independence. Ruled by the hereditary Raymondine dynasty from their ancient Roman seat at Toulouse on the Garonne River, the counts exercised paramount authority over Languedoc, Rouergue and Septimania. Sponsoring Occitan language traditions and municipal self-government, the county preserved autonomous legal and fiscal institutions, detached from royal oversight in Paris until much later thirteenth-century crusades and treaties integrated the southern territory into the Kingdom of France. \n\n Status: Nominal possession; Capital: Toulouse; Official languages: Medieval Latin; Common languages: Old Occitan and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal principality; Ruler title: Count of Toulouse; Currency: Tolosan denier; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 889; Disestablished: 987; Succeeded by: Kingdom of France

name: Kingdom of the Iberians
description: The Kingdom of the Iberians was a medieval Georgian monarchy founded in Tao-Klarjeti around 888 when Adarnase IV of the Bagrationi dynasty formally revived the royal title of King of the Iberians. Centred along the deep mountain gorges of the Coruh and Kura rivers with major royal fortresses at Artanuji and Bana, the realm served as a vital bulwark of Christian Georgian culture. The kingdom's political leadership and monastic patronage proved decisive in overcoming regional fragmentation, culminating in 1008 when King Bagrat III united Iberia with Abkhazia to forge the unified Kingdom of Georgia. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Artanuji; Common languages: Georgian; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King of the Iberians; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 888; Disestablished: 1008; Preceded by: Principality of Iberia; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Georgia

name: Kingdom of Italy
label: barbarian kingdoms;frankish polities
description: The Kingdom of Italy during this contentious interlude was ruled by Duke Guy III of Spoleto after he defeated Berengar of Friuli at the Battle of the Trebbia in early 889. Consecrated King of Italy at Pavia and subsequently crowned Roman Emperor by Pope Stephen V in 891, Guy asserted imperial hegemony over the Lombard and Tuscan nobilities. description: The Kingdom of Italy constituted during this specific phase the northeastern territorial domain maintained by Berengar of Friuli following his expulsion from the capital at Pavia in 889. name: Fraxinetum

description: Fraxinetum was an autonomous Muslim military stronghold and naval base established on the forested heights of modern La Garde-Freinet near Saint-Tropez in Provence. Founded by Andalusian seafarers around 890, the settlement dominated the Mediterranean shoreline and projected military force far into the hinterland. Controlling vital passes across the Western Alps, the garrison raided northwards into the Rhone Valley, Piedmont and Switzerland until Count William I of Provence assembled a combined Provençal and Italian army that crushed the base at the Battle of Tourtour in 973. \n\n Status: Autonomous military stronghold; Capital: La Garde-Freinet; Common languages: Andalusian Arabic, Latin and Old Occitan; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Military emirate; Ruler title: Commander; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 890; Disestablished: 974; Succeeded by: County of Provence

name: Hamdanid Emirate
description: The Hamdanid Emirate was an illustrious Arab Shia dynasty originating from the Banu Taghlib tribe that held dominion across Upper Mesopotamia and northern Syria from capitals at Mosul and Aleppo. Ascending under the charismatic emir Sayf al-Dawla, the court in Aleppo flourished as a radiant sanctuary of Arabic poetry and philosophy, hosting literary giants such as al-Mutanabbi and the scholar al-Farabi. The emirs stood as the principal military champions of the Islamic frontier against aggressive Byzantine imperial offensives until mounting Byzantine pressure and internal revolts fragmented the emirate in the late tenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign emirate; Capital: Aleppo; Common languages: Arabic; Religion: Shia Islam; Government: Hereditary emirate; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 890; Disestablished: 1004; Preceded by: Abbasid Caliphate; Succeeded by: Mirdasid dynasty and Uqaylid dynasty

name: Sajid Dynasty
label: iranian intermezzo
description: The Sajid dynasty was an autonomous Islamic principality established in Azerbaijan during the Iranian Intermezzo by commanders originating from Central Asian Ushrusana. Operating initially from Maragha before transferring their seat to Ardabil, the dynasty exploited waning Abbasid authority to consolidate sovereign power across the region. Their reigns were characterised by sustained military campaigns to subjugate neighbouring Armenian principalities until the lineage collapsed following internal turbulence in 929. \n\n Status: Autonomous emirate; Capital: Maragha; Common languages: Persian and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Sajid; Ruler title: Afshin; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Sallarid dynasty

name: Baekje
description: Baekje, recognised in Korean historiography as Later Baekje, was a revived monarchical realm founded in southwestern Korea during the Later Three Kingdoms period. Established by the dissident military commander Kyon Hwon, the kingdom rallied local populations claiming descent from ancient Baekje and governed from Wansanju. The state commanded formidable agrarian and military resources throughout the Jeolla region until internal succession disputes enabled the rival kingdom of Goryeo to conquer its territories in 936. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Wansanju; Common languages: Old Korean and Classical Chinese; Religion: Buddhism and Confucianism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 892; Succeeded by: Goryeo

name: Samanid Empire
label: iranian intermezzo
description: The Samanid Empire was a major Persianate realm centred in Transoxiana and Khorasan that flourished as an autonomous power during the Iranian Intermezzo. Governed from Bukhara following its unification under Ismail Samani, the dynasty fostered a profound revival of Persian literature, scholarship and administrative culture alongside Islamic orthodoxy. Although regional governors and Turkic military commanders gradually eroded central control in the late tenth century, the state remained a vital intellectual beacon until its partition by Karakhanid and Ghaznavid invaders. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Bukhara; Official languages: Persian and Arabic; Common languages: Eastern Iranian languages and Sogdian; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: Amir; Historical era: Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Ghaznavid dynasty and Karakhanids

name: Kingdom of Hereti
description: The Kingdom of Hereti was a medieval Caucasian monarchy established along the mountainous frontiers of eastern Georgia and Caucasian Albania. Governed from the fortified city of Shaki, the realm asserted sovereign independence amid shifting alliances between neighbouring Armenian, Georgian and Islamic powers. Its monarchs fostered both Georgian Orthodox traditions and local Caucasian cultural heritage until the kingdom was formally integrated into the unified realm of Kakheti-Hereti in the eleventh century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Shaki; Official languages: Georgian; Common languages: Georgian and Caucasian Albanian; Religion: Georgian Orthodoxy; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 893; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Kakheti-Hereti

name: Kingdom of the Isles
label: norse/viking polities;celtic polities
description: The Kingdom of the Isles was a maritime Norse-Gaelic domain encompassing the Isle of Man, the Hebrides and the Firth of Clyde under the suzerainty of the Norwegian crown. Seafaring rulers administered this insular territory through shifting regional assemblies and strong naval fleets, maintaining distinctive hybrid Norse and Celtic cultural institutions. Despite frequent dynastic conflicts and competing interventions from Scottish and Irish lords, Norwegian overlordship endured until the archipelago was formally ceded to the Kingdom of Scotland following the Treaty of Perth. \n\n Status: Vassal kingdom under Norwegian suzerainty; Capital: Castletown; Common languages: Old Norse, Middle Irish and Latin; Religion: Norse paganism and Roman Catholicism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 849; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Scotland

name: Principality of Hungary
description: The Principality of Hungary was the initial Magyar state established in the Carpathian Basin following the nomadic settlement led by Grand Prince Arpad. Operating from centres such as Esztergom, the confederation combined tribal autonomy with expansive cavalry raids across Central and Western Europe throughout the tenth century. The realm underwent gradual sedentarisation and Christianisation under princes Taksony and Geza, culminating in the coronation of Stephen I and the establishment of the Christian Kingdom of Hungary on Christmas Day in 1000. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Esztergom; Common languages: Old Hungarian; Religion: Hungarian paganism, Tengrism and Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Tribal principality; Ruling dynasty: Arpad; Ruler title: Grand Prince; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 895; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Hungary

name: Jin
label: five dynasties and ten kingdoms - other countries  (chinese history)
description: Jin, also recorded as Former Jin or Hedong, was a powerful northern Chinese regional state founded by the Shatuo military commander Li Keyong. Centred at Taiyuan in modern Shanxi, the realm developed a fearsome cavalry apparatus that fiercely contested the legitimacy of the rival Later Liang dynasty following the fall of the Tang court. Under Li Keyong's son and successor Li Cunxu, Jin expanded aggressively across the Central Plains, ultimately overthrowing the Later Liang in 923 to inaugurate the Later Tang dynasty. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Taiyuan; Common languages: Middle Chinese and Shatuo Turkic; Religion: Buddhism and Chinese folk religion; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Prince of Jin; Historical era: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms; Disestablished: 923; Succeeded by: Later Tang

name: Sultanate of Showa
description: The Sultanate of Showa was a medieval Islamic polity established in the highlands of central and eastern Ethiopia by the Makhzumi dynasty. Governed from its principal settlement at Walale, the state maintained vital trade links connecting the interior plateau with coastal ports along the Gulf of Aden. The sultanate fostered early Islamic scholarship and urban culture in the region for nearly four centuries until internal fragmentation facilitated its annexation by the rising Sultanate of Ifat in 1286. \n\n Status: Sovereign sultanate; Capital: Walale; Official languages: Arabic; Common languages: Harla and Argobba; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Makhzumi; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Middle Ages; Disestablished: 1286; Succeeded by: Sultanate of Ifat

name: Zaydi Imamate
description: The Zaydi Imamate was an ecclesiastical state founded in the rugged northern highlands of Yemen by Imam al-Hadi ila'l-Haqq Yahya of the Rassid lineage. Centred at Sa'dah, the polity integrated theological authority with tribal leadership, requiring its imams to demonstrate profound religious scholarship alongside martial capability. Despite periodic friction with local highland clans and lowland dynasties, the imamate maintained autonomous governance across upper Yemen, establishing an enduring institutional framework that shaped the region for centuries. \n\n Status: Sovereign imamate; Capital: Sa'dah; Official languages: Arabic; Religion: Zaydi Shia Islam; Government: Theocratic elective imamate; Ruling dynasty: Rassid; Ruler title: Imam; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 897

name: Kingdom of Lotharingia
label: barbarian kingdoms;frankish polities
description: The Kingdom of Lotharingia functioned as an autonomous Carolingian realm re-established in the borderlands between East and West Francia under King Zwentibold. Operating from historic administrative centres including Metz, the monarch struggled to balance the competing ambitions of powerful local counts and ecclesiastical dignitaries. Zwentibold's brief sovereign tenure ended violently when he fell in combat against rebellious nobles in August 900, after which the territory was reintegrated into the wider East Frankish realm. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Metz; Common languages: Old Frankish, Old High German, Old French and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Carolingian; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Disestablished: 13 August 900; Succeeded by: East Francia

name: Kingdom of the East Franks
label: barbarian kingdoms;frankish polities
description: The Kingdom of the East Franks constituted the eastern partition of the former Carolingian Empire, governing Germanic territories spanning Saxony, Franconia, Swabia and Bavaria. Following the death of Emperor Arnulf in December 899, the crown passed to his infant son Louis the Child, with governance largely steered by aristocratic regents and leading bishops from centres like Frankfurt and Regensburg. During this brief juncture, the kingdom maintained separate administration while Arnulf's illegitimate son Zwentibold held Lotharingia until his death in the summer of 900. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Frankfurt and Regensburg; Common languages: Old High German, Old Saxon, Old Low German and Latin; Religion: Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Carolingian; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Germany

name: Principality of Benevento and Capua
label: lombard polities
description: The Principality of Benevento and Capua was a Lombard monarchy in southern Italy created in 900 when Count Atenulf of Capua conquered Benevento and united the two states. Governed from the historic ducal citadel of Benevento, the combined realm formed the primary bulwark of independent Lombard authority in the Mezzogiorno. The princes successfully mobilised regional coalitions against Saracen encampments along the Garigliano and navigated complex diplomatic rivalries with both the Byzantine Empire and the Papacy throughout the tenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Benevento; Common languages: Early Italian vernaculars, Lombardic and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Prince; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 900; Preceded by: Duchy of Benevento and County of Capua

name: Qarmatians
description: The Qarmatians constituted an Ismaili Shia theocratic state established across the oasis settlements of eastern Arabia by followers of Abu Sa'id al-Jannabi. Centred at al-Ahsa, the community instituted a distinctive millenarian and communal governance structure that rejected the political and religious authority of both the Abbasid and Fatimid caliphates. Renowned for their formidable desert cavalry, the Qarmatians mounted devastating expeditions across Iraq and the Levant, famously seizing the Black Stone from Mecca in 930 before gradually succumbing to tribal insurrections in the late eleventh century. \n\n Status: Sovereign theocratic state; Capital: Al-Ahsa; Common languages: Arabic and Persian; Religion: Ismaili Shia Islam; Government: Theocratic republic; Ruler title: Chief missionary; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 899; Succeeded by: Uyunid Emirate

name: Kingdom of Italy

description: The Kingdom of Italy entered a period of dynastic union under King Louis the Blind of Provence, who crossed the Alps and was crowned Italian monarch at Pavia in October 900. After securing the imperial crown from Pope Benedict IV the following year, Louis sought to impose effective royal authority over turbulent Lombard and Frankish magnates across northern Italy. His reign faced fierce resistance from Berengar of Friuli, who captured and blinded Louis in July 905, abruptly ending Provencal rule over the peninsula. \n\n Status: Kingdom in personal union with Provence; Capital: Pavia; Common languages: Early Italian vernaculars, Old Occitan and Medieval Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Elective monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Bosonid; Ruler title: King of Italy; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 12 October 900; Disestablished: 21 July 905

name: Chandra Dynasty
description: The Chandra dynasty was a sovereign Buddhist monarchy that governed the regions of Samatata and Vanga in southeastern Bengal alongside portions of coastal Arakan. Based at their royal seat in Vikramapura, the Chandra rulers presided over an era of flourishing maritime commerce, monumental monastic endowments and intellectual vitality. Maintaining complicated diplomatic relations with the neighbouring Pala Empire to the north and kingdoms in southern India, the dynasty preserved regional autonomy until succumbing to internal succession crises and external invasions in the mid-eleventh century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Vikramapura; Common languages: Sanskrit and Old Bengali; Religion: Buddhism and Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Maharajadhiraja; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 900; Disestablished: 1050; Succeeded by: Pala Empire

name: Cuilapan
label: mesoamerican polities
description: Cuilapan was an autonomous Mesoamerican city-state situated in the central valley of Oaxaca that reasserted full independence following the political fragmentation of nearby Monte Alban around 900 CE. Developing into a prosperous urban centre inhabited by both Mixtec and Zapotec populations, the polity commanded rich agricultural lands and exerted substantial influence across the surrounding valleys. Cuilapan maintained its political institutions, sophisticated crafts and defensive alliances through centuries of regional warfare until the arrival of Spanish forces in the 1520s ended its sovereign existence. \n\n Status: Sovereign city-state; Capital: Cuilapan; Common languages: Mixtec and Zapotec; Religion: Mesoamerican polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Lord; Historical era: Postclassic Mesoamerica; Established: 901; Succeeded by: New Spain

name: Kamarupa Kingdom
description: The Kamarupa Kingdom was an ancient realm in the Brahmaputra Valley and neighbouring tracts of eastern Bengal that operated as a vassal polity subordinate to the Pala Empire during the tenth century. Governed by local dynasties from major riverine capitals in Assam, the state preserved its distinct administrative customs, religious endowments and vibrant cultural traditions while offering nominal allegiance to Pala overlords. As imperial Pala authority fluctuated across northeastern India, Kamarupa continued to defend its regional frontiers and maritime river routes against external encroachment. \n\n Status: Vassal kingdom under the Pala Empire; Capital: Durjaya; Common languages: Kamarupi Prakrit and Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism and Animism; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruler title: Maharajadhiraja; Historical era: Classical India; Established: 350; Disestablished: 1140

name: Kingdom of Alania
description: The Kingdom of Alania was a medieval Caucasian state established by the Iranian-speaking Alans in the fertile foothills and northern passes of the Caucasus mountains. Having emancipated itself from Khazar hegemony, the kingdom governed from its fortified capital at Maghas and embraced Eastern Orthodox Christianity through extensive Byzantine missionary contact. Controlling the strategic Darial Pass, Alania prospered as a vital trade conduit and supplied renowned cavalry forces to regional alliances until devastating Mongol invasions shattered the realm and razed Maghas in 1239. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Maghas; Common languages: Alanic; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy and Alanic paganism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 900; Succeeded by: Mongol Empire

name: Kingdom of Tonga
description: The Kingdom of Tonga was an expansive Polynesian monarchy established in the South Pacific, whose dynastic lineage emerged under the first Tu'i Tonga, Aho'eitu, around the tenth century. Centred on the island of Tongatapu, the realm evolved into a sophisticated maritime empire whose naval canoes and trading networks exerted hegemony over neighbouring archipelagoes, including Samoa, Niue and parts of Fiji. The kingdom preserved its sacred political institutions and social hierarchy across centuries of insular history, maintaining indigenous independence until entering a British protectorate treaty in 1900. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Nuku'alofa; Official languages: Tongan; Common languages: Tongan; Religion: Polynesian religion and later Christianity; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Tu'i Tonga; Ruler title: Tu'i Tonga; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 900

name: Sultanate of Mogadishu
description: The Sultanate of Mogadishu was a prosperous medieval maritime state centred around the coastal emporium of Mogadishu in southern Somalia. Founded in the tenth century under the Fakhr al-Din dynasty, the sultanate commanded extensive commercial networks across the Indian Ocean, linking the African interior with Arabia, Persia and India. The city-state minted its own distinctive coinage, erected monumental mosques and stone residences, and maintained undisputed naval and mercantile pre-eminence along the Benadir coast before yielding regional dominance to the Ajuran Sultanate. \n\n Status: Sovereign sultanate; Capital: Mogadishu; Common languages: Somali and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Sultanate; Ruling dynasty: Fakhr al-Din; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Ajuran Sultanate

name: Tambralinga Kingdom
description: The Tambralinga Kingdom was an Indianised maritime state situated along the eastern coast of the Malay Peninsula, centred at the city of Nakhon Si Thammarat in present-day southern Thailand. Benefiting from vital trans-isthmian overland trade routes between the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea, the kingdom fostered vibrant Buddhist and Hindu court traditions. Although frequently interacting with the maritime empire of Srivijaya, Tambralinga maintained sovereign diplomatic ties with Song China and exerted significant commercial and naval influence across the region throughout the high medieval period. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Nakhon Si Thammarat; Common languages: Old Mon, Old Khmer, Austronesian languages and Sanskrit; Religion: Buddhism and Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Middle Ages; Disestablished: 1277; Succeeded by: Nakhon Si Thammarat Kingdom

name: Toltec Empire
label: mesoamerican polities
description: The Toltec Empire was a dominant Postclassic Mesoamerican political entity centred at the urban citadel of Tollan-Xicocotitlan in central Mexico. Renowned for its militaristic ideology, monumental pillared architecture and artisan craftsmanship, the state exercised profound cultural and economic hegemony over the Valley of Mexico and extended trade contacts across Mesoamerica. Toltec dynastic legends and administrative concepts exerted lasting prestige throughout the region, serving as the foundational model of legitimate royal authority for subsequent Nahua civilisations, including the Aztecs. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Tollan-Xicocotitlan; Common languages: Nahuatl and Otomi; Religion: Toltec religion; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Tlatoani; Historical era: Postclassic Mesoamerica; Established: 900; Succeeded by: Azcapotzalco and Tenochtitlan

name: Tomara Dynasty
description: The Tomara dynasty was a sovereign Rajput ruling house that controlled the strategic plains of Delhi and Haryana in northern India during the early medieval era. Having originally governed as feudatories of the Gurjara-Pratihara Empire, the Tomaras attained full independence as imperial authority waned in the tenth century and established fortified settlements, including Lal Kot. The dynasty presided over substantial urban growth, defensive fortification and religious patronage in the Delhi basin until being supplanted by the rival Chahamanas of Shakambhari in the mid-twelfth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign monarchy; Capital: Lal Kot; Common languages: Apabhramsha and Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Tomara; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 736; Succeeded by: Chahamanas of Shakambhari

name: Tondo
label: barangay states
description: Tondo was an influential precolonial maritime trading polity established along the northern reaches of the Pasig River delta on the island of Luzon. Attested in the historic Laguna Copperplate Inscription of 900 CE, the settlement was governed by a hereditary lakan and maintained a loose confederation of local barangay communities. Controlling extensive mercantile exchanges of Chinese porcelain, silk and local gold throughout the archipelago, Tondo flourished as a premier commercial hub until the Spanish expeditionary force under Miguel Lopez de Legazpi seized the Pasig delta in May 1571. \n\n Status: Sovereign maritime polity; Capital: Tondo; Common languages: Old Tagalog, Kapampangan and Classical Malay; Religion: Tagalog polytheism and Hinduism; Government: Feudal bayan; Ruler title: Lakan; Currency: Piloncitos and gold rings; Historical era: Post-classical; Disestablished: 19 May 1571; Succeeded by: Captaincy General of the Philippines

name: Tzʼutujil Kingdom
label: mesoamerican polities
description: The Tzutujil Kingdom was a Postclassic Maya state centred around the southern shores and volcanic highlands of Lake Atitlan in southwestern Guatemala. Governed from the fortified hilltop citadel of Chuitinamit, the kingdom commanded fertile valleys and obsidian trade routes while defending its borders against rival K'iche' and Kaqchikel neighbours. The monarchy preserved robust ritual traditions, agricultural terraces and civic administration until Spanish conquistador Pedro de Alvarado allied with neighbouring highland groups to overthrow the citadel in April 1524. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Chuitinamit; Common languages: Tzutujil; Religion: Maya religion; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Ajpop; Historical era: Postclassic Mesoamerica; Established: 901; Disestablished: 18 April 1524; Succeeded by: New Spain

name: Venad Kingdom
description: The Venad Kingdom was a prominent medieval principality located between the Western Ghats and the Arabian Sea at the southwestern tip of the Indian subcontinent. Governed from the thriving port city of Kollam, the state emerged as an autonomous successor to the ancient Chera dynasty and prospered through extensive Indian Ocean spice commerce with Arab, Persian and Chinese merchants. Under ambitious rulers like Ravi Varma Kulasekhara, the kingdom asserted military power across the Tamil country before consolidating into the early modern Kingdom of Travancore. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Kollam; Official languages: Malayalam; Common languages: Malayalam and Tamil; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Kulasekhara; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Travancore

name: Goryeo
description: Goryeo was a dynastic Korean state founded by King Taejo following the collapse of Taebong during the Later Three Kingdoms period. Administered from its primary capital at Gaegyeong, the kingdom successfully unified the Korean Peninsula by assimilating the remnants of Silla, Later Baekje and northern refugees from Balhae into a shared cultural identity. The realm fostered a magnificent golden age of Buddhist art, bureaucratic civil examinations and celadon ceramic production, maintaining its sovereignty until the establishment of the Joseon dynasty in 1392. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Gaegyeong; Common languages: Middle Korean and Classical Chinese; Religion: Buddhism and Confucianism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Wang; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Joseon

name: Dachanghe
description: Dachanghe was a short-lived imperial realm established in modern Yunnan following the violent overthrow of the Nanzhao dynasty by the chief minister Zheng Maisi. Governed from the historic lakeside capital of Yangjumie, the kingdom sought legitimacy by portraying itself as the rightful heir to both Nanzhao and Tang imperial heritage. The state engaged in military skirmishes and marriage alliances with neighbouring Chinese regional kingdoms until the ruling Zheng lineage was overthrown in an aristocratic coup led by Yang Ganzhen in 928. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Yangjumie; Common languages: Bai, Nuosu and Middle Chinese; Religion: Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Zheng; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms; Succeeded by: Datianxing

name: Majin
description: Majin was a short-lived Korean kingdom established during the Later Three Kingdoms period when the monarch Kung Ye renamed his realm of Later Goguryeo. Operating from its newly established fortress capital at Cheorwon, the state functioned as a militarised Buddhist theocracy where Kung Ye proclaimed himself the living Maitreya Buddha. The kingdom expanded vigorously across central Korea against Unified Silla and Later Baekje before the ruler reorganised the polity under the dynastic title of Taebong in 911. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Cheorwon; Common languages: Old Korean and Classical Chinese; Religion: Buddhism; Government: Theocratic monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 904; Succeeded by: Taebong

name: Xiliangfu
description: Xiliangfu was a regional Tibetan tribal confederation that ruled Liangzhou along the vital Hexi Corridor in modern Gansu province. Emerging from the dissolution of Tang and Tibetan imperial administration in the late ninth century, the confederation brought local Tibetan and Han populations under the collective leadership of the Liugu clans. Controlling profitable Silk Road overland trade and defending its strategic oasis against neighbouring nomad powers, the polity retained autonomy until Tangut Western Xia forces and allied Uyghurs conquered Liangzhou in the early eleventh century. \n\n Status: Sovereign tribal confederation; Capital: Liangzhou; Common languages: Old Tibetan and Middle Chinese; Religion: Buddhism; Government: Tribal confederation; Historical era: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms; Established: 906; Succeeded by: Western Xia and Tsongkha

name: Chu
label: five dynasties and ten kingdoms - ten kingdoms  (chinese history)
description: Chu, commonly designated in Chinese historiography as Ma Chu or Southern Chu, was an autonomous kingdom established in modern Hunan during the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period. Founded by the military governor Ma Yin with its royal court at Changsha, the state prospered by promoting extensive commercial trade in tea, silk and timber with northern regimes. The kingdom maintained internal stability and minted distinctive iron coinage until fratricidal succession struggles following Ma Yin's death invited invasion and absorption by the neighbouring Southern Tang in 951. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Changsha; Common languages: Middle Chinese and Medieval Xiang; Religion: Buddhism, Taoism and Confucianism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Ma; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms; Succeeded by: Southern Tang

name: Great Han
label: five dynasties and ten kingdoms - ten kingdoms  (chinese history)
description: Great Han, known historically as Southern Han, was an imperial coastal state founded by Liu Yan across present-day Guangdong and Guangxi during the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period. Operating from its magnificent commercial capital at Xingwang Fu, the realm accumulated immense wealth by taxing maritime trade routes linking China with Southeast Asia, India and the Persian Gulf. Despite domestic political cruelty and failed military expeditions into northern Vietnam, the dynasty maintained its maritime prosperity until Northern Song armies conquered the territory in 971. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Xingwang Fu; Common languages: Middle Chinese and Medieval Yue; Religion: Buddhism and Taoism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Liu; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms; Succeeded by: Song dynasty

name: Min
label: five dynasties and ten kingdoms - ten kingdoms  (chinese history)
description: Min was an independent coastal kingdom established in the rugged maritime province of Fujian by Wang Shenzhi during the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms era. Centred at Fuzhou, the monarchy fostered overseas commerce, encouraged agricultural reclamation and patronised Buddhist monastic foundations to develop a previously peripheral border region. Following Wang Shenzhi's death, internal palace strife and violent fratricidal warfare severely weakened the state, culminating in its military defeat and territorial partition by the neighbouring Southern Tang and Wuyue in 945. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Fuzhou; Common languages: Middle Chinese and Medieval Min; Religion: Buddhism and Taoism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Wang; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms; Succeeded by: Southern Tang and Wuyue

name: Qi
label: five dynasties and ten kingdoms - other countries  (chinese history)
description: Qi was a northern Chinese principality established around Fengxiang in modern Shaanxi by the veteran Tang warlord Li Maozhen at the onset of the Five Dynasties period. Clinging to Tang royal traditions and refusing to recognise the usurping Later Liang dynasty, Li Maozhen exercised autonomous military authority over territories spanning Shaanxi, Gansu and northern Sichuan. Constant warfare against powerful neighbours gradually constricted the realm to the environs of Fengxiang, prompting Li Maozhen to submit to the Later Tang dynasty shortly before his death in 924. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Fengxiang; Common languages: Middle Chinese; Religion: Buddhism and Confucianism; Government: Principality; Ruling dynasty: Li; Ruler title: Prince of Qi; Historical era: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms; Succeeded by: Later Tang

name: Shu
label: five dynasties and ten kingdoms - ten kingdoms  (chinese history)
description: Shu, designated by historians as Former Shu, was an autonomous imperial state founded in the fertile Sichuan Basin by the military governor Wang Jian following the collapse of the Tang dynasty. Headquartered at the affluent metropolis of Chengdu, the empire was protected by rugged mountain barriers and became a celebrated sanctuary for northern poets, artists and Buddhist scholars fleeing war. Despite its agricultural wealth and refined court culture, administrative decadence under Wang Jian's son Wang Zongyan allowed invading Later Tang armies to swiftly conquer the realm in 925. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Chengdu; Common languages: Middle Chinese and Ba-Shu Chinese; Religion: Buddhism, Taoism and Confucianism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Wang; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms; Succeeded by: Later Tang

name: Wu
label: five dynasties and ten kingdoms - ten kingdoms  (chinese history)
description: Wu, known in historiography as Southern Wu or Yang Wu, was a prominent eastern Chinese state established along the lower Yangtze and Huai River valleys during the Five Dynasties era. Governed from the bustling canal city of Guangling, the kingdom originated under the military commander Yang Xingmi and derived vast revenue from riverine grain transport and salt monopolies. Although Yang Xingmi's sons formally occupied the throne, actual power fell into the hands of the regent Xu Wen and his adopted son Xu Zhigao, who eventually usurped authority in 937 to found the Southern Tang. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Guangling; Common languages: Middle Chinese; Religion: Buddhism and Taoism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Yang; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms; Succeeded by: Southern Tang

name: Wuyue
label: five dynasties and ten kingdoms - ten kingdoms  (chinese history)
description: Wuyue was an economically prosperous coastal kingdom founded by Qian Liu around modern Zhejiang and Shanghai during the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period. Governed from its primary capital at Qiantang, the kingdom pursued prudent diplomatic submission towards northern imperial dynasties while concentrating domestic resources on coastal dyke construction, agricultural reclamation and maritime commerce. Under successive monarchs of the Qian clan, Wuyue emerged as a magnificent cultural centre and patron of Buddhist scholarship until peacefully submitting its territory to the reunifying Northern Song dynasty in 978. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Qiantang; Common languages: Middle Chinese and Medieval Wu; Religion: Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Qian; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms; Succeeded by: Northern Song dynasty

name: Jinghai Circuit
label: five dynasties and ten kingdoms - other countries  (chinese history)
description: The Jinghai Circuit was a quasi-independent military commandery covering the Red River Delta in northern Vietnam during the fragmentation of the Tang Empire. Centred at Dai La, the circuit was administered by native Vietnamese notables of the Khuc family, who exercised de facto autonomy as hereditary military governors while maintaining nominal tributary ties with Chinese regimes. The administration reduced tax burdens and restored local stability until the neighbouring Southern Han dynasty launched a maritime invasion in 930, temporarily disrupting indigenous self-rule. \n\n Status: Semi-independent military circuit under nominal Chinese suzerainty; Capital: Dai La; Common languages: Middle Chinese and Old Vietnamese; Religion: Vietnamese folk religion and Buddhism; Government: Military commandery; Ruler title: Jiedushi; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Southern Han

name: Khamag Mongol
description: Khamag Mongol was an influential nomadic tribal confederation that dominated the steppes of the Mongolian Plateau along the Onon, Kherlen and Tuul river basins. Functioning as the primary political predecessor to the Mongol Empire, the confederation unified core clans including the Khiyad, Taichiud and Jalairs under the leadership of Khabul Khan. The pastoral alliance maintained formidable cavalry forces that repeatedly checked Jurchen Jin border encroachments and contested rival Tatar tribes, culminating in the rise of Genghis Khan and the proclamation of the Mongol Empire in 1206. \n\n Status: Sovereign tribal confederation; Capital: Avraga; Common languages: Middle Mongol; Religion: Tengrism; Government: Nomadic confederation; Ruling dynasty: Borjigin; Ruler title: Khan; Historical era: Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Mongol Empire

name: Khitan Confederation
description: The Khitan Confederation was a unified nomadic alliance that organised the pastoral tribes of Manchuria and the eastern Mongolian Plateau under the charismatic leadership of Yelu Abaoji. Operating from early seasonal headquarters that preceded the imperial capital of Shangjing, the confederation consolidated eight traditional Khitan clans and subjugated neighbouring steppe peoples following the disintegration of the Tang dynasty. Through innovative dual civil and tribal military institutions, Abaoji transformed this nomadic federation into a centralised imperial polity, formally inaugurating the Great Liao dynasty in 916. \n\n Status: Sovereign nomadic confederation; Capital: Shangjing; Common languages: Khitan and Middle Chinese; Religion: Khitan animism, Shamanism and Buddhism; Government: Tribal confederation; Ruling dynasty: Yelu; Ruler title: Khagan; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Great Liao

name: Zhao
label: five dynasties and ten kingdoms - other countries  (chinese history)
description: Zhao was an autonomous regional principality established in central Hebei during the chaotic interregnum between the Tang and Song dynasties. Centred at Zhenzhou, the polity arose from the former Chengde military commandery under its long-serving warlord Wang Rong, who navigated precarious diplomatic ties between the rival regimes of Jin and Later Liang. The state preserved local autonomy and agrarian revenues until a violent military mutiny in 921 overthrew the Wang family, allowing neighbouring Shatuo forces from Jin to annex the territory shortly thereafter. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Zhenzhou; Common languages: Middle Chinese; Religion: Buddhism and Taoism; Government: Principality; Ruling dynasty: Wang; Ruler title: Prince of Zhao; Historical era: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms; Succeeded by: Jin

name: Great Liao
description: Great Liao was a powerful empire founded by the Yelu clan of the Khitan people that held sway over Manchuria, the Mongolian Plateau and the northern fringes of China. Governed from Shangjing and several secondary capitals, the state implemented an innovative dual administrative system that preserved traditional nomadic governance for northern tribes while applying Chinese-style civil bureaucracy to sedentary subjects. At the height of its military strength, Liao seized the strategic Sixteen Prefectures and commanded international prestige along the eastern Silk Road until collapsing under combined Jurchen and Song assaults in 1125. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Shangjing; Common languages: Khitan and Middle Chinese; Religion: Buddhism and Khitan animism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Yelu; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Jin dynasty and Western Liao

name: Fatimid Caliphate
description: The Fatimid Caliphate was a major Islamic empire established in North Africa by the Ismaili Shia dynasty tracing descent from the Prophet's daughter Fatima. Inaugurated at Raqqada and Mahdia through the military backing of Kutama Berbers, the caliphate challenged Abbasid religious and political hegemony throughout the Mediterranean basin. After conquering Egypt in 969, the Fatimids established Cairo as their imperial capital, fostering flourishing international trade, architectural splendour and scholarship at al-Azhar until Saladin abolished the dynasty in 1171. \n\n Status: Sovereign caliphate; Capital: Cairo; Common languages: Arabic, Berber and Coptic; Religion: Ismaili Shia Islam; Government: Theocratic hereditary caliphate; Ruling dynasty: Fatimid; Ruler title: Caliph; Historical era: Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Ayyubid Sultanate

name: Kingdom of Asturias
description: The Kingdom of Asturias entered its final autonomous phase following the territorial partition of 910 among the sons of King Alfonso III. Governed from Oviedo by King Fruela II, this northern Cantabrian realm preserved the traditional institutional heartland of the early Christian Reconquista. Fruela maintained cordial dynastic ties with his brothers in neighbouring Leon and Galicia, ultimately reuniting the separated crowns under his rule shortly before his death in 925. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Oviedo; Common languages: Latin and Old Leonese; Religion: Catholic Christianity; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Astur-Leonese; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Kingdom of León

name: Kingdom of Galicia
description: The Kingdom of Galicia emerged as an autonomous political realm following the division of the Asturian crown in 910, passing to King Ordono II.
