Centred in the northwest of the Iberian Peninsula with its spiritual heart at Santiago de Compostela, the kingdom possessed extensive agricultural resources and experienced maritime communities. Galician nobility played a decisive role in regional expansion against Moorish strongholds, remaining closely tied by dynastic inheritance to the neighbouring thrones of Leon and Asturias. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Santiago de Compostela; Common languages: Latin and Old Galician-Portuguese; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Astur-Leonese; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Kingdom of León

name: Kingdom of Jinshan
label: five dynasties and ten kingdoms - other countries  (chinese history)
description: The Kingdom of Jinshan, officially styled the Jinshan Kingdom of the Western Han, was a short-lived monarchical regime established along the eastern Silk Road by the warlord Zhang Chengfeng. Operating from Dunhuang in the Guiyi Circuit, Zhang broke formal allegiance with the collapsing Tang Empire and assumed imperial titles. The fledgling desert state struggled to withstand aggressive pressure from neighbouring Ganzhou Uyghur nomads, who defeated its armies and forced the regime to abandon imperial pretensions by 914. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Dunhuang; Common languages: Middle Chinese, Old Tibetan and Sogdian; Religion: Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Zhang; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms; Succeeded by: Guiyi Circuit

name: Kingdom of León
description: The Kingdom of León was established when King Garcia I transferred the royal seat from Oviedo south across the Cantabrian mountains to the fortified city of Leon. Commanding the fertile plains of the Duero river basin, the new realm spearheaded military frontier defence and Christian repopulation initiatives against the Caliphate of Cordoba. Garcia and his successor Ordono II consolidated royal authority over regional counts, transforming Leon into the pre-eminent Christian monarchy of the northwestern Iberian Peninsula. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: León; Common languages: Old Leonese, Latin and Galician-Portuguese; Religion: Latin Christianity; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Astur-Leonese; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Crown of Castile

name: Yiwu Circuit
label: five dynasties and ten kingdoms - other countries  (chinese history)
description: The Yiwu Circuit was an autonomous northern Chinese military commandery centred at Dingzhou during the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period. Governed by the hereditary warlord Wang Chuzhi and his successors, the territory retained significant fiscal and military independence from the central imperial courts. Yiwu played a delicate diplomatic balancing game between the rival regimes of Jin and Later Liang until the expanding Later Tang dynasty laid siege to Dingzhou and extinguished local autonomy in March 929. \n\n Status: Autonomous military circuit; Capital: Dingzhou; Common languages: Middle Chinese; Religion: Buddhism and Taoism; Government: Military commandery; Ruling dynasty: Wang; Ruler title: Jiedushi; Historical era: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms; Succeeded by: Later Tang

name: Duchy of Normandy
label: norse/viking polities
description: The Duchy of Normandy originated as a semi-autonomous feudal fiefdom granted to the Scandinavian leader Rollo under the Treaty of Saint-Clair-sur-Epte in 911. Headquartered at the cathedral city of Rouen, the Norse settlers agreed to accept Christian baptism and protect the lower Seine valley from rival Viking incursions on behalf of King Charles III of West Francia. Blending Scandinavian maritime institutions with Frankish feudal law, Rollo and his successors expanded their territorial jurisdiction while providing nominal vassal allegiance to the West Frankish crown. \n\n Status: Feudal duchy under West Frankish suzerainty; Capital: Rouen; Common languages: Old Norman, Old Norse and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Normandy; Ruler title: Duke of Normandy; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 911

name: Great Yan
label: five dynasties and ten kingdoms - other countries  (chinese history)
description: Great Yan, recorded in Chinese annals as Jie Yan, was a short-lived imperial realm established around Youzhou in modern Beijing by the militarist Liu Shouguang. Having wrested control of the Lulong Circuit from his father and brother, Liu audaciously assumed the title of emperor in 911 amidst the collapse of northern order. Characterised by extreme political cruelty and isolation from neighbouring courts, the regime was swiftly besieged by Li Cunxu of Jin, whose Shatuo armies captured Youzhou and dissolved the state in early 914. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Youzhou; Common languages: Middle Chinese; Religion: Buddhism and Taoism; Government: Empire; Ruling dynasty: Liu; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms; Succeeded by: Jin

name: Taebong
description: Taebong was the final incarnation of the northern Korean kingdom established by the charismatic monarch Kung Ye during the Later Three Kingdoms period. Headquartered at the fortified central city of Cheorwon, the realm operated as an authoritarian Buddhist theocracy with ambitions to subjugate both Unified Silla and Later Baekje. Kung Ye's increasingly erratic purges of the court nobility alienated military elites, culminating in an aristocratic coup in 918 that elevated General Wang Kon to the throne and transformed the realm into Goryeo. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Cheorwon; Common languages: Old Korean and Classical Chinese; Religion: Buddhism; Government: Theocratic monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Preceded by: Majin; Succeeded by: Goryeo

name: Kingdom of Bali
description: The Kingdom of Bali was a sovereign Hindu-Buddhist realm established across the volcanic island of Bali, whose historical epigraphy traces back to King Sri Kesari Warmadewa in 914. Maintaining seats of power at settlements such as Bedulu and Gelgel, the monarchy harmonised native ancestor veneration with classical Indianised court rituals, irrigation management and sophisticated temple architecture. The state retained strong commercial and religious interactions with neighbouring Javanese kingdoms, flourishing as an independent island redoubt of Indo-Javanese culture throughout the medieval era. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Gelgel; Official languages: Balinese; Common languages: Balinese, Kawi and Sanskrit; Religion: Balinese Hinduism and Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Warmadewa; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 914

name: Norman State in Brittany
label: norse/viking polities
description: The Norman State in Brittany was a Scandinavian military regime that ruled the Breton peninsula for two decades following the collapse of the unified Kingdom of Brittany. Operating from their primary maritime base at Nantes along the Loire estuary, Norse warlords exacted tribute, raided inland monasteries and controlled local commercial shipping routes. Breton resistance consolidated under Alan Twistedbeard, who returned from English exile with Anglo-Saxon assistance, routed the Norse garrison at the Battle of Trans and ended Scandinavian occupation in August 939. \n\n Status: Sovereign military lordship; Capital: Nantes; Common languages: Old Norse, Breton, Old French and Latin; Religion: Norse paganism and Christianity; Government: Military occupation; Ruler title: Jarl; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Duchy of Brittany

name: Sallarid Dynasty
label: iranian intermezzo
description: The Sallarid dynasty, also known as the Musafirids, was an Iranian Shia ruling house of Daylami origin that gained prominence during the Iranian Intermezzo. Having originated from the mountain fortress of Tarom, the dynasty expanded across northwestern Iran and Transcaucasia, establishing royal governance at Ardabil and controlling Azerbaijan, Arran and eastern Armenia. The Sallarids contended with Rus raiders on the Caspian Sea and rival regional dynasts until dynastic rivalries allowed the Rawadids and Shaddadids to displace their regional hegemony in the eleventh century. \n\n Status: Sovereign monarchy; Capital: Ardabil; Common languages: Persian, Daylami and Talysh; Religion: Shia Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Sallarid; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Rawadid dynasty and Shaddadids

name: Kingdom of Deheubarth
label: celtic polities in britain;celtic polities
description: The Kingdom of Deheubarth was a prominent realm in southwestern Wales formed in 920 when King Hywel Dda amalgamated the territories of Seisyllwg and Dyfed. Administered from strategic royal centres including Dinefwr and Carmarthen, the state became celebrated for Hywel's comprehensive codification of traditional Welsh legal principles, known as the Laws of Hywel. Deheubarth commanded major pastoral valleys and coastal trade routes, exerting dominant influence across southern Wales while balancing diplomatic interactions with Anglo-Saxon neighbours until later Anglo-Norman pressures reshaped the Welsh borderlands. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Dinefwr; Common languages: Old Welsh and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Dinefwr; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Middle Ages; Preceded by: Seisyllwg and Kingdom of Dyfed

name: Kingdom of Italy
label: barbarian kingdoms;frankish polities
description: The Kingdom of Italy entered a dynastic union with the Kingdom of Upper Burgundy when King Rudolph II crossed the Alps upon the invitation of dissident Italian nobles. Following his decisive victory over Berengar of Friuli at the Battle of Fiorenzuola in 923, Rudolph was acclaimed king at Pavia, attempting to stabilise northern Italian governance. Facing mounting aristocratic opposition orchestrated by rivals who preferred Provencal leadership, Rudolph was compelled to relinquish the Italian throne to Hugh of Arles in July 926. \n\n Status: Kingdom in personal union with Upper Burgundy; Capital: Pavia; Common languages: Early Italian vernaculars, Franco-Provencal and Medieval Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Elective monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Elder House of Welf; Ruler title: King of Italy; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 923; Disestablished: 6 July 926

name: Kingdom of Lotharingia
label: barbarian kingdoms;frankish polities
description: The Kingdom of Lotharingia served as the final royal redoubt of the Carolingian monarch Charles the Simple after he was deposed from the West Frankish throne in 922. Operating from historic Lotharingian centres such as Metz, Charles retained the allegiance of local magnates who recognised his legitimate Carolingian royal lineage against rival Robertian claimants. His autonomous sovereign tenure proved precarious, collapsing when Count Herbert of Vermandois lured Charles into captivity, where the dispossessed monarch remained confined until his death in October 929. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Metz; Common languages: Old Frankish, Old French, Old High German and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Carolingian; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Succeeded by: East Francia

name: Principality of Serbia
description: The Principality of Serbia briefly operated as a subordinate client realm under the First Bulgarian Empire during the winter of 923. Tsar Simeon I of Bulgaria intervened militarily across the Serbian highlands to suppress pro-Byzantine rebellions and secure his western frontier against imperial encirclement. Although local tribal zupans retained administrative control from regional strongholds near the Danubian and Sava frontiers, direct Bulgarian political oversight severely constrained sovereign domestic initiatives during this turbulent diplomatic confrontation. \n\n Status: Client principality under Bulgarian suzerainty; Capital: Belgrade; Common languages: Old Serbian; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Principality; Ruling dynasty: Vlastimirovic; Ruler title: Knez; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 923; Disestablished: 923

name: Principality of Serbia
description: The Principality of Serbia functioned as a client state allied with the Eastern Roman Empire between 923 and 925 under Prince Zaharija Pribislavljevic. Renouncing Bulgarian suzerainty, Zaharija aligned his highland realm with Constantinople, receiving imperial subsidies and recognition to harass western Bulgarian border positions. This pro-Byzantine stance provoked a devastating punitive expedition launched by Bulgarian Tsar Simeon, who dispatched a punitive army that deposed Zaharija and temporarily depopulated and annexed the Serbian interior around 925. \n\n Status: Client principality under Byzantine suzerainty; Capital: Ras; Common languages: Old Serbian; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Principality; Ruling dynasty: Vlastimirovic; Ruler title: Knez; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Succeeded by: First Bulgarian Empire

name: Tang
label: five dynasties and ten kingdoms - five dynasties (chinese history)
description: Tang, recorded in Chinese historiography as the Later Tang, was an imperial dynasty established by the Shatuo military leader Li Cunxu following his conquest of the Later Liang in 923. Headquartered at Luoyang, the regime claimed legitimate restoration of the ancient Tang dynasty, combining traditional Chinese civil administration with elite Shatuo cavalry divisions. The empire incorporated Former Shu and dominated the Central Plains until military insurrections and foreign interventions culminated in its defeat by Shi Jingtang and allied Khitan forces in 936. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Luoyang; Common languages: Middle Chinese and Shatuo Turkic; Religion: Buddhism, Confucianism and Taoism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Li; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms; Succeeded by: Later Jin

name: Jingnan
label: five dynasties and ten kingdoms - ten kingdoms  (chinese history)
description: Jingnan, also known as Nanping or Northern Chu, was a compact autonomous state established along the middle Yangtze River in modern Hubei during the Five Dynasties period. Founded by Gao Jixing with its capital at Jingzhou, the principality leveraged its strategic geographical crossroads to profit from inter-regional commerce while remaining the smallest of the Ten Kingdoms. To safeguard its vulnerable borders, the ruling Gao family maintained diplomatic flexibility by offering nominal tributary allegiance to all neighbouring imperial dynasties until peacefully yielding to the Song dynasty in 963. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Jingzhou; Common languages: Middle Chinese; Religion: Buddhism and Taoism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Gao; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms; Succeeded by: Song dynasty

name: Chandelas of Jejakabhukti
description: The Chandelas of Jejakabhukti were a sovereign Rajput dynasty that governed the Bundelkhand region of central India following their emancipation from Gurjara-Pratihara suzerainty. Governed from their celebrated capital at Khajuraho and fortified hill citadels such as Kalanjara, the monarchs established formidable military dominance across the northern plains. Under rulers Yashovarman and Dhanga, the dynasty commissioned the world-renowned temple complexes of Khajuraho, demonstrating exquisite sculptural artistry and devout religious patronage before encountering recurrent invasions from northern sultanates. \n\n Status: Sovereign monarchy; Capital: Khajuraho; Common languages: Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism and Jainism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Chandela; Ruler title: Maharajadhiraja; Historical era: Medieval India; Established: 831; Disestablished: 1315

name: Kingdom of Croatia
description: The Kingdom of Croatia emerged as an independent South Slavic realm in the western Balkans under its first monarch, King Tomislav, who received royal recognition from Pope John X around 925. Administered from key royal seats including Knin and Nin, the kingdom successfully defended its frontiers against Hungarian incursions and decisively routed Bulgarian invasion forces. Tomislav established a powerful naval fleet in the Adriatic and fostered Christian ecclesiastical assemblies in Split, creating a stable medieval kingdom that united coastal Dalmatian towns with inland territories. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Knin; Common languages: Old Croatian and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Trpimirovic; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Personal union with Hungary

name: Kingdom of Ngari Khorsum
label: tibetan era of fragmentation
description: The Kingdom of Ngari Khorsum was an autonomous Himalayan realm established in western Tibet during the Era of Fragmentation following the collapse of the Tibetan Empire. Founded by Kyide Nyimagon, a royal scion of the ancient Yarlung dynasty, the kingdom established its administrative base at Purang near Mount Kailash. The state served as an essential sanctuary for Tibetan cultural continuity and Buddhist scholarship, maintaining mountain trade routes connecting the Tibetan plateau with Kashmir, Ladakh and northern India for several centuries. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Purang; Common languages: Old Tibetan; Religion: Tibetan Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Yarlung; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Tibetan Era of Fragmentation; Established: 926

name: Kingdom of Italy
label: barbarian kingdoms;frankish polities
description: The Kingdom of Italy entered an eight-year period of dynastic union under King Hugh of Arles, who assumed the iron crown at Pavia in July 926 following the expulsion of Rudolph of Burgundy. Supported by loyal Provencal retainers and Italian partisans, Hugh sought to rebuild centralised monarchical power amidst persistent feudal rebellions and private wars among Lombard margraves. His administration actively reorganised royal finances and negotiated delicate alliances with the Roman papacy before consolidating his Italian domains into a more unified sovereign regime by 934. \n\n Status: Kingdom in personal union with Provence; Capital: Pavia; Common languages: Early Italian vernaculars, Old Occitan and Medieval Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Elective monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Bosonid; Ruler title: King of Italy; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 6 July 926; Disestablished: 934

name: Dongdan Kingdom
description: The Dongdan Kingdom was a dependent puppet realm established in eastern Manchuria by Emperor Abaoji of the Khitan Liao dynasty following his conquest of Balhae in 926. Administered by Abaoji's eldest son Yelu Bei from Huhan and subsequently Liaoyang, the state was created to govern former Balhae populations while preventing native insurrections. As succession rivalries in the Liao imperial court deepened, the territory lost its administrative autonomy and was progressively dismantled and incorporated directly into the regular prefecture system of the Liao Empire. \n\n Status: Puppet kingdom under Liao dynasty suzerainty; Capital: Liaoyang; Common languages: Khitan and Balhae languages; Religion: Buddhism, Shamanism and Confucianism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Yelu; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Liao dynasty

name: Wajihids
description: The Wajihids were an autonomous Arab dynastic house that ruled coastal Oman throughout the middle of the tenth century. Headquartered at the flourishing port emporium of Suhar, the dynasty controlled maritime trade routes traversing the Persian Gulf, the Gulf of Oman and the wider Indian Ocean. The Wajihid emirs maintained a capable naval force, repelling aggressive incursions launched by the Qarmatians of eastern Arabia and navigating delicate ties with Abbasid and regional Iranian potentates before being overcome by the Buyids around 966. \n\n Status: Sovereign emirate; Capital: Suhar; Official languages: Arabic; Religion: Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Banu Wajih; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Buyid dynasty

name: Kingdom of England
description: The Kingdom of England emerged as a unified sovereign monarchy in 927 when King Athelstan of the House of Wessex subjugated the last Scandinavian kingdom of York. Operating from administrative capitals at Winchester and London, the realm established a sophisticated shire system, uniform royal law codes and an advanced national currency. Athelstan and his successors consolidated Anglo-Saxon and Anglo-Scandinavian populations into a single realm, exerting paramount overlordship across Great Britain and defending the coast against recurrent Viking incursions throughout the tenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Winchester; Common languages: Old English and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Wessex; Ruler title: King of the English; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Great Britain

name: Datianxing
description: Datianxing was an ephemeral monarchical regime established in modern Yunnan following the violent overthrow of the Dachanghe kingdom in 928. Instigated by the influential military officer Yang Ganzhen, the state placed the high official Zhao Shanzheng upon the throne in the lakeside capital of Dali. Characterised by intense palace factionalism and an acute lack of institutional cohesion, the regime survived barely ten months before Yang Ganzhen deposed Zhao and proclaimed the subsequent state of Dayining in 930. \n\n Status: Sovereign monarchy; Capital: Dali; Common languages: Bai, Nuosu and Middle Chinese; Religion: Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Zhao; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms; Succeeded by: Dayining

name: Caliphate of Córdoba
description: The Caliphate of Cordoba was an illustrious Islamic empire established across al-Andalus when Emir Abd al-Rahman III proclaimed himself caliph on 16 January 929. Governed from the glittering metropolis of Cordoba and the palatine city of Madinat al-Zahra, the realm fostered a dazzling golden age of Mediterranean commerce, scientific learning and architectural splendour. The caliphs unified central and southern Iberia, checked Christian kingdoms in the north and expanded naval influence into North Africa until internal civil strife shattered the polity into regional taifas in 1031. \n\n Status: Sovereign caliphate; Capital: Córdoba; Common languages: Andalusi Arabic, Andalusi Romance and Hebrew; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Theocratic hereditary monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Umayyad; Ruler title: Caliph; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Taifa kingdoms

name: Dayining
description: Dayining was an autonomous kingdom that governed the territory of modern Yunnan during the turbulent aftermath of the collapse of Nanzhao. Established in 930 by the military commander Yang Ganzhen after deposing the ephemeral regime of Datianxing, the monarchy ruled from the historic lakeside citadel of Dali. Facing domestic unpopularity and fierce resistance from neighbouring regional clans, the Yang brothers struggled to maintain political cohesion until Duan Siping led a broad tribal coalition that overthrew Dayining in 937 to found the enduring Dali Kingdom. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Dali; Common languages: Bai, Nuosu and Middle Chinese; Religion: Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Yang; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms; Succeeded by: Dali Kingdom

name: Marca Geronis
description: The Marca Geronis was a sprawling military frontier province established along the eastern borders of the Duchy of Saxony under the command of Margrave Gero. Headquartered at Merseburg, the march served as the vanguard of East Frankish territorial expansion and Christianisation across the lands of the Polabian Slavs. Operating under the royal authority of King Otto I, Gero conducted relentless military campaigns, constructed frontier fortifications and levied tribute on Slavic tribes until his death in 965 led to the division of his massive domain into five distinct border marches. \n\n Status: Vassal march under East Frankish suzerainty; Capital: Merseburg; Common languages: Old High German, Old Saxon, Polabian and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Military march; Ruler title: Margrave; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Succeeded by: March of Meissen and Saxon Eastern March

name: Icelandic Commonwealth
label: norse/viking polities
description: The Icelandic Commonwealth was a unique medieval free state established across the North Atlantic island of Iceland by Norse settlers around 930. Administered without an executive monarchy, public governance was conducted through regional assemblies and the annual Althing held at the volcanic plains of Thingvellir, where chieftains deliberated law and resolved legal disputes. The commonwealth adopted Christianity peacefully at the turn of the eleventh century and produced exceptional skaldic and saga literature before factional clan wars during the Sturlung Era led to Norwegian annexation in 1262. \n\n Status: Sovereign commonwealth; Capital: Thingvellir; Common languages: Old Norse and Old Icelandic; Religion: Old Norse religion and Roman Catholicism; Government: Stateless assembly republic; Legislature: Logretta of the Althing; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Norway

name: Kingdom of Detsugon
label: tibetan era of fragmentation
description: The Kingdom of Detsugon was an autonomous Tibetan principality formed during the Era of Fragmentation following the partition of western Tibetan territories among the royal scions of Kyide Nyimagon. Centred in the upper valleys of western Tibet with historic ties to the spiritual traditions of Lhasa, the realm preserved imperial Yarlung administrative norms amidst regional decentralisation. The monarchy fostered Buddhist revival, supported monastic establishments and maintained trade caravans across high Himalayan passes until political consolidation reintegrated its lands into broader regional western Tibetan polities. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Lhasa; Common languages: Old Tibetan; Religion: Tibetan Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Yarlung; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Tibetan Era of Fragmentation; Preceded by: Tibetan Empire

name: Maryul
label: tibetan era of fragmentation
description: Maryul was a sovereign Himalayan kingdom encompassing Ladakh and adjacent western Tibetan uplands, founded around 930 by Prince Lhachen Palgyigon following the partition of his father's realm. Headquartered initially at Shey and later at Leh, the kingdom commanded vital mountain passes along trans-Himalayan trade routes linking Tibet, Kashmir and Central Asia. Maryul cultivated a distinctive Ladakhi Buddhist culture, sustained monumental fortresses and monasteries, and maintained independent dynastic rule under the Lhachen and Namgyal houses until Dogra forces incorporated the territory into Jammu and Kashmir in 1842. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Shey; Common languages: Ladakhi and Classical Tibetan; Religion: Tibetan Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Lhachen; Ruler title: Gyalpo; Historical era: Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Jammu and Kashmir

name: Purang-Guge Kingdom
label: tibetan era of fragmentation
description: The Purang-Guge Kingdom was an influential western Himalayan realm founded in western Tibet following the political fragmentation of the Yarlung Empire. Governing initially from Purang and later from Tholing in the dramatic Sutlej River canyon, the kingdom became the primary driving force behind the second diffusion of Buddhism across the Tibetan plateau. Under devout monarchs such as King Yeshe-O, the state sponsored scholar-translators, founded magnificent monastic complexes including Tholing and Tabo, and preserved regional autonomy until dividing into separate dynastic branches around the late eleventh century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Burang; Common languages: Old Tibetan; Religion: Tibetan Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Yarlung; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Tibetan Era of Fragmentation; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Guge

name: Ziyarid Dynasty
label: iranian intermezzo
description: The Ziyarid dynasty was an autonomous Iranian ruling house of Gilaki origin that controlled Tabaristan and the Caspian littoral during the Iranian Intermezzo. Founded in 931 by the charismatic general Mardavij, who briefly swept across northern and western Iran with ambitions to revive ancient Sasanian glory, the dynasty later consolidated its court at Gorgan. The Ziyarids engaged in protracted military and diplomatic rivalries with the Buyids and Samanids, fostering a brilliant intellectual court that patronised renowned scholars including al-Biruni before falling under Seljuk suzerainty. \n\n Status: Sovereign monarchy; Capital: Gorgan; Common languages: Persian, Gilaki and Tabari; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Ziyarid; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Nizari Ismaili state

name: Kingdom of Guiyi
label: five dynasties and ten kingdoms - other countries  (chinese history)
description: The Kingdom of Guiyi, historically rooted in the Guiyi Circuit, was an autonomous oasis realm centred at Dunhuang along the Gansu corridor during the Five Dynasties and Northern Song periods. Ruled by the Cao family from 914 onwards, the government pursued diplomatic conciliation with the Ganzhou Uyghurs and Khotan, safeguarding the northern Silk Road caravan networks. The court distinguished itself through lavish patronage of the Mogao Caves and Buddhist translation projects, preserving Chinese literary and administrative institutions until the Tangut Western Xia conquered Dunhuang in 1036. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Dunhuang; Common languages: Middle Chinese, Old Tibetan and Sogdian; Religion: Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Cao; Ruler title: King of Guiyi; Historical era: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms; Succeeded by: Western Xia

name: Banu Ilyas
description: The Banu Ilyas, also known as the Ilyasids, was an autonomous Iranian dynasty of Sogdian origin that governed the province of Kerman from 932 to 968. Established by the former Samanid military commander Muhammad ibn Ilyas, the dynasty established its administrative capital at Bardsir and maintained effective independence amidst the rivalries of the Iranian Intermezzo. Controlling crucial overland trade arteries connecting the Iranian plateau with the Persian Gulf, the principality flourished until intra-dynastic conflicts enabled the expanding Buyid ruler Adud al-Dawla to conquer Kerman. \n\n Status: Sovereign emirate; Capital: Bardsir; Common languages: Persian and Sogdian; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Banu Ilyas; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Buyid dynasty

name: Kingdom of Burgundy
label: holy roman empire
description: The Kingdom of Burgundy, frequently termed the Kingdom of Arles, was a sovereign realm formed in 933 through the unification of Upper and Lower Burgundy under King Rudolph II. Stretching from the Mediterranean coast to the High Rhine and encompassing western Switzerland, the kingdom maintained its primary royal seat at Arles. Governed by the Elder House of Welf until 1032, the realm integrated diverse Provencal, Burgundian and Alemannic territories before being bequeathed to Emperor Conrad II, thereby becoming one of the three constituent kingdoms of the Holy Roman Empire. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Arles; Common languages: Old Occitan, Franco-Provencal and Medieval Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Elder House of Welf; Ruler title: King of Burgundy; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Holy Roman Empire

name: Kingdom of Italy
label: holy roman empire
description: The Kingdom of Italy was a premier post-Carolingian monarchy encompassing northern and central Italy, whose traditional administrative seat and coronation site remained the ancient Lombard capital of Pavia. During the mid-tenth century, indigenous Italian magnates and rival dynasts including Hugh of Arles and Berengar of Ivrea contended fiercely for sovereign control over the realm. German King Otto I intervened decisively in Italian affairs in 951, capturing Pavia and eventually securing imperial coronation at Rome in 962, which permanently incorporated the Italian crown into the Holy Roman Empire. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Pavia; Common languages: Early Italian vernaculars and Medieval Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Elective monarchy; Ruler title: King of Italy; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 934; Succeeded by: Holy Roman Empire

name: Maboum
description: Maboum was an autonomous precolonial polity established in the western highlands and fertile plateau regions of central Cameroon. Governed from its ancestral royal seat at Maboum, the kingdom rested upon a hereditary chieftaincy system supported by council elders, secret societies and traditional agrarian lineage networks. The polity commanded vital regional trading routes connecting the southern forest zone with northern savannah markets, sustaining its political autonomy and indigenous cultural practices across centuries until the consolidation of German colonial administration in the early twentieth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Maboum; Common languages: Grassfields Bantu languages; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Chief; Historical era: Precolonial Africa; Established: 934; Succeeded by: Kamerun

name: Shu
label: five dynasties and ten kingdoms - ten kingdoms  (chinese history)
description: Shu, designated in Chinese historiography as Later Shu, was an autonomous imperial state established in the Sichuan Basin by the military commander Meng Zhixiang in 934. Centred at Chengdu, the realm enjoyed three decades of remarkable political stability, agricultural wealth and vibrant urban culture while northern China was engulfed in war. Under Meng Chang, the kingdom patronised the compilation of renowned lyrical poetry anthologies and expanded regional irrigation networks before being overwhelmed and annexed by the reunifying armies of the Song dynasty in 965. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Chengdu; Common languages: Middle Chinese and Ba-Shu Chinese; Religion: Buddhism, Taoism and Confucianism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Meng; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms; Succeeded by: Song dynasty

name: Buyid Dynasty
label: iranian intermezzo
description: The Buyid dynasty was an influential Shia confederation of Daylamite origin that dominated southern and central Iran alongside Iraq during the Iranian Intermezzo. Founded by Ali ibn Buya and his brothers, who established regional courts at Shiraz, Ray and Baghdad, the dynasty took control of the Abbasid capital in 945 and reduced the caliphs to figureheads. Reviving ancient Sasanian imperial traditions and adopting the title of Shahanshah, the Buyids presided over an era of profound cultural brilliance, philosophical inquiry and urban reconstruction until Seljuk conquests in the mid-eleventh century. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Shiraz and Baghdad; Common languages: Arabic, Persian and Daylami; Religion: Shia Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Buyid; Ruler title: Shahanshah; Historical era: Islamic Golden Age; Succeeded by: Seljuk Empire

name: Billung March
description: The Billung March was an essential frontier territory situated across the northeastern borders of the Duchy of Saxony, established by King Otto I under the military command of Margrave Hermann Billung. Governed from regional fortifications including Luneburg, the march was charged with safeguarding the lower Elbe frontier and levying tribute upon the Obotrite confederation and neighbouring Polabian Slavic groups. Billung wielded broad military authority on behalf of the East Frankish crown, fostering regional security and church foundations until the Slavic uprising of 983 permanently disrupted German border control. \n\n Status: Vassal march under East Frankish suzerainty; Capital: Luneburg; Common languages: Old Saxon, Polabian and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Military march; Ruling dynasty: House of Billung; Ruler title: Margrave; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Preceded by: Duchy of Saxony

name: Ikhshidid Dynasty
description: The Ikhshidid dynasty was an autonomous princely realm established in Egypt and parts of the Levant by the Turkic military commander Muhammad ibn Tughj al-Ikhshid in 935. Operating from the administrative seat of Fustat, the rulers governed as hereditary viceroys under nominal Abbasid caliphal suzerainty, maintaining internal fiscal independence while extending their dominion over the holy cities of Mecca and Medina. The dynasty successfully repelled Fatimid naval and land assaults for over three decades until the regent Abu al-Misk Kafur died, enabling Fatimid forces to conquer Fustat in 969. \n\n Status: Vassal emirate under Abbasid suzerainty; Capital: Fustat; Common languages: Arabic and Coptic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Ikhshidid; Ruler title: Wali; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Fatimid Caliphate

name: Jin
label: five dynasties and ten kingdoms - five dynasties (chinese history)
description: Jin, known in historiography as the Later Jin, was an imperial Chinese dynasty established in 936 by the Shatuo general Shi Jingtang with crucial military support from the Khitan Liao Empire. Headquartered at Kaifeng, Shi Jingtang ruled as a subordinate vassal to the Liao monarch, formally styling himself an imperial son and ceding the strategic Sixteen Prefectures along the northern frontier. Despite widespread domestic resentment against Khitan hegemony, the regime maintained tributary compliance and administrative control across the Yellow River basin until Shi Jingtang died in 942. \n\n Status: Vassal empire under Liao dynasty suzerainty; Capital: Kaifeng; Common languages: Middle Chinese and Shatuo Turkic; Religion: Buddhism, Taoism and Confucianism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Shi; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms; Succeeded by: Later Jin

name: Dali Kingdom
description: The Dali Kingdom was an autonomous Bai-led monarchy established in southwestern China across the fertile valleys of modern Yunnan. Founded by Duan Siping in 937 following the overthrow of the short-lived Dayining regime, the state governed from its magnificent lakeside capital at Yangjumie. The kingdom maintained harmonious tributary relations with the Song dynasty, fostered esoteric Azali Buddhist traditions and constructed renowned architectural monuments including the Three Pagodas, sustaining its regional independence until the Mongol conquest of 1253. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Yangjumie; Common languages: Bai and Classical Chinese; Religion: Esoteric Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Duan; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Mongol Empire

name: Tang
label: five dynasties and ten kingdoms - ten kingdoms  (chinese history)
description: Tang, recognised historically as the Southern Tang, was a prominent Chinese realm founded in 937 by Li Bian following his usurpation of the Wu kingdom. Administered from the cultural metropolis of Jinling, the dynasty claimed direct descent from the glorious Tang imperial house and promoted peaceful agricultural rehabilitation alongside maritime commerce. The state expanded rapidly by annexing the kingdoms of Min and Chu, presiding over an illustrious literary and artistic renaissance until mounting military pressure from the Northern Song extinguished the dynasty in 975. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Jinling; Common languages: Middle Chinese; Religion: Buddhism, Taoism and Confucianism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Li; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms; Succeeded by: Northern Song dynasty

name: Ngô Dynasty
description: The Ngo dynasty was an independent Vietnamese monarchy founded by Ngo Quyen following his decisive naval triumph over the Southern Han fleet at the Bach Dang River in 938. Establishing his royal seat at the ancient citadel of Co Loa, Ngo Quyen ended nearly a millennium of Chinese imperial domination and laid the institutional groundwork for autonomous Vietnamese statehood. Following his death, the realm fractured into violent regional civil conflict known as the Anarchy of the Twelve Warlords, until national reunification was achieved under the Dinh dynasty. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Co Loa; Common languages: Old Vietnamese and Middle Chinese; Religion: Vietnamese folk religion and Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Ngo; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Medieval Asia; Succeeded by: Anarchy of the Twelve Warlords

name: Tamna
description: Tamna was an insular maritime realm encompassing Jeju Island that maintained autonomous internal self-governance while acknowledging the suzerainty of the Goryeo dynasty from 938 onwards. Governed by hereditary local dynasties including the Go and Moon clans from its primary settlement at Jeju, the kingdom retained distinct cultural traditions, maritime trading networks and island livestock husbandry. Tamna rendered regular tribute and naval assistance to the Goryeo court throughout the medieval era until the newly founded Joseon dynasty dissolved its regional autonomy and absorbed the island in 1404. \n\n Status: Vassal kingdom under Goryeo suzerainty; Capital: Jeju City; Common languages: Tamna and Middle Korean; Religion: Shamanism and Buddhism; Government: Autonomous principality; Ruler title: Seongju; Historical era: Middle Ages; Disestablished: 1404; Succeeded by: Joseon

name: Jin
label: five dynasties and ten kingdoms - five dynasties (chinese history)
description: Jin, functioning during its final sovereign phase as the Later Jin dynasty, renounced its former tributary vassalage to the Khitan Liao Empire following the accession of Emperor Shi Chonggui in July 942. Governing northern China from Kaifeng, the monarch adopted a defiant stance towards the Khitan court, declaring himself an imperial grandson rather than an obedient subject. This assertion of complete sovereignty provoked massive Liao punitive invasions that ravaged the Central Plains, culminating in the sack of Kaifeng and the overthrow of the dynasty in January 947. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Kaifeng; Common languages: Middle Chinese and Shatuo Turkic; Religion: Buddhism, Confucianism and Taoism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Shi; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms; Succeeded by: Liao dynasty and Later Han

name: Chaulukya Dynasty
description: The Chaulukya dynasty, also designated as the Solankis of Gujarat, was a powerful Rajput realm that governed substantial portions of modern Gujarat and Rajasthan. Established around 940 by King Mularaja with its royal court at Anahilavada, the dynasty commanded profitable Arabian Sea maritime trade ports and rich agricultural plains. The monarchs repelled regional rivals and sponsored exceptional architectural monuments, including magnificent stepwells and Jain temple complexes, maintaining sovereign authority across northwestern India until being supplanted by their Vaghela feudatories in the thirteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Anahilavada; Common languages: Sanskrit and Old Gujarati; Religion: Hinduism and Jainism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Chaulukya; Ruler title: Maharajadhiraja; Historical era: Medieval India; Succeeded by: Vaghela dynasty

name: Duchy of Brittany
label: celtic polities of brittany;celtic polities
description: The Duchy of Brittany was a semi-autonomous Celtic feudal realm reconstituted in the northwestern peninsula of France after the expulsion of Scandinavian invaders. Following the liberation campaigns of Duke Alan Twistedbeard, the Breton ruler rendered formal feudal homage to King Louis IV of West Francia in the early 940s, placing the realm under royal Frankish suzerainty. Operating from aristocratic centres including Rennes and Nantes, the dukes maintained distinctive Breton legal traditions and regional autonomy while defending their eastern marches against expanding Norman influence. \n\n Status: Feudal duchy under West Frankish suzerainty; Capital: Rennes and Nantes; Common languages: Breton, Gallo and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Nantes; Ruler title: Duke of Brittany; Historical era: Early Middle Ages

name: Great Yin
label: five dynasties and ten kingdoms - ten kingdoms  (chinese history)
description: Great Yin was a brief imperial splinter state established in northern Fujian during the violent dynastic dissolution of the Min Kingdom. Proclaimed in 943 by Wang Yanzheng from his fortified power base at Jianzhou, the regime asserted imperial status in direct opposition to rival relatives holding the court at Fuzhou. After his brother was assassinated in 945, Wang Yanzheng assumed the broader Min crown and reintegrated his territory, bringing an abrupt end to Yin as a distinct polity shortly before Southern Tang armies invaded the region. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Jianzhou; Common languages: Middle Chinese and Medieval Min; Religion: Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Wang; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms; Succeeded by: Min

name: Han
label: five dynasties and ten kingdoms - five dynasties (chinese history)
description: Han, known in historiography as the Later Han, was an imperial Chinese dynasty established in 947 by the Shatuo military commander Liu Zhiyuan following the sudden withdrawal of Khitan forces from northern China. Headquartered at Luoyang and Kaifeng, the state represented the fourth of the Five Dynasties, asserting royal legitimacy over the turbulent Central Plains. Plagued by chronic court paranoia and severe conflict between juvenile emperors and senior military commanders, the short-lived regime collapsed in 951 when General Guo Wei mutinied and established the Later Zhou. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Luoyang; Common languages: Middle Chinese and Shatuo Turkic; Religion: Buddhism, Confucianism and Taoism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Liu; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms; Succeeded by: Later Zhou

name: Kingdom of Northumbria
label: saxon polities in britain
description: The Kingdom of Northumbria experienced a dramatic final revival of Scandinavian sovereign independence when the exiled Norwegian ruler Eric Bloodaxe seized royal power at York. Governing northern England between the Humber and the Scottish border, Eric rallied Norse-Gaelic and Anglo-Danish settlers to defy the expanding hegemony of the English House of Wessex. His turbulent reign was characterised by fierce factional conflicts against rival Northumbrian magnates and southern armies until Eric was ambushed and slain at Stainmore in 954, permanently extinguishing Northumbria as an independent realm. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: York; Common languages: Old Norse and Old English; Religion: Norse paganism and Roman Catholicism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Fairhair; Ruler title: King of Northumbria; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Disestablished: 954; Succeeded by: Kingdom of England

name: Emirate of Sicily
description: The Emirate of Sicily was a flourishing Islamic maritime power that governed the central Mediterranean island of Sicily under the hereditary rule of the Kalbid dynasty. Centred at the cosmopolitan capital of Palermo, the emirate developed a remarkably sophisticated agrarian and urban civilisation characterised by extensive irrigation canal works, lucrative international commerce and harmonious Arab-Byzantine architectural traditions. Sicilian fleets projected naval influence across southern Italy and the Mediterranean until dynastic fragmentation in the eleventh century exposed the emirate to progressive Norman conquest. \n\n Status: Sovereign emirate; Capital: Palermo; Common languages: Sicilian Arabic, Byzantine Greek and Sicilian; Religion: Sunni Islam, Shia Islam and Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Kalbid; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: Middle Ages; Succeeded by: County of Sicily

name: Paramara Dynasty
description: The Paramara dynasty was a sovereign Rajput monarchy that governed the fertile Malwa plateau of west-central India from the mid-tenth century onwards. Rising from feudatory status under King Siyaka, who sacked the Rashtrakuta capital to secure sovereign independence, the dynasty established its royal court at Dhara. The realm reached its zenith under King Bhoja, renowned across the subcontinent for profound polymath scholarship, educational endowments and monumental temple construction, maintaining regional power until suffering eventual conquest by the Delhi Sultanate in the early fourteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Dhara; Common languages: Sanskrit and Prakrit; Religion: Shaivism and Jainism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Paramara; Ruler title: Maharajadhiraja; Historical era: Medieval India; Succeeded by: Delhi Sultanate

name: Qingyuan Circuit
label: five dynasties and ten kingdoms - other countries  (chinese history)
description: The Qingyuan Circuit, later renamed Pinghai, was an autonomous maritime military commandery that governed southern Fujian during the Five Dynasties and early Song eras. Established in 949 under the local warlord Liu Congxiao with its administrative seat at Quanzhou, the circuit maintained de facto independence while tendering nominal diplomatic submission to northern courts. The regime revitalised overseas trade networks with Southeast Asia and expanded harbour facilities until its final military governor, Chen Hongjin, peacefully surrendered his territory to Emperor Taizong of Song in 978. \n\n Status: Autonomous military circuit; Capital: Quanzhou; Common languages: Middle Chinese and Medieval Min; Religion: Buddhism; Government: Military commandery; Ruler title: Jiedushi; Historical era: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms; Established: 949; Disestablished: 978; Succeeded by: Northern Song dynasty

name: Chahamanas of Naddula
description: The Chahamanas of Naddula, known also as the Chauhans of Nadol, were an autonomous Rajput dynasty that ruled the Marwar region of southern Rajasthan. Founded around 950 by Prince Lakshmana as a cadet branch of the Shakambhari royal house, the kingdom established its administrative stronghold at Naddula. The dynasty defended its desert frontier against incursions from the Ghaznavids and engaged in fierce regional conflicts with neighbouring Chaulukya and Paramara monarchs until Ghurid forces under Qutb al-Din Aibak overwhelmed the kingdom in 1197. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Naddula; Common languages: Sanskrit and Old Rajasthani; Religion: Hinduism and Jainism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Chahamana; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Medieval India; Succeeded by: Ghurid dynasty

name: Chahamanas of Shakambhari
description: The Chahamanas of Shakambhari were a prominent sovereign Rajput dynasty that governed the historic territory of Sapadalaksha in modern Rajasthan. Having discarded their vassalage to the Gurjara-Pratiharas during the tenth century under Simharaja, the monarchs initially ruled from Shakambhari before King Ajayaraja II established Ajayameru as their fortified capital. The kingdom reached extensive power across northern India, successfully confronting Chaulukya and Tomara rivals until King Prithviraja III was defeated by the invading Ghurid army at the second Battle of Tarain in 1192. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Shakambhari and Ajayameru; Common languages: Sanskrit and Old Rajasthani; Religion: Hinduism and Jainism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Chahamana; Ruler title: Maharajadhiraja; Historical era: Medieval India; Succeeded by: Ghurid dynasty

name: County of Provence
label: holy roman empire
description: The County of Provence was an autonomous feudal principality situated along the lower Rhone River and Mediterranean coastline of southeastern France. Originating in the mid-tenth century under Count Boson II with its capital at Aix-en-Provence, the county exercised de facto sovereign authority while maintaining nominal ties to the Kingdom of Arles. The counts repelled Saracen raiders from their alpine strongholds, fostered thriving Mediterranean maritime trade and patronised early troubadour culture before dynastic matrimonial alliances transferred the territory to the Crown of Aragon in the twelfth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign county; Capital: Aix-en-Provence; Common languages: Old Occitan and Medieval Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Provence; Ruler title: Count of Provence; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Crown of Aragon

name: Emirate of Multan
description: The Emirate of Multan was a sovereign Islamic state centred upon the historic oasis city of Multan along the Chenab River in southern Punjab. Originally governed by the Arab Banu Munabbih clan, the realm was transformed in the mid-tenth century when Ismaili missionaries established a prosperous Qarmatian theocracy allied with the Fatimid Caliphate. The emirate derived immense wealth from controlling northern Indian commercial trade arteries and pilgrim revenues from the ancient Sun Temple until Sultan Mahmud of Ghazni invaded the region and annexed Multan in 1006. \n\n Status: Sovereign emirate; Capital: Multan; Common languages: Arabic, Sindhi and Saraiki; Religion: Ismaili Shia Islam; Government: Theocratic monarchy; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 951; Disestablished: 1006; Succeeded by: Ghaznavid Empire

name: Jämtland
description: Jamtland was an autonomous peasant commonwealth established across the forested lakes and central valleys of the Scandinavian interior around Lake Storsjon. Operating without a crowned monarch, the free farmers managed collective political affairs, administered justice and resolved communal disputes through their annual parliamentary assembly, the Jamtamot. The community maintained its own legal customs, traded furs and iron with neighbouring Norwegian and Swedish territories and preserved sovereign self-rule until King Sverre of Norway defeated the Jamtish forces in battle in 1178 and imposed royal taxation. \n\n Status: Sovereign peasant commonwealth; Capital: Froson; Common languages: Old Jamtish and Old Norse; Religion: Norse paganism and Roman Catholicism; Government: Assembly republic; Legislature: Jamtamot; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Norway

name: Lordship of Cuzcatlán
label: mesoamerican polities
description: The Lordship of Cuzcatlan was a sovereign Nahua state confederation established across western and central El Salvador between the Paz and Lempa rivers. Founded by migratory Pipil populations originating from the Toltec cultural sphere of central Mexico, the polity governed from its primary urban settlement of Cuzcatlan. The confederation commanded fertile volcanic soils, produced valuable cacao and cotton harvests and maintained formidable military alliances that fiercely resisted Spanish invasion under Pedro de Alvarado in 1524 until subjugated by colonial expeditionary forces in 1526. \n\n Status: Sovereign confederation; Capital: Cuzcatlan; Common languages: Nawat; Religion: Mesoamerican polytheism; Government: Tributary monarchy; Ruler title: Tagatecu; Historical era: Postclassic Mesoamerica; Disestablished: 1526; Succeeded by: New Spain

name: Zhou
label: five dynasties and ten kingdoms - five dynasties (chinese history)
description: Zhou, designated in historiography as the Later Zhou, was an imperial Chinese dynasty founded by the military commander Guo Wei following his overthrow of the Later Han in 951. Headquartered at Kaifeng, the state was the final of the Five Dynasties and underwent sweeping administrative, agrarian and fiscal restructuring under Emperor Shizong. Through disciplined professional armies, the dynasty reconquered northern frontier zones and compelled the Southern Tang to cede vital riverine territories, providing the stable political and military foundation for the rise of the Northern Song in 960. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Kaifeng; Common languages: Middle Chinese; Religion: Confucianism, Taoism and Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Guo; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms; Succeeded by: Northern Song dynasty

name: Han
label: five dynasties and ten kingdoms - ten kingdoms  (chinese history)
description: Han, known in Chinese history as the Northern Han, was an autonomous splinter regime established in modern Shanxi by Liu Min following the collapse of the Later Han in 951. Governed from the fortified northern stronghold of Taiyuan, the state relied upon crucial military protection and diplomatic patronage from the Khitan Liao Empire to resist conquest by the Later Zhou. Despite its harsh mountain terrain and depleted agricultural resources, the kingdom held out as the last of the Ten Kingdoms until Emperor Taizong of Song finally conquered Taiyuan in 979. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Taiyuan; Common languages: Middle Chinese and Shatuo Turkic; Religion: Buddhism, Taoism and Confucianism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Liu; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms; Succeeded by: Northern Song dynasty

name: Shaddadids
label: kurdish principalities;iranian intermezzo
description: The Shaddadids were a sovereign Kurdish Muslim dynasty that governed Arran and eastern Armenia during the Iranian Intermezzo. Originating at Dvin before establishing their primary administrative capital at Ganja, the dynasty exercised paramount authority across the fertile plains between the Kura and Aras rivers. The Shaddadid emirs intermarried with the Armenian Bagratuni royal house, defended their borders against Byzantine expansion and repelled Caspian Rus raids before internal succession disputes compelled them to acknowledge the suzerainty of the Seljuk Empire in 1075. \n\n Status: Sovereign emirate; Capital: Ganja; Common languages: Persian, Kurdish and Armenian; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Shaddadid; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Seljuk Empire

name: Wuping Circuit
label: five dynasties and ten kingdoms - ten kingdoms  (chinese history)
description: The Wuping Circuit was an autonomous Chinese military regime centred at Langzhou in modern Hunan following the collapse of the Kingdom of Chu. Established when local commanders led by Liu Yan and Zhou Xingfeng expelled occupying Southern Tang forces, the circuit restored regional stability across the Xiang River basin. The military governors promoted domestic reconstruction, suppressed regional banditry and maintained de facto sovereignty over southern agrarian communities until civil strife following Zhou Xingfeng's death enabled the invading Song dynasty to annex the circuit in 963. \n\n Status: Autonomous military circuit; Capital: Langzhou; Common languages: Middle Chinese and Medieval Xiang; Religion: Buddhism and Taoism; Government: Military commandery; Ruler title: Jiedushi; Historical era: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms; Succeeded by: Song dynasty

name: Duchy of Amalfi
label: maritime republics;byzantine successors in southern italy
description: The Duchy of Amalfi was a pioneering Italian maritime republic that flourished along the steep coastal cliffs of the Gulf of Salerno. Having shaken off Byzantine administrative oversight, the citizens elected Mastalus II as their first duke in 958, consolidating sovereign municipal institutions and codifying advanced maritime jurisprudence in the Tavole Amalfitane. Amalfitan merchants established thriving commercial quarters across the Levant, Egypt and Constantinople, accumulating tremendous commercial wealth until aggressive Norman expansion under Robert Guiscard extinguished the republic's independence in 1073. \n\n Status: Sovereign maritime republic; Capital: Amalfi; Common languages: Early Italian, Neapolitan and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Elective duchy; Ruler title: Duke; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 958; Disestablished: 1073; Succeeded by: Norman County of Apulia

name: Rawadid Dynasty
label: iranian intermezzo
description: The Rawadid dynasty was an autonomous ruling house of Arab origin that became culturally Kurdicised while governing Azerbaijan and portions of southern Armenia. Operating from their capital at Tabriz, the Rawadids supplanted the declining Sallarid dynasty in the mid-tenth century and established firm control over lucrative trade routes crossing northwestern Iran. The emirs patronised Persian court poetry, fortified key regional mountain strongholds and successfully defended their frontiers against neighbouring Daylami and Byzantine armies until submitting to the expanding Great Seljuk Empire in 1054. \n\n Status: Sovereign emirate; Capital: Tabriz; Common languages: Persian, Kurdish and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rawadid; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Seljuk Empire

name: Song
description: Song was a Chinese imperial dynasty founded on 4 February 960 when General Zhao Kuangyin was proclaimed Emperor Taizu following a bloodless military mutiny at Chenqiao. Governed initially from the vast metropolis of Kaifeng and later from Hangzhou as the Southern Song, the empire brought an end to the chaotic Five Dynasties period by systematically reunifying southern China. Celebrated for pioneering paper currency, technological innovations and flourishing neo-Confucian scholarship, the dynasty sustained an extraordinary demographic and economic expansion until falling to the Mongol Yuan dynasty. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Kaifeng; Common languages: Middle Chinese; Religion: Buddhism, Taoism and Confucianism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Zhao; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Post-classical; Succeeded by: Yuan dynasty

name: Duchy of Poland
description: The Duchy of Poland was an early medieval Western Slavic realm established across the basins of the Warta and Vistula rivers under the Piast dynasty. Administered from royal strongholds at Gniezno and Poznan, Duke Mieszko I consolidated diverse Lechitic tribes into a unified state and embraced Latin Christianity in 966. This baptism integrated Poland into Western Christendom, enabling Mieszko and his successor Boleslaw the Brave to expand sovereign borders against Saxon and Bohemian rivals until Boleslaw was formally crowned king in 1025. \n\n Status: Sovereign duchy; Capital: Gniezno; Common languages: Old Polish and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Piast; Ruler title: Duke; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Poland

name: Kingdom of Denmark
description: The Kingdom of Denmark emerged as a unified Scandinavian realm in the tenth century under King Harald Bluetooth of the House of Jelling. Headquartered initially at Jelling and subsequently at Roskilde, the kingdom united the Jutland peninsula with the Danish archipelago and southern Scandinavian coastal territories. Harald erected formidable circular ring fortresses, consolidated royal administration and formally converted the Danes to Christianity, establishing a powerful maritime state that projected naval authority across the Baltic Sea and laid the foundations for the North Sea Empire. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Jelling; Common languages: Old Norse and Old Danish; Religion: Norse paganism and Roman Catholicism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Jelling; Ruler title: King of Denmark; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 960

name: Hasanwayhid Emirate
label: kurdish principalities;iranian intermezzo
description: The Hasanwayhid Emirate was an autonomous Kurdish principality that governed the rugged mountainous territories of Jibal in western Iran from 959 to 1015. Founded by the Kurdish chieftain Hasanwayh ibn Husayn with his fortress capital at Sarmaj near Dinavar, the dynasty adhered to Twelver Shia Islam and adroitly balanced relations with neighbouring Buyid rulers. Controlling major caravan passes through the Zagros Mountains, the emirs accumulated significant wealth, built extensive bridges and maintained internal stability until dynastic disputes enabled the rival Annazids to supplant their rule. \n\n Status: Sovereign emirate; Capital: Sarmaj; Common languages: Kurdish and Persian; Religion: Twelver Shia Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Hasanwayhid; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Annazids

name: Abbey of Saint Blaise
label: holy roman empire
description: The Abbey of Saint Blaise was an ecclesiastical territory in the southern Black Forest that possessed imperial immediacy within the Holy Roman Empire from 962 onwards. Governed by a Benedictine prince-abbot from the monastic complex at Saint Blasien, the abbey exercised sovereign temporal jurisdiction over surrounding valleys, timber forests and agricultural holdings in Swabia. Supported by imperial privileges and aristocratic patrons, the monastery flourished as an influential centre of monastic reform, religious scholarship and rural economic management throughout the high and late medieval periods. \n\n Status: Imperial abbey of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Saint Blasien; Common languages: Middle High German, Alemannic and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Ecclesiastical principality; Ruler title: Prince-Abbot; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 962; Disestablished: 1379

name: Abbey of Saint-Hubert
label: holy roman empire
description: The Abbey of Saint-Hubert was a sovereign ecclesiastical territory situated in the dense Ardennes forest of present-day Belgium, exercising imperial immediacy within the Holy Roman Empire. Centred upon the historic Benedictine monastery dedicated to Saint Hubert, the abbey held extensive feudal manors, forest jurisdictions and judicial rights across the Meuse borderlands. Pilgrims flocked to the abbey shrine for spiritual intercession, generating revenue that sustained monastic autonomy against encroaching regional counts until revolutionary French forces suppressed the institution and annexed its lands in the late eighteenth century. \n\n Status: Imperial abbey of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Saint-Hubert; Common languages: Walloon, French and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Ecclesiastical principality; Ruler title: Prince-Abbot; Historical era: Middle Ages to Early Modern; Succeeded by: French First Republic

name: Archbishopric of Mainz
label: holy roman empire
description: The Archbishopric of Mainz was a pre-eminent ecclesiastical principality of the Holy Roman Empire, whose prince-archbishops held the prestigious status of Archchancellor of Germany and premier imperial elector. Headquartered at the cathedral city of Mainz along the Rhine, the territory comprised discontinuous swathes of land spanning Franconia, the Rhineland and Hesse. The archbishops exercised paramount political influence over imperial elections and diets, presiding as primates of Germany and acting as essential constitutional arbiters between the emperor and the Imperial Estates until the dissolution of the electorate in 1803. \n\n Status: Ecclesiastical principality and electorate; Capital: Mainz; Common languages: German and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Ecclesiastical elective monarchy; Ruler title: Prince-Elector and Archbishop; Historical era: Middle Ages to Early Modern; Established: 780; Disestablished: 1803

name: Archbishopric of Trier
label: holy roman empire
description: The Archbishopric of Trier was a venerable ecclesiastical principality and electorate within the Holy Roman Empire, originating from an ancient Roman episcopal see along the Moselle River. Governed from Trier and subsequently Koblenz, the prince-archbishops served as hereditary archchancellors of Burgundy and wielded one of the three ecclesiastical votes in the imperial electoral college. The state commanded strategic river valleys and fortified castles throughout the Rhineland, preserving its sovereign constitutional rights through centuries of European warfare until French revolutionary annexation in the late eighteenth century. \n\n Status: Ecclesiastical principality and electorate; Capital: Trier and Koblenz; Common languages: German and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Ecclesiastical elective monarchy; Ruler title: Prince-Elector and Archbishop; Historical era: Middle Ages to Early Modern; Established: 962; Disestablished: 1803

name: Billung March
label: holy roman empire
description: The Billung March was an imperial frontier command situated northeast of the Elbe River, established within the Holy Roman Empire to protect Saxon borders and subjugate the Polabian Slavs. Administered by Margrave Hermann Billung and his successors, the territory enforced German imperial authority, established bishoprics and collected tribute from the Obotrite and Wagrian tribal confederacies. The march retained significant operational autonomy as a vital military bulwark of the Ottonian realm until the widespread Slavic insurrection of 983 overran German garrisons and dissolved effective frontier governance. \n\n Status: Imperial frontier march; Capital: Luneburg; Common languages: Old Saxon, Polabian and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Military march; Ruling dynasty: House of Billung; Ruler title: Margrave; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Preceded by: Duchy of Saxony

name: Bormio
label: holy roman empire
description: Bormio was an autonomous alpine community and county situated in the upper Valtellina valley of the central Alps within the Holy Roman Empire. Headquartered at the fortified market town of Bormio, the local municipality exercised self-governance and judicial privileges confirmed by imperial charters. The territory derived strategic and economic significance from controlling crucial alpine transit routes, including mountain passes connecting Lombardy with the Engadin and Tyrol, sustaining its municipal liberties against neighbouring feudal lords until being absorbed into broader regional Lombard confederations in the fourteenth century. \n\n Status: Autonomous imperial county; Capital: Bormio; Common languages: Lombard, Romansh and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Municipal county; Ruler title: Podesta; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 962; Disestablished: 1301

name: County of Bouillon
label: holy roman empire
description: The County of Bouillon was an autonomous feudal estate in the Ardennes region of modern Belgium that possessed imperial immediacy within the Holy Roman Empire from 962. Centred upon the formidable promontory fortress of Bouillon Castle over the Semois River, the lordship formed the ancestral patrimony of the illustrious House of Ardennes. Its most celebrated lord, Godfrey of Bouillon, pledged the estate to the Prince-Bishopric of Liege in 1095 to finance his leadership of the First Crusade, after which the territory became a distinct ducal apanage. \n\n Status: Imperial county of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Bouillon; Common languages: Walloon, Old French and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal lordship; Ruling dynasty: House of Ardennes; Ruler title: Count of Bouillon; Historical era: Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Prince-Bishopric of Liège

name: County of Ceccano
label: holy roman empire
description: The County of Ceccano was an autonomous feudal lordship situated in the Sacco River valley of southern Lazio that held imperial immediacy within the Holy Roman Empire from 962. Governed by the counts of the de Ceccano lineage from their hilltop fortress of Ceccano, the county maintained strategic control over the inland corridors linking Rome with southern Italy. Fiercely jealous of their political autonomy, the counts frequently allied with imperial forces against encroaching papal authority, preserving their local seigneurial privileges and castles until the mid-fifteenth century. \n\n Status: Imperial county of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Ceccano; Common languages: Early Italian, Central Italian dialects and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal lordship; Ruling dynasty: De Ceccano; Ruler title: Count of Ceccano; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 962; Disestablished: 1451

name: County of Dillingen
label: holy roman empire
description: The County of Dillingen was a sovereign feudal territory situated along the upper Danube River in Swabia that enjoyed imperial immediacy within the Holy Roman Empire from 962. Headquartered at the fortified castle town of Dillingen, the counts of Dillingen were influential magnates closely linked to the bishoprics of Augsburg and Constance, counting Saint Ulrich among their celebrated lineage. The dynasty administered extensive agricultural estates and market towns across northern Swabia until the direct comital lineage became extinct in 1258, whereupon their domains were partitioned between the Bishopric of Augsburg and the House of Wittelsbach. \n\n Status: Imperial county of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Dillingen; Common languages: Middle High German, Swabian and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Dillingen; Ruler title: Count of Dillingen; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Bishopric of Augsburg

name: County of Geneva
label: holy roman empire
description: The County of Geneva was an autonomous feudal state established around Lake Geneva and the surrounding Prealps, holding imperial status within the Holy Roman Empire. Governed by the hereditary House of Geneva from regional strongholds including La Roche and Annecy, the counts exercised seigneurial jurisdiction over the Genevois plateau while contesting temporal authority over Geneva with the local prince-bishops. The county preserved its judicial independence and alpine toll revenues through centuries of territorial rivalry until its dynastic extinction in 1401 led to its sale and incorporation into the rising County of Savoy. \n\n Status: Imperial county of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Annecy; Common languages: Franco-Provencal, Old French and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Geneva; Ruler title: Count of Geneva; Historical era: Middle Ages; Succeeded by: County of Savoy

name: County of Hainaut

name: Prince-Bishopric of Chur
label: holy roman empire

Originating from the ancient Roman province of Raetia Curiensis, the bishops were invested with imperial immediacy and comital rights by Ottonian and Salian monarchs to control strategic transalpine transit passes like the Septimer and Julier.
