name: Prince-Bishopric of Eichstätt
label: holy roman empire
description: The Prince-Bishopric of Eichstätt was a compact ecclesiastical principality of the Holy Roman Empire located in central Bavaria along the Altmühl river. Elevated to imperial immediacy by medieval emperors, the prince-bishops combined episcopal governance with territorial administration from their residence at Willibaldsburg. The principality suffered extensive devastation during the Thirty Years' War but rebuilt into an exquisite baroque residential state, which persevered within the Franconian Circle until its secularisation and annexation to the Electorate of Bavaria in 1802. \n\n Status: Ecclesiastical principality of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Eichstätt; Common languages: East Franconian, Bavarian and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Ecclesiastical principality; Ruler title: Prince-Bishop; Historical era: Middle Ages to Early Modern; Disestablished: 1802; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Bavaria

name: Prince-Bishopric of Freising
label: holy roman empire
description: The Prince-Bishopric of Freising was an ecclesiastical state of the Holy Roman Empire centred on the cathedral hill of Freising north of Munich along the Isar river. Over the course of the Middle Ages, the bishops acquired imperial immediacy and assembled a fragmented network of territorial enclaves across Upper Bavaria, Tyrol and Carniola, including Garmisch-Partenkirchen and Innichen. The prince-bishops retained their secular sovereignty and cultural prominence as an imperial estate of the Bavarian Circle until the realm was mediatised and absorbed by the Kingdom of Bavaria in 1802. \n\n Status: Ecclesiastical principality of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Freising; Common languages: Central Bavarian and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Ecclesiastical principality; Ruler title: Prince-Bishop; Historical era: Middle Ages to Early Modern; Disestablished: 1802; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Bavaria

name: Prince-Bishopric of Verdun
label: holy roman empire
description: The Prince-Bishopric of Verdun was an ecclesiastical state of the Holy Roman Empire occupying a strategic reach of the Meuse river in Upper Lorraine. Granted imperial immediacy and comital rights over the County of Verdun by Emperor Otto III in 997, the prince-bishops defended their autonomous jurisdiction amidst border conflicts with neighbouring Lorraine, Bar and France. Imperial authority over Verdun came to an effective end in 1552 when French troops under King Henry II occupied the city, formalising the annexation of the Three Bishoprics under the Peace of Westphalia. \n\n Status: Ecclesiastical principality of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Verdun; Common languages: Lorrain, French and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Ecclesiastical principality; Ruler title: Prince-Bishop; Historical era: Middle Ages to Early Modern; Established: 997; Disestablished: 1552; Succeeded by: Three Bishoprics

name: Princely Abbey of Stavelot-Malmedy
label: holy roman empire
description: The Princely Abbey of Stavelot-Malmedy was a sovereign ecclesiastical principality of the Holy Roman Empire situated in the Ardennes forest of the southern Low Countries. Formed around a double Benedictine foundation established in 651, the prince-abbot held imperial immediacy and sat on the Ecclesiastical Bench of the Imperial Diet with a full vote alongside prince-bishops. The principality preserved its autonomy within the Lower Rhenish-Westphalian Circle until French revolutionary forces overran the Ardennes in 1795, abolishing monastic secular rule and annexing the territory into the department of Ourthe. \n\n Status: Ecclesiastical principality of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Malmedy; Common languages: Walloon, German, French and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Ecclesiastical principality; Ruler title: Prince-Abbot; Historical era: Middle Ages to Early Modern; Established: 651; Disestablished: 1795; Succeeded by: French First Republic

name: Rani Tribes
description: The Rani Tribes were a seafaring West Slavic tribal confederacy inhabiting the island of Rügen and the adjacent Baltic shoreline across the Strelasund. Renowned for their formidable naval power and unyielding adherence to Slavic paganism, the Rani centred their religious life and governance on the fortified sanctuary of Svantevit at Cape Arkona and their princely stronghold at Charenza. The Rani resisted Saxon and Danish Christian expansion for centuries until King Valdemar I of Denmark conquered Arkona in 1168, destroying the pagan idols and subordinating the island as the Christian Principality of Rügen. \n\n Status: West Slavic pagan tribal principality; Capital: None (decentralised); Administrative seat: Charenza; Common languages: Rani dialect of Polabian; Religion: Slavic paganism; Government: Theocratic tribal principality; Historical era: Early Middle Ages to High Middle Ages; Disestablished: 1168; Succeeded by: Principality of Rügen

name: Slavic Tribes
description: The Slavic Tribes comprised a broad continuum of Polabian and Pomeranian tribal communities inhabiting the river valleys and forests between the middle Elbe, Oder and Vistula. Lacking a centralised monarchical authority, these tribes organised themselves into local territorial clans governed by elected elders, clan councils and seasonal religious assemblies. Despite intense pressure from German eastward colonisation and the expansion of the Piast monarchy in Poland, these pagan and semi-autonomous groups retained customary communal governance until the progressive Christianisation and Germanisation of Pomerania in the thirteenth century. \n\n Status: Decentralised West Slavic tribal grouping; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Polabian and Pomeranian Slavic dialects; Religion: Slavic paganism; Government: Clan-based tribal confederacy; Historical era: Middle Ages; Disestablished: 1246; Succeeded by: Duchy of Pomerania

name: Duchy of Bohemia
label: holy roman empire
description: The Duchy of Bohemia was an important Central European realm of the Holy Roman Empire, encompassing the fertile Bohemian Basin around the Vltava and Elbe rivers. Ruled from Prague Castle by the native Přemyslid dynasty, the duchy was Christianised in the tenth century and integrated into the imperial framework as an Imperial State in 1002 under Duke Vladivoj. Bohemian dukes expanded their influence over Moravia, participated prominently in imperial politics and secured the elevation of their state into the hereditary Kingdom of Bohemia under Ottokar I in 1198. \n\n Status: Imperial state of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Prague; Common languages: Old Czech and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal duchy; Ruling dynasty: Přemyslid dynasty; Ruler title: Duke of Bohemia; Historical era: Middle Ages; Preceded by: Great Moravia; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Bohemia

name: Kadambas of Goa
description: The Kadambas of Goa were a prominent regional Hindu dynasty that ruled the coastal Konkan territory of Goa from the late tenth century. Established by Shasthadeva upon displacing the Shilaharas, the rulers initially governed from Chandor before transferring their commercial and administrative capital to Gopakapattana on the Zuari river. Flourishing through maritime trade with the Indian Ocean and the Persian Gulf, the dynasty patronised grand Shaivite temple architecture and retained substantial autonomy before succumbing to the Yadavas of Devagiri and subsequent Islamic conquests. \n\n Status: Regional coastal kingdom; Capital: Chandor; Common languages: Kannada and Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Kadamba dynasty; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Classical to Postclassical India; Established: 960; Disestablished: 1310; Preceded by: Shilahara dynasty

name: March of Lusatia
label: holy roman empire
description: The March of Lusatia was an eastern frontier territory of the Holy Roman Empire established in the Slavic lands along the Spree and Oder rivers. Created in 965 following the partition of the vast Marca Geronis, the margraviate served as an imperial military borderland aimed at subduing the local Sorbian tribes. Governed from Lübben and contested repeatedly by Polish rulers and the margraves of Brandenburg, the territory fostered extensive German eastward settlement before being incorporated into the Lands of the Bohemian Crown. \n\n Status: Frontier march of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Lübben; Common languages: Lower Sorbian, Upper Sorbian, German and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal margraviate; Ruler title: Margrave; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 965; Preceded by: Marca Geronis

name: March of Merseburg
label: holy roman empire
description: The March of Merseburg was a short-lived eastern frontier command of the Holy Roman Empire established on the lower Saale river following the death of Margrave Gero in 965. Centred on the fortified royal residence and episcopal see of Merseburg, the march safeguarded the eastern marches of Saxony against neighbouring Polabian Slavic tribes. The military district operated as an imperial bastion until the widespread Slavic uprising of 983, after which its defensive duties and territories were absorbed into the emerging Margraviate of Meissen. \n\n Status: Frontier march of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Merseburg; Common languages: Old Saxon, Polabian Slavic and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Military border march; Ruler title: Margrave; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 965; Disestablished: 983; Preceded by: Marca Geronis

name: March of Zeitz
label: holy roman empire
description: The March of Zeitz was a temporary frontier province of the Holy Roman Empire established in 965 along the White Elster river following the division of the Marca Geronis. Established to secure imperial influence and support missionary activities among the surrounding Sorbian populations, the march was closely connected to the newly founded Bishopric of Zeitz. The outpost suffered devastating setbacks during the great Slavic rebellion of 983, which sacked the episcopal see and prompted imperial authorities to consolidate the remaining frontier administration under Meissen. \n\n Status: Frontier march of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Zeitz; Common languages: Old Saxon, Sorbian and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Military border march; Ruler title: Margrave; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 965; Disestablished: 983; Preceded by: Marca Geronis

name: Margraviate of Meissen
label: holy roman empire
description: The Margraviate of Meissen was a prominent eastern border state of the Holy Roman Empire centred on the Elbe river valley in modern Saxony. Formed in 965 from the division of the Marca Geronis to subjugate the local Slavic Sorbs, the march became a lasting powerhouse after Emperor Henry IV granted it to the House of Wettin in 1089. Under Wettin rule, the margraviate expanded through German eastward settlement and silver mining, eventually acquiring the electoral duchy of Saxe-Wittenberg in 1423 to form the foundation of the modern Saxon state. \n\n Status: Imperial margraviate of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Meissen; Common languages: Upper Saxon German, Sorbian and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal margraviate; Ruling dynasty: House of Wettin; Ruler title: Margrave of Meissen; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 965; Succeeded by: Electorate of Saxony

name: Northern March
label: holy roman empire
description: The Northern March was a frontier march of the Holy Roman Empire created in 965 along the middle Elbe and Havel rivers to control the Polabian Slavic tribes. Governed from strongholds in the Altmark, including Tangermünde, under Margrave Dietrich of Haldensleben, the march attempted to extend imperial and ecclesiastical domination over the Lutici and Hevelli. The great Slavic rebellion of 983 decisively overran German garrisons and destroyed episcopal sees east of the Elbe, reducing imperial control to a narrow defensive corridor along the western riverbank. \n\n Status: Frontier march of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Tangermünde; Common languages: Old Saxon, Polabian Slavic and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Military border march; Ruler title: Margrave; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 965; Disestablished: 983; Preceded by: Marca Geronis

name: Volga Bulgaria
description: Volga Bulgaria was a wealthy medieval Bulgar state centred at the strategic confluence of the Volga and Kama rivers in eastern Europe. Having embraced Sunni Islam in the early tenth century following diplomatic contacts with the Abbasid Caliphate, the state developed a lucrative trading monopoly connecting Scandinavia, the Rus principalities and the Islamic world. Governed from formidable fortified capitals at Bolghar and Bilyar, the realm maintained a sophisticated urban culture and agrarian economy until suffering catastrophic destruction during the Mongol invasion of 1236. \n\n Status: Medieval emirate and trading empire; Capital: Bilyar; Common languages: Volga Bulgar, Kipchak Turkic and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Islamic monarchy; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 9th century; Disestablished: 1 December 1236; Succeeded by: Golden Horde

name: Kale State
label: shan states
description: Kale State was an early Shan principality located in the fertile Myittha river valley upstream from the Chindwin in northwestern Myanmar. Founded in the late tenth century with its capital at Kalemyo, the state guarded crucial overland trade and communication passages linking the central dry zone of Burma with the Manipur hills and eastern India. The sawbwas of Kale maintained regional autonomy and distinctive Tai cultural traditions for centuries, balancing diplomatic relations with the Kingdom of Pagan and neighbouring Chin communities before becoming embroiled in the Ava-Hanthawaddy wars. \n\n Status: Autonomous Shan principality; Capital: Kalemyo; Common languages: Shan, Old Burmese and Chin; Religion: Theravada Buddhism and animism; Government: Feudal principality; Ruler title: Sawbwa; Historical era: Classical to Postclassical Burma; Established: 3 February 966; Disestablished: 1407

name: Emirate of Aleppo
description: The Emirate of Aleppo was a northern Syrian Islamic principality that operated as a protectorate of the Eastern Roman Empire during the late tenth and early eleventh centuries. Following devastating Byzantine military expeditions under Emperor Nikephoros II Phokas, the ruling Hamdanid amirs accepted the 969 Treaty of Safar, agreeing to pay annual tribute and assist imperial armies against common enemies. Centred on the fortified ancient citadel of Aleppo, the emirate served as a crucial buffer between Byzantine Antioch and the expanding power of the Fatimid Caliphate in southern Syria. \n\n Status: Protectorate of the Eastern Roman Empire; Capital: Aleppo; Common languages: Arabic and Medieval Greek; Religion: Shia Islam and Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Tributary Islamic emirate; Ruling dynasty: Hamdanid dynasty; Ruler title: Amir; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 969; Disestablished: 1018

name: Marquisate of Montferrat
label: holy roman empire
description: The Marquisate of Montferrat was an autonomous imperial principality of the Holy Roman Empire located in the hilly wine-growing heartland of Piedmont south of the Po river. Created as a border march for Count Aleramo in the late tenth century, the state was ruled by the Aleramici dynasty, whose marquesses gained international renown through prominent leadership in the Crusades. Governing from Casale Monferrato from the early fourteenth century under a cadet branch of the Byzantine Palaiologos dynasty, the marquisate skilfully defended its independence against Milan and Savoy until the sixteenth century. \n\n Status: Imperial marquisate of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Casale Monferrato; Common languages: Piedmontese, Latin and Italian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal marquisate; Ruling dynasty: House of Montferrat; Ruler title: Marquess; Historical era: Middle Ages to Early Modern; Established: 967; Succeeded by: Duchy of Montferrat

name: Đại Cồ Việt

Establishing his fortified capital amidst the limestone karsts of Hoa Lư, the monarch proclaimed imperial sovereignty, issued native bronze coinage and established an autonomous administrative hierarchy independent of Chinese provincial governance. Despite entering into formal tributary relations with the Song dynasty to secure peace, the Đinh court retained internal imperial dignity until dynastic succession passed to the Early Lê dynasty in 980. \n\n Status: Sovereign imperial monarchy; Capital: Hoa Lư; Official languages: Literary Chinese; Common languages: Old Vietnamese; Religion: Buddhism and Vietnamese folk religion; Government: Imperial monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Đinh dynasty; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Postclassical Asia; Established: 1 February 968; Disestablished: 980

name: Bishopric of Zeitz
label: holy roman empire
description: The Bishopric of Zeitz was an imperial ecclesiastical diocese of the Holy Roman Empire established in 968 by Emperor Otto I to Christianise the Slavic Sorbs along the White Elster river. Placed under the ecclesiastical jurisdiction of the Archdiocese of Magdeburg, the bishops governed a vulnerable frontier domain exposed to frequent pagan revolts, culminating in the sack of Zeitz during the Slavic uprising of 983. Because of persistent security risks and local flooding, the episcopal see was transferred westward to the better-fortified town of Naumburg in 1029, forming the Prince-Bishopric of Naumburg-Zeitz. \n\n Status: Ecclesiastical principality of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Zeitz; Common languages: Old Saxon, Sorbian and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Ecclesiastical bishopric; Ruler title: Bishop; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 968; Disestablished: 1029; Succeeded by: Prince-Bishopric of Naumburg-Zeitz

name: Bulgarian Empire
description: The Bulgarian Empire endured a critical phase as a client state of Kievan Rus between 969 and 971 following the swift invasion led by Prince Sviatoslav I. Operating from the imperial capital at Great Preslav, Sviatoslav captured Tsar Boris II and compelled the Bulgarian court into military alliance against the Eastern Roman Empire. Bulgarian forces fought alongside the Rus in Thrace until Emperor John I Tzimiskes launched a decisive counter-offensive in 971, storming Preslav, capturing Boris II and forcing the Rus to withdraw across the Danube. \n\n Status: Client state of Kievan Rus; Capital: Preslav; Common languages: Old Church Slavonic and Old East Slavic; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Vassal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Krum dynasty; Ruler title: Tsar; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Preceded by: First Bulgarian Empire; Succeeded by: Byzantine Empire

name: Chalukyas of Lata
description: The Chalukyas of Lata were a regional Indian ruling dynasty that controlled the fertile coastal province of Lata around the lower Narmada and Tapti rivers in present-day southern Gujarat. Founded in the late tenth century by Barappa, the house initially served as military feudatories of the Western Chalukya Empire before asserting practical autonomy over coastal trade routes. The dynasty engaged in recurrent warfare with neighbouring powers including the Paramaras of Malwa and the Cholas, until being completely subdued and annexed by the Chaulukyas of Gujarat in the late eleventh century. \n\n Status: Regional feudal kingdom; Capital: Unrecorded; Common languages: Sanskrit and Old Gujarati; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Chalukya dynasty; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Medieval India; Established: 970; Disestablished: 1070; Succeeded by: Chaulukya dynasty

name: Kingdom of Norway
description: The Kingdom of Norway entered a brief personal union with the Kingdom of Denmark between 971 and 977 under the rule of King Harald Bluetooth. Following the assassination of King Harald Greycloak, Harald Bluetooth claimed supreme Norwegian kingship and installed Earl Haakon Sigurdsson of Lade as his governing regent and tributary earl in Trondheim. Haakon oversaw regional defence and administrative affairs while paying tribute to the Danish monarch, until mounting Danish interference and Christianisation demands provoked Haakon to break the union and rule Norway independently. \n\n Status: Kingdom in personal union with Denmark; Capital: Trondheim; Common languages: Old West Norse; Religion: Norse paganism and Latin Christianity; Government: Early medieval feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Gorm; Head of state: Harald Bluetooth; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Viking Age

name: Kingdom of Sweden
label: barbarian kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of Sweden took shape in the late tenth century through the consolidation of the Svear and Geatish realms under King Eric the Victorious. Centred on the Lake Mälaren basin and the royal minting town of Sigtuna, the early monarchy exercised sovereign authority through regional things and aristocratic alliances rather than centralised bureaucracy. Under King Olof Skötkonung, the realm adopted Christianity and integrated into western European trade networks, preserving royal autonomy across Scandinavia until dynastic conflicts led to the rise of the House of Sverker in 1156. \n\n Status: Early medieval kingdom; Capital: Sigtuna; Common languages: Old Swedish and Old East Norse; Religion: Norse paganism transitioning to Roman Catholicism; Government: Elective monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Munsö; Ruler title: King of the Swedes and Geats; Historical era: Viking Age to Early Middle Ages; Established: 970

name: Kingdom of Viguera
description: The Kingdom of Viguera was a short-lived sub-kingdom established in 970 in the upper Ebro basin of modern La Rioja. Carved out of the southern borderlands of the Kingdom of Pamplona by King García Sánchez I for his younger son Ramiro Garcés, the principality served to defend the Iregua valley against Muslim incursions from the Caliphate of Córdoba. Governed from the fortress of Viguera, the tiny kingdom remained closely subordinated to the court at Pamplona and was peacefully reabsorbed into the Navarrese realm following the death of its second ruler around 1005. \n\n Status: Appanage kingdom under Pamplona; Capital: Viguera; Common languages: Old Spanish, Basque and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal sub-kingdom; Ruling dynasty: Jiménez dynasty; Ruler title: King of Viguera; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 970; Disestablished: 1005; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Pamplona

name: Ma-i
label: barangay states
description: Ma-i was an influential precolonial maritime trading polity located in the Philippine archipelago, likely centred on the island of Mindoro or the Laguna de Bay basin. Documented in imperial Chinese records from 971 onwards during the Song dynasty, the state commanded lucrative trade networks exchanging gold, pearls, beeswax, betel nuts and tortoise shells for Chinese porcelain, iron vessels and silk fabrics. Governed by coastal merchant-chieftains who adhered strictly to contractual trade customs, Ma-i maintained commercial partnerships across Island Southeast Asia until declining in the fourteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign maritime trade polity; Capital: Ma-i; Common languages: Proto-Tagalog and Hanunoo; Religion: Philippine indigenous religion; Government: Maritime chieftaincy and thalassocracy; Historical era: Postclassical Southeast Asia; Established: 971; Disestablished: 1340

name: Abbey of San Colombano
label: holy roman empire
description: The Abbey of San Colombano was a renowned monastic principality of the Holy Roman Empire located at Bobbio in the Trebbia valley of northern Italy. Founded in 614 by the Irish missionary Saint Columbanus, the monastery became an illustrious centre of Western intellectual culture, preserving one of the finest scriptoriums and libraries of the Middle Ages. In the late tenth century, Ottonian emperors granted the abbots imperial immediacy, secular comital prerogatives and extensive territorial holdings across Liguria and Emilia, which the community defended until urban communes and neighbouring dioceses gradually dismantled its secular authority. \n\n Status: Imperial abbey of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Bobbio; Common languages: Medieval Latin, Early Italian and Ligurian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Monastic abbacy; Ruler title: Abbot; Historical era: Early Middle Ages to High Middle Ages; Established: 614; Disestablished: 1228; Succeeded by: Diocese of Bobbio

name: County of Lenzburg
label: holy roman empire
description: The County of Lenzburg was a prominent Swabian comital estate of the Holy Roman Empire encompassing substantial parts of the Aargau and Zürichgau in northern Switzerland. Governing from their imposing hilltop stronghold at Lenzburg Castle, the counts held imperial immediacy, administered lucrative alpine trade routes and controlled important bailiwicks over imperial abbeys such as Beromünster and Schänis. The comital dynasty maintained significant influence across the High Middle Ages until the extinction of their male lineage in 1173, whereupon their vast territorial domains were partitioned among the houses of Kyburg, Zähringen and Hohenstaufen. \n\n Status: Comital estate of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Lenzburg; Common languages: Alemannic German and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal comital monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Counts of Lenzburg; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 10th century; Disestablished: 1173; Succeeded by: County of Kyburg

name: Western Chalukya Empire
description: The Western Chalukya Empire was a formidable Kannada imperial power that dominated the western Deccan Plateau of southern India from the late tenth to the late twelfth century. Founded in 973 by Tailapa II after overthrowing the Rashtrakuta dynasty, the realm initially ruled from Manyakheta before establishing its regal capital at Kalyani. The empire engaged in prolonged warfare against the Chola dynasty for supremacy over the Krishna-Godavari delta and the Vengi region, while fostering an extraordinary renaissance in Kannada literature and pioneering distinct vesara architectural styles until fragmenting into the Hoysala, Kakatiya and Seuna kingdoms. \n\n Status: Imperial dynasty; Capital: Manyakheta; Common languages: Kannada and Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism and Jainism; Government: Imperial monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Western Chalukya dynasty; Ruler title: Emperor; First ruler: Tailapa II; Historical era: Early Medieval India; Established: 973; Disestablished: 1189; Succeeded by: Hoysala Empire

name: Chiefdom of Shuidong
label: four great native chiefdoms in guizhou
description: The Chiefdom of Shuidong was an autonomous indigenous tribal polity located in the mountainous Guizhou plateau of southwestern China, counted among the legendary Four Great Native Chiefdoms. Established in 975 by Song Jingyang after conquering the Manzhou prefecture from local Yi clans, the hereditary Song family was formally confirmed as autonomous chieftains by the imperial Song court. Governed through a hereditary tusi administration, Shuidong preserved indigenous customary law and military independence across rugged valleys until increasing Yuan and Ming centralisation culminated in direct imperial bureaucratic integration. \n\n Status: Autonomous native chiefdom; Capital: Guiyang; Common languages: Bouyei, Hmong and Chinese; Religion: Indigenous animism and ancestor worship; Government: Hereditary tribal chieftaincy; Ruling dynasty: Song clan; Ruler title: Chieftain; Historical era: Postclassical China; Established: 975; Succeeded by: Ming dynasty

name: Duchy of Carinthia
label: holy roman empire
description: The Duchy of Carinthia was an autonomous imperial principality of the Holy Roman Empire located across southern Austria and northern Slovenia along the Drava river basin. Separated from the Duchy of Bavaria in 976 by Emperor Otto II, it became the first newly established Imperial State created after the original German stem duchies. Governed initially from Sankt Veit an der Glan and later from Klagenfurt, the dukes commanded vital southeastern Alpine passes and presided over unique installation ceremonies at the Prince's Stone in the Slovene language until dynastic successions eventually brought the territory under the House of Habsburg. \n\n Status: Imperial duchy of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Klagenfurt; Common languages: Southern Bavarian, Carinthian Slovene and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal duchy; Ruler title: Duke of Carinthia; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 976; Preceded by: Duchy of Bavaria; Succeeded by: Habsburg Carinthia

name: Ghaznavid Sultanate
description: The Ghaznavid Sultanate was an influential Persianate Islamic empire of Turkic origin that dominated eastern Iran, Transoxiana, Afghanistan and northwestern India from the late tenth to the late twelfth century. Founded by Sabuktigin, a former Samanid military commander, the realm achieved its zenith under Sultan Mahmud of Ghazni, who launched regular campaigns into the Indo-Gangetic Plain and transformed his capital at Ghazni into a magnificent metropolis of Islamic scholarship and courtly literature. After losing western territories to the Great Seljuk Empire, the dynasty retreated eastward to Lahore before being extinguished by the Ghurids in 1186. \n\n Status: Islamic empire; Capital: Ghazni; Common languages: Persian, Arabic and Turkic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Islamic sultanate; Ruling dynasty: Ghaznavid dynasty; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 977; Disestablished: 1186; Succeeded by: Ghurid dynasty

name: Bishopric of Acqui
label: holy roman empire
description: The Bishopric of Acqui was an autonomous ecclesiastical lordship of the Holy Roman Empire located in southern Piedmont along the Bormida river. Invested with temporal comital prerogatives and imperial immediacy by Emperor Otto II in 978, the bishops governed the historic thermal city of Acqui Terme and its surrounding rural districts. The episcopal administration fortified local castles and asserted feudal jurisdiction over regional nobles until the rise of independent civic communes and the territorial consolidation of the Aleramici marquesses eclipsed the bishop's secular power during the twelfth century. \n\n Status: Ecclesiastical principality of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Acqui Terme; Common languages: Piedmontese, Ligurian and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Prince-bishopric; Ruler title: Bishop; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 978; Disestablished: 1136

name: Principality of Benevento, Capua and Salerno
label: lombard polities
description: The Principality of Benevento, Capua and Salerno was a unified Lombard realm in southern Italy briefly created under the autocratic rule of Prince Pandulf Ironhead. By inheriting Capua and Benevento and subsequently conquering Salerno in 978, Pandulf consolidated almost the entirety of Langobardia Minor under a single ruler for the first time since the eighth century. Governed from Benevento as an imperial ally against Byzantine and Saracen expansion, this fragile coalition of southern Italian principalities fractured immediately upon Pandulf's death in 981, when his domains were divided among his competing sons. \n\n Status: Unified Lombard principality; Capital: Benevento; Common languages: Vulgar Latin, Lombardic and Medieval Italian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Capua; Head of state: Pandulf Ironhead; Ruler title: Prince; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 979; Disestablished: 1 April 981

name: Commune of Bibbiena
label: holy roman empire
description: The Commune of Bibbiena was a self-governing hill town and medieval city-state of the Holy Roman Empire situated in the Casentino valley of eastern Tuscany along the upper Arno. Developing around an ancient Etruscan settlement, the commune established autonomous consular institutions and fortified city walls to safeguard its agrarian territory against neighbouring feudal magnates and the assertive bishops of Arezzo. Bibbiena guarded regional trade routes connecting Romagna with central Tuscany until mounting military conflict during the Guelph-Ghibelline wars led to its conquest by Florence and Arezzo in the late thirteenth century. \n\n Status: Autonomous medieval commune; Capital: Bibbiena; Common languages: Tuscan Italian and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Communal republic; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 980; Disestablished: 1291; Succeeded by: Republic of Florence

name: Đại Cồ Việt
description: Đại Cồ Việt under the Early Lê dynasty functioned as a consolidated Vietnamese empire following the accession of Emperor Lê Hoàn in 980. Governing from the fortified stronghold of Hoa Lư, the regime secured its sovereignty by repelling an imperial Chinese invasion by the Song dynasty in 981 and campaigning southward against the Kingdom of Champa. The Early Lê monarchs expanded hydraulic infrastructure, promoted Buddhist monastic institutions and established a resilient central administration that prepared the nation for its subsequent golden age under the Lý dynasty. \n\n Status: Sovereign imperial monarchy; Capital: Hoa Lư; Official languages: Literary Chinese; Common languages: Old Vietnamese; Religion: Buddhism and Vietnamese folk religion; Government: Imperial monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Early Lê dynasty; Historical era: Postclassical Asia; Succeeded by: Lý dynasty

name: Hasanwayhid Emirate
label: kurdish principalities;iranian intermezzo
description: The Hasanwayhid Emirate was a Kurdish Shia principality that held sway over the central Zagros mountains and the Jibal province of western Iran from the tenth century. Centred on the ancient city of Dinawar and the mountain fortress of Sarmaj, the dynasty recognised the suzerainty of the Buyid amirs while exercising extensive administrative autonomy over local Kurdish tribes and transit trade routes. Under Emir Badr ibn Hasanwayh, the realm enjoyed unprecedented domestic stability, public works and legal order, until internal dynastic strife after his death allowed the rival Annazid dynasty and the Buyids to dismantle the state in 1015. \n\n Status: Autonomous vassal emirate; Capital: Dinawar; Common languages: Kurdish, Persian and Arabic; Religion: Shia Islam; Government: Hereditary emirate; Ruling dynasty: Hasanwayhid dynasty; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 959; Disestablished: 1016; Preceded by: Buyid dynasty; Succeeded by: Annazids

name: Kingdom of Galicia
description: The Kingdom of Galicia functioned as a sovereign medieval realm in northwestern Iberia between 982 and 985 during a bitter civil war that split the Crown of León. Galician and Portuguese aristocrats dissatisfied with King Ramiro III crowned Bermudo II as independent monarch at the cathedral of Santiago de Compostela in 982. Governing from Compostela with the fervent support of local bishops and counts, Bermudo defended northwestern Iberia against Muslim raids before triumphing over Ramiro III in 985, which reunited Galicia with the Leonese monarchy. \n\n Status: Sovereign medieval kingdom; Capital: Santiago de Compostela; Common languages: Galician-Portuguese and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Astur-Leonese dynasty; Head of state: Bermudo II; Ruler title: King of Galicia; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 1 September 982; Disestablished: 26 June 985; Succeeded by: Kingdom of León

name: Great Xia
description: Great Xia, known historically as the Western Xia or the Tangut Empire, was a powerful Buddhist empire established by the Tangut people across the Ordos Loop and the Hexi Corridor in northwestern China. Ruled by the Weiming clan from their magnificent walled capital at Xingqing, the state developed a sophisticated written script, maintained a formidable mobile army and controlled vital northern arteries of the Silk Road. The Tangut emperors successfully balanced diplomatic and military rivalries against the Song, Liao and Jin dynasties, preserving their independence until becoming a vassal of Genghis Khan in 1210. \n\n Status: Sovereign imperial state; Capital: Yinchuan; Official languages: Tangut and Chinese; Religion: Tibetan Buddhism, Chinese Buddhism and Taoism; Government: Imperial monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Weiming clan; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Postclassical Asia; Established: 983; Preceded by: Dingnan Jiedushi; Succeeded by: Mongol Empire

name: Marwanids
label: kurdish principalities;iranian intermezzo
description: The Marwanids were an influential Kurdish Sunni dynasty that ruled the Diyar Bakr province of Upper Mesopotamia from the late tenth century following the collapse of Buyid and Hamdanid authority. Governing from Mayyafariqin and the walled fortress city of Amida, the dynasty maintained a prosperous commercial hub along the upper Tigris that linked northern Syria, Armenia and Azerbaijan. Under the long and enlightened reign of Emir Nasr al-Dawla Ahmad, the state experienced an intellectual and architectural renaissance until growing military pressure from the Great Seljuk Empire led to its formal annexation in 1085. \n\n Status: Sovereign Islamic emirate; Capital: Diyarbakır; Common languages: Kurdish, Arabic, Syriac and Persian; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Hereditary emirate; Ruling dynasty: Marwanid dynasty; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 983; Disestablished: 1085; Succeeded by: Seljuk Empire

name: Obotrite Confederation
description: The Obotrite Confederation was a powerful medieval league of West Slavic Polabian tribes inhabiting the coastal lowlands of modern Mecklenburg and eastern Holstein between the Trave and Warnow rivers. Centred on princely fortresses at Veligrad and Liubice, the confederation threw off German imperial overlordship during the great Slavic uprising of 983, re-establishing pagan religious traditions and political sovereignty. The princes defended their maritime territory against Saxon crusaders and Danish naval attacks until internal feuds and the Wendish Crusade culminated in Henry the Lion subordinating the realm, transforming the ruling dynasty into the Christian House of Mecklenburg. \n\n Status: Tribal confederation and principality; Capital: Liubice; Common languages: Polabian Slavic and Old Saxon; Religion: Slavic paganism transitioning to Christianity; Government: Elective tribal principality; Ruling dynasty: House of Niklot; Ruler title: Prince; Historical era: Middle Ages; Disestablished: 1167; Succeeded by: Principality of Mecklenburg

name: Norse Settlements in Greenland
label: norse/viking polities
description: The Norse Settlements in Greenland were autonomous medieval Scandinavian colonies established in southwestern Greenland beginning in 986 under the leadership of Erik the Red. Organised into the Eastern and Western settlements along deep, sheltered fjords, the colonists established pastoral farming communities governed by a communal Althing assembly meeting at Brattahlid and later Gardar. The settlers exported walrus ivory, polar bear pelts and furs to Europe in exchange for timber, grain and iron, maintaining independent communal institutions until formally submitting to the sovereignty of the Kingdom of Norway in 1261. \n\n Status: Autonomous Norse colonial republic; Capital: Brattahlid; Common languages: Old Norse; Religion: Norse paganism transitioning to Roman Catholicism; Government: Communal assembly democracy; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 986; Disestablished: 1261; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Norway

name: Prince-Bishopric of Liège
label: holy roman empire
description: The Prince-Bishopric of Liège was an important ecclesiastical state of the Holy Roman Empire encompassing the Meuse valley and the Ardennes plateau in modern Belgium. Secular principality status was consolidated between 980 and 985 when Bishop Notker received comital prerogatives over Huy and surrounding lands from Emperor Otto II, securing imperial immediacy and a seat in the Imperial Diet. Developing into an industrial centre known for armaments, metalworking and coal extraction, the principality tenaciously preserved its sovereignty against Burgundian and Habsburg encirclement until annexed by the French First Republic in 1795. \n\n Status: Ecclesiastical principality of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Liège; Common languages: Walloon, Old French, Dutch and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Elective prince-bishopric; Ruler title: Prince-Bishop; Historical era: Middle Ages to Early Modern; Established: 980; Disestablished: 28 December 1794; Succeeded by: French First Republic

name: County of Toulouse
description: The County of Toulouse was an expansive and virtually independent feudal principality in southern France encompassing the lower Garonne basin and large portions of Languedoc. Nominally recognising the suzerainty of the French Capetian crown after 987, the counts of the House of Saint-Gilles ruled as sovereign monarchs who fostered vibrant Occitan troubadour culture and extensive municipal freedoms. The spread of the Cathar heresy across the county provoked the devastating Albigensian Crusade in the early thirteenth century, culminating in the 1229 Treaty of Paris that subordinated Toulouse to the French royal domain. \n\n Status: Feudal county nominally under the French Crown; Capital: Toulouse; Common languages: Old Occitan and Medieval Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Catharism; Government: Feudal comital monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Toulouse; Ruler title: Count of Toulouse; Historical era: Middle Ages; Disestablished: 1229; Succeeded by: Kingdom of France

name: Duchy of Brittany
label: celtic polities of brittany;celtic polities
description: The Duchy of Brittany was a semi-autonomous Celtic feudal state occupying the Armorican peninsula between the English Channel and the Bay of Biscay. Founded in 939 following the expulsion of Viking raiders, the duchy was nominally a vassal of the French crown but maintained distinct Breton legal traditions, language and aristocratic liberties. Governed from historic capitals at Rennes and Nantes, the dukes navigated intense geopolitical rivalry between England and France throughout the High and Late Middle Ages until royal marriages and the 1532 edict permanently incorporated Brittany into the Kingdom of France. \n\n Status: Feudal duchy under the French Crown; Capital: Rennes; Common languages: Breton, Gallo, French and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal duchy; Ruler title: Duke of Brittany; Historical era: Middle Ages to Early Modern; Established: 939; Disestablished: 13 August 1547; Succeeded by: Kingdom of France

name: Duchy of Normandy
label: norse/viking polities
description: The Duchy of Normandy was a powerful and practically independent maritime state established in northern France along the lower Seine and the English Channel. Originating from the 911 Treaty of Saint-Clair-sur-Epte between the Frankish king Charles the Simple and the Viking chieftain Rollo, the duchy rapidly evolved into a disciplined feudal and military power based at Rouen. Under leaders such as Duke Richard I and Duke William the Conqueror, the Normans adopted the French language, constructed formidable castles and established a centralised administration that culminated in the successful invasion and conquest of England in 1066. \n\n Status: Autonomous feudal duchy; Capital: Rouen; Common languages: Old Norman, Old Norse and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal duchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Normandy; Ruler title: Duke of Normandy; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 911; Disestablished: 14 October 1066; Succeeded by: Kingdom of England

name: Kingdom of France
description: The Kingdom of France emerged as a sovereign European monarchy following the election and coronation of Hugh Capet as King of the Franks on 3 July 987. From their ancestral royal domain in the Île-de-France around Paris, the Capetian monarchs and their cadet branches steadily consolidated power over regional dukes and counts, transforming a fragmented feudal territory into a heavily centralised absolutist state. France developed into a leading global power, patron of arts and sciences and extensive colonial empire until the abolition of the monarchy during the French Revolution in 1792 and its final fall in 1848. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Paris; Official languages: French and Medieval Latin; Common languages: French, Occitan, Breton and regional languages; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy transitioning to absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Capet; Ruler title: King of France; Historical era: Middle Ages to Modern; Established: 3 July 987

name: Sabuktiginids
description: The Sabuktiginids formed an ascendant eastern Islamic ruling dynasty based in the highlands of eastern Afghanistan and eastern Khorasan. Founded by the Turkic commander Sabuktigin following his appointment over Ghazni, the house established sovereign authority while expanding southward into Balochistan and eastward across the Hindu Kush. Sabuktigin and his successors campaigned aggressively against the Hindu Shahi kings of Kabul, securing the strategic mountain passes of northwestern India and laying the territorial foundation for the extensive Ghaznavid Empire under Mahmud of Ghazni. \n\n Status: Sovereign Islamic dynasty; Capital: Ghazni; Common languages: Persian, Arabic and Turkic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Military emirate; Ruling dynasty: Sabuktiginid dynasty; Ruler title: Amir; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 977; Disestablished: 1001; Succeeded by: Ghaznavid Sultanate

name: County of Besalú
label: catalan counties
description: The County of Besalú was an independent Catalan feudal state of the Marca Hispanica situated in the foothills of the eastern Pyrenees in northern Catalonia. Centred on the fortified river town of Besalú, the county broke away from Frankish suzerainty in the late tenth century under Count Bernard I Tallaferro, who established autonomous comital minting and courtly administration. The comital dynasty defended its border valleys and patronised important Romanesque monasteries such as Sant Pere de Besalú until the death of Count Bernard III in 1111, when the county was permanently annexed to the County of Barcelona. \n\n Status: Sovereign Catalan county; Capital: Besalú; Common languages: Old Catalan and Medieval Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal comital monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Barcelona (Besalú branch); Ruler title: Count of Besalú; Historical era: Early Middle Ages to High Middle Ages; Established: 878; Disestablished: 1111; Succeeded by: County of Barcelona

name: Principality of Andorra
description: The Principality of Andorra is an ancient sovereign microstate nestled high in the eastern Pyrenees between France and Spain, centred along the Gran Valira basin. Origins trace to 988 when Count Borrell II of Urgell ceded the mountain valleys to the Diocese of Urgell, establishing an enduring clerical lordship over the agrarian communities. To settle bitter territorial disputes between the bishops and the counts of Foix, the historic Paréage treaties of 1278 created a unique co-principality under the joint sovereignty of the Bishop of Urgell and the French head of state, preserving Andorran autonomy into modern times. \n\n Status: Sovereign co-principality; Capital: Andorra la Vella; Official languages: Catalan; Common languages: Catalan, Spanish and French; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Parliamentary co-principality; Co-princes: Bishop of Urgell and President of France; Historical era: Middle Ages to Contemporary; Established: 988

name: County of Empúries
label: catalan counties
description: The County of Empúries was a sovereign maritime county of Catalonia situated along the Gulf of Roses and the Empordà coastal plain south of the Pyrenees. Following the partition of comital estates upon the death of Gausfred I in 989, the territory formed an autonomous principality governed from Castelló d'Empúries under Count Hugh I. The counts maintained a formidable Mediterranean fleet, engaged in maritime commerce and fortified coastal defences against Saracen corsairs, retaining fierce independence against the growing regional dominance of the neighbouring counts of Barcelona. \n\n Status: Sovereign Catalan county; Capital: Castelló d'Empúries; Common languages: Old Catalan and Medieval Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal comital monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Empúries; Ruler title: Count of Empúries; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 989; Disestablished: 1079; Preceded by: County of Roussillon

name: Uqaylid Dynasty
description: The Uqaylid Dynasty was an influential Shia Arab realm that dominated Upper Mesopotamia, northern Syria and northern Iraq from the late tenth century. Originating from the Bedouin Banu Uqayl tribe, the dynasty established its political seat at Mosul in 990 under Al-Muqallad, quickly displacing the weakened Hamdanids and challenging Buyid supremacy in Baghdad. The Uqaylid maliks maintained a powerful desert-cavalry army, patronised Arabic literature and secured significant commercial revenue from Euphrates trade routes until becoming tributary vassals of the expanding Great Seljuk Empire in the mid-eleventh century. \n\n Status: Sovereign Arab emirate; Capital: Mosul; Common languages: Arabic, Syriac and Persian; Religion: Shia Islam; Government: Hereditary emirate; Ruling dynasty: Uqaylid dynasty; Ruler title: Malik; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 990; Preceded by: Hamdanid dynasty; Succeeded by: Seljuk Empire

name: Annazids
label: kurdish principalities;iranian intermezzo
description: The Annazids were a Kurdish Sunni dynasty that ruled the Zagros borderlands between western Iran and central Iraq from the late tenth century. Founded by Abu'l-Fath Muhammad ibn Annaz in 990, the dynasty established its capital at the strategic pass city of Hulwan and asserted authority over Kermanshah and Dinawar after eclipsing the neighbouring Hasanwayhids. The Annazid amirs navigated shifting alliances with the Buyid emirs, the Kakuyids and local Kurdish and Arab tribes until the rapid expansion of the Seljuk Turks dissolved their principality in the early twelfth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign Islamic emirate; Capital: Hulwan; Common languages: Kurdish, Persian and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Hereditary emirate; Ruling dynasty: Annazid dynasty; Ruler title: Amir; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 991; Disestablished: 1117; Preceded by: Hasanwayhids; Succeeded by: Seljuk Empire

name: Kalachuris of Tripuri
description: The Kalachuris of Tripuri were a formidable medieval Hindu dynasty that dominated the Chedi region of central India along the upper Narmada river valley. Ruling from their grand capital at Tripuri near modern Jabalpur, the monarchs attained imperial status under Gangeyadeva and his son Lakshmikarna, who assumed the universal title of Chakravartin after triumphant military expeditions across northern and eastern India. The dynasty lavishly patronised Sanskrit poetry, temple architecture and Shaivite monastic settlements until sustained warfare with the Chandelas, Paramaras and Gahadavalas caused their gradual decline in the thirteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign imperial kingdom; Capital: Tripuri; Common languages: Sanskrit and Prakrit; Religion: Hinduism and Jainism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Kalachuri dynasty; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical era: Early Medieval India; Established: 9th century; Disestablished: 1251

name: Numayrid Dynasty
description: The Numayrid Dynasty was a prominent Arab Bedouin realm that controlled the fertile plains of Diyar Mudar in western Upper Mesopotamia along the Balikh and Euphrates rivers. Established in 990 by Waththab ibn Sabiq al-Numayri, the dynasty governed key commercial towns including Harran, Saruj and Raqqa, ruling through urban deputies while maintaining their primary nomadic encampments in the surrounding pastures. The Numayrid amirs successfully preserved their independence against Byzantine advances and Fatimid encroachment, fostering local commerce until Seljuk expansion and regional Uqaylid pressure eroded their authority. \n\n Status: Sovereign Arab emirate; Capital: Harran; Common languages: Arabic; Religion: Shia Islam; Government: Tribal emirate; Ruling dynasty: Numayrid dynasty; Ruler title: Amir; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 990; Disestablished: 1081; Preceded by: Hamdanid dynasty; Succeeded by: Uqaylid dynasty

name: Vinland
label: norse/viking polities
description: Vinland was an ephemeral Norse overseas settlement and exploratory outpost established on the northern tip of Newfoundland around the turn of the eleventh century. Documented in the Icelandic Vinland sagas and evidenced by timber and turf longhouses excavated at L'Anse aux Meadows, the outpost served Scandinavian seafarers journeying from Greenland to harvest timber, wild grapes and furs. Because of vulnerable maritime supply lines across the North Atlantic and violent clashes with the indigenous Beothuk or Dorset populations, the Norse abandoned permanent colonisation after several decades. \n\n Status: Norse exploratory outpost and settlement; Capital: L'Anse aux Meadows; Common languages: Old Norse; Religion: Norse paganism and Roman Catholicism; Government: Monastic and communal expeditionary council; Historical era: Viking Age; Established: 991; Disestablished: 1051

name: County of Chiny
label: holy roman empire
description: The County of Chiny was a sovereign feudal estate of the Holy Roman Empire located along the Semois river and the southern Ardennes in the borderlands of modern Belgium and France. Emerging from the ancient pagus of Ivois during the tenth century under Otto of Warcq, the counts erected robust fortresses and cultivated fruitful relations with neighbouring episcopal sees, particularly Verdun. The comital house governed thriving market towns including Chiny, Florenville and Virton until dynastic intermarriage united the territory with the County of Looz, after which it was ultimately sold to the Duchy of Luxembourg in 1364. \n\n Status: County of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Chiny; Common languages: Old French, Walloon and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal comital monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Chiny; Ruler title: Count of Chiny; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 971; Disestablished: 1379; Succeeded by: Duchy of Luxembourg

name: Imperial Abbey of Quedlinburg
label: holy roman empire
description: The Imperial Abbey of Quedlinburg was a prestigious autonomous ecclesiastical principality of the Holy Roman Empire situated along the Bode river north of the Harz mountains. Established in 936 by Queen Mathilda as a collegiate foundation for unmarried noblewomen, the abbey enjoyed imperial immediacy and served as an esteemed royal residence and memorial site for the Ottonian dynasty. The princess-abbesses held a virile vote in the Imperial Diet and exercised direct temporal jurisdiction over the town of Quedlinburg and extensive landed estates until the foundation was secularised and mediatised into Prussia in 1802. \n\n Status: Imperial abbey of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Quedlinburg; Common languages: Middle Low German, German and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism transitioning to Lutheranism; Government: Ecclesiastical collegiate principality; Ruler title: Princess-Abbess; Historical era: Middle Ages to Early Modern; Established: 936; Disestablished: 25 February 1803; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Prussia

name: Ma'munids
description: The Ma'munids were an Iranian Muslim dynasty that briefly ruled the oasis civilisation of Khwarazm along the lower Amu Darya south of the Aral Sea. Founded in 995 by Ma'mun I ibn Muhammad, who unified northern and southern Khwarazm and established his court at Gurganj, the dynasty assumed the ancient regal title of Khwarazmshah. The Ma'munid court became celebrated throughout Central Asia for lavish patronage of science and philosophy, hosting intellectual luminaries including Avicenna and al-Biruni, before being overthrown and annexed by the Ghaznavid Empire in 1017. \n\n Status: Sovereign Islamic monarchy; Capital: Gurganj; Common languages: Khwarezmian, Persian and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Ma'munid dynasty; Ruler title: Khwarazmshah; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 995; Disestablished: 1017; Preceded by: Afrighids; Succeeded by: Ghaznavid Sultanate

name: Abbey of Vangadizza
label: holy roman empire
description: The Abbey of Vangadizza was an autonomous Benedictine monastic territory of the Holy Roman Empire located at Badia Polesine in the fertile lowlands along the lower Adige river. Endowed with sweeping territorial immunities and direct imperial protection by Emperor Otto III in 996, the monastery functioned as an independent ecclesiastical lordship in the Polesine region. The abbots exercised civil and judicial authority over neighbouring agrarian settlements and river tolls, maintaining their sovereign status until increasing Venetian and Ferrarese territorial ambitions absorbed the monastic domain in the early fifteenth century. \n\n Status: Imperial abbey of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Badia Polesine; Common languages: Venetian and Medieval Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Monastic lordship; Ruler title: Abbot; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 26 December 996; Disestablished: 1401; Succeeded by: Republic of Venice

name: Tsongkha
label: tibetan era of fragmentation
description: Tsongkha was an influential Buddhist theocracy that governed northeastern Tibet across the fertile Huangshui river basin and the Qinghai region during the Tibetan Era of Fragmentation. Founded at the end of the tenth century and brought to prominence by the monarch Gusiluo, the state established prominent administrative centres at Qingtang and Miaochuan. Tsongkha formed a thriving trading and religious crossroads between China, Central Asia and Tibet, maintaining cordial tributary and diplomatic relations with the Northern Song dynasty until Song military campaigns conquered the territory in 1104. \n\n Status: Sovereign Tibetan theocracy; Capital: Miaochuan; Common languages: Old Tibetan; Religion: Tibetan Buddhism; Government: Theocratic monarchy; Ruler title: King; First ruler: Gusiluo; Historical era: Postclassical Asia; Established: 997; Disestablished: 1104; Succeeded by: Song dynasty

name: Margraviate of Namur
label: holy roman empire
description: The Margraviate of Namur was a strategic feudal state of the Holy Roman Empire located at the confluence of the Sambre and Meuse rivers in modern Wallonia. Originating as a county around the rocky promontory and citadel of Namur under Count Albert I, the territory was later elevated to a margraviate and held imperial immediacy within the Lower Lotharingian realm. The margraves navigated competing territorial claims from the Duchy of Brabant, the County of Hainaut and the Prince-Bishopric of Liège until the childless Margrave John III sold the realm to Duke Philip the Good of Burgundy in 1421. \n\n Status: Imperial margraviate of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Namur; Common languages: Walloon, Old French and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal margraviate; Ruling dynasty: House of Namur; Ruler title: Margrave of Namur; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 998; Disestablished: 1421; Succeeded by: Burgundian Netherlands

name: Prince-Bishopric of Passau
label: holy roman empire
description: The Prince-Bishopric of Passau was an important ecclesiastical state of the Holy Roman Empire located at the picturesque three-river confluence of the Danube, Inn and Ilz in eastern Bavaria. Endowed with extensive imperial immunities, customs privileges and urban jurisdiction by Ottonian and Salian emperors around the year 1000, the prince-bishops administered a prosperous domain known as the Ilzstadt and Obernzell. The episcopal state derived vast wealth from the Alpine salt trade and Danube navigation, preserving its imperial immediacy within the Bavarian Circle until its secularisation into the Electorate of Bavaria in 1803. \n\n Status: Ecclesiastical principality of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Passau; Common languages: Central Bavarian and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Ecclesiastical principality; Ruler title: Prince-Bishop; Historical era: Middle Ages to Early Modern; Established: 739; Disestablished: 1803; Succeeded by: Electorate of Bavaria

name: Prince-Bishopric of Sion
label: holy roman empire
description: The Prince-Bishopric of Sion was an autonomous Alpine ecclesiastical state of the Holy Roman Empire encompassing the Upper Rhône valley within the modern Swiss canton of Valais. In 999, King Rudolf III of Burgundy invested Bishop Hugo of Sion with the comital rights of the County of Valais, establishing a powerful prince-bishopric that was subsequently integrated into the Holy Roman Empire in 1032. The prince-bishops governed from the twin hilltop castles of Valère and Tourbillon, guarding vital transit routes across the Great Saint Bernard Pass until regional peasant communes coalesced to form the Republic of the Seven Zenden. \n\n Status: Ecclesiastical principality of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Sion; Common languages: Franco-Provençal, German and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Ecclesiastical principality; Ruler title: Prince-Bishop; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 999; Disestablished: 1351; Succeeded by: Republic of the Seven Zenden

name: Kingdom of Norway
description: The Kingdom of Norway functioned as a subordinate territorial possession of the Kingdom of Denmark between 1000 and 1001 following the historic naval Battle of Svolder. After the defeat and death of King Olaf Tryggvason, King Sweyn Forkbeard of Denmark claimed sovereignty over the Norwegian coast and partitioned governance with his Swedish and Norwegian allies. Operating from the administrative centre at Trondheim, the Danish king delegated regional authority in western Norway to Earl Eiríkr Hákonarson as a loyal jarl, maintaining tributary suzerainty over the realm before royal power transitioned to local dynastic rule. \n\n Status: Conquered possession under Denmark; Capital: Trondheim; Common languages: Old West Norse; Religion: Norse paganism and Latin Christianity; Government: Early medieval feudal dependency; Ruling dynasty: House of Gorm; Head of state: Sweyn Forkbeard; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Viking Age; Established: 9 September 1000; Disestablished: 1001

name: Kingdom of Hungary
description: The Kingdom of Hungary was founded on Christmas Day in the year 1000 with the coronation of Saint Stephen I at Esztergom, receiving a royal crown sent by Pope Sylvester II. Spanning the fertile Carpathian Basin and the middle Danube, the kingdom converted rapidly to Latin Christianity, established an advanced county administration and developed into a major Central European power under the native Árpád dynasty. The realm successfully repelled nomadic incursions, established a codified legal order and integrated diverse ethnic communities, flourishing as an independent European monarchy until modern times. \n\n Status: Sovereign medieval kingdom; Capital: Esztergom; Common languages: Hungarian and Medieval Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Árpád dynasty; Ruler title: King of Hungary; First ruler: Stephen I; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 25 December 1000

name: Alempois
label: ancient estonian counties
description: Alempois was an independent landlocked Finnic tribal county situated in central Estonia, bordered by Harjumaa, Järvamaa, Sakala and Nurmekund. Covering an area of roughly four hundred agricultural hides along the upper Navesti river basin, the community was governed by a traditional council of elders meeting in seasonal folk assemblies. The inhabitants maintained an agrarian way of life, practised indigenous Finnic pagan customs and coordinated mutual regional defence with neighbouring Estonian counties until the Livonian Crusade subjugated the region in the early thirteenth century. \n\n Status: Autonomous ancient Estonian county; Capital: Alempois; Common languages: Ancient Estonian and Finnic dialects; Religion: Finnic paganism; Government: Tribal council of elders; Ruler title: Elder; Historical era: Early Middle Ages to High Middle Ages; Established: 1001; Disestablished: 1224; Succeeded by: Livonian Brothers of the Sword

name: Amuzgos
label: mesoamerican polities
description: The Amuzgos formed an autonomous Mesoamerican indigenous polity located in the rugged Sierra Madre del Sur along the present-day border between Guerrero and Oaxaca. description: The K'iche' Kingdom of Q'umarkaj was a powerful pre-Columbian Maya state centred in the fertile volcanic highlands of modern Guatemala.
