The kingdom attained its zenith during the fifteenth century before splintering through internal rivalries, leaving it vulnerable to the Spanish invasion led by Pedro de Alvarado in 1524. \n\n Status: Sovereign monarchy; Capital: Q'umarkaj; Common languages: Classical K'iche'; Religion: Maya religion; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Ajpop; Historical era: Postclassic Mesoamerica; Disestablished: 1525; Succeeded by: New Spain

name: Kalachuris of Ratnapura
description: The Kalachuris of Ratnapura were an offshoot of the central Indian Tripuri Kalachuri lineage who established independent dominion over the upper Mahanadi basin in modern Chhattisgarh. Governed from the fortified city of Ratnapura, the dynasty expanded through successful military encounters with the Eastern Gangas and neighbouring regional chieftains. Royal patronage supported the erection of ornate Shaivite temple complexes and the development of extensive tank irrigation systems, sustaining economic prosperity throughout the twelfth and early thirteenth centuries. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Ratnapura; Common languages: Sanskrit and Prakrit; Religion: Hinduism and Jainism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Medieval India; Preceded by: Kalachuris of Tripuri; Succeeded by: Later Haihayas of Ratanpur

name: Kingdom of Ajtony
description: The Kingdom of Ajtony was an early eleventh-century tribal realm established in the Banat region along the lower Mureș and Danube rivers. Seated at the fortress of Urbs Morisena, modern Cenad, the chieftain Ajtony commanded extensive herds of livestock and controlled lucrative salt trade routes entering the Pannonian basin. Rejecting Hungarian royal supremacy, Ajtony embraced Eastern Orthodox Christianity before being defeated and killed by the army of King Stephen I under the commander Csanád around 1030. \n\n Status: Sovereign tribal kingdom; Capital: Cenad; Common languages: Old Hungarian and Slavic; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy and Paganism; Government: Tribal monarchy; Ruler title: Chieftain; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Disestablished: 1031; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Hungary

name: Kingdom of Kano
label: hausa states
description: The Kingdom of Kano was a foundational Hausa city-state located in modern northern Nigeria, developing around the iron-smelting and spiritual settlement of Dala Hill. Guided by the Bagauda dynasty, the polity established defensive earthen walls and created an influential council of state known as the Taran Kano to advise the sovereign sarki. The realm functioned as a critical marketplace for trans-Saharan merchants trading in leather, woven textiles and salt before its gradual Islamisation during the fourteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Kano; Common languages: Hausa; Religion: Hausa animism and Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Sarki; Legislature: Taran Kano; Historical era: Middle Ages; Currency: Cowrie shells

name: Kingdom of Siang
description: The Kingdom of Siang was a maritime and agricultural polity that flourished along the western coast of the South Sulawesi peninsula. Anchored at its central estuary port of Siang, the kingdom exerted political hegemony over neighbouring Bugis and Makassarese settlements, coordinating regional shipping networks and rice production. Recorded by early Portuguese travellers as a populous trading centre in the early sixteenth century, the kingdom lost its independence and commercial dominance amidst the rapid military ascendancy of Gowa and Talloq. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Siang; Common languages: Makassarese and Buginese; Religion: Indigenous animism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Precolonial Southeast Asia; Disestablished: 1551; Succeeded by: Sultanate of Gowa

name: Kingdom of Zimbabwe
description: The Kingdom of Zimbabwe was a medieval Shona monarchy centred on the monumental granite architectural complex of Great Zimbabwe in southern Africa. Succeeding Mapungubwe as the principal interior power, the state extracted vast wealth from alluvial gold mining and cattle husbandry, exchanging precious metals and ivory with Swahili trading networks along the Indian Ocean coast. Shifting trade routes, demographic pressure and ecological depletion precipitated the abandonment of its stone metropolis in the late fifteenth century, prompting succession by the Mutapa and Butua kingdoms. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Great Zimbabwe; Common languages: Shona; Religion: Shona traditional religion; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Mambo; Historical era: Medieval Southern Africa; Disestablished: 1481; Succeeded by: Mutapa Empire and Kingdom of Butua

name: Läänemaa
label: ancient estonian counties
description: Läänemaa was an autonomous maritime county encompassing the coastal lowlands of western Estonia and its adjacent archipelago waters. The territory was structured into decentralised parishes governed by village elders who met in assembly to organise naval expeditions and mutual territorial defence. Fortified coastal settlements, predecessor to later medieval Haapsalu, provided defensive refuge and commercial staging points until German and Scandinavian crusaders systematically overran the county during the Livonian Crusade in the early thirteenth century. \n\n Status: Autonomous county; Administrative seat: Haapsalu; Common languages: Old Estonian; Religion: Estonian paganism; Government: Tribal eldership; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Historical region: Ancient Estonia; Disestablished: 1208; Succeeded by: Livonian Brothers of the Sword

name: Lordship of Commercy
label: holy roman empire
description: The Lordship of Commercy was a feudal seigneury within the Holy Roman Empire, situated along the Meuse River in the borderlands of Lorraine. Held successively by the Houses of Broyes and Saarbrücken, the lordship controlled critical river crossings and maintained a heavily fortified castle around which the market town developed. The barons navigated complex diplomatic rivalries between the Duchy of Lorraine and the French crown until the territory was absorbed into the ducal estates of Lorraine in the late fifteenth century. \n\n Status: Lordship of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Commercy; Common languages: Old French and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal seigneury; Ruler title: Lord of Commercy; Historical era: Middle Ages; Disestablished: 1478; Succeeded by: Duchy of Lorraine

name: Lordship of Faucigny
label: holy roman empire
description: The Lordship of Faucigny was an Alpine feudal domain of the Holy Roman Empire nestled in the upper Arve valley south of Lake Geneva. Centred on the hilltop castle of Faucigny, the local dynasts expanded their influence across Mont Blanc passes through advantageous marital alliances and military service. The territory became a contested battleground between the Counts of Savoy and the Dauphins of Viennois, ultimately passing to the Dauphiné in 1305 before its final cession to the House of Savoy. \n\n Status: Imperial lordship; Capital: Faucigny; Common languages: Arpitan and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal lordship; Ruler title: Lord of Faucigny; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Disestablished: 1305; Succeeded by: Dauphiné of Viennois

name: Lordship of Hohenburg
label: holy roman empire
description: The Lordship of Hohenburg was a territorial barony of the Holy Roman Empire located along the Lauterach River in the Upper Palatinate region of Bavaria. Governed from the fortified stronghold of Hohenburg, the lords held imperial immediacy and exercised regional jurisdiction over surrounding agricultural villages and forestry lands. Following the extinction of the original comital line, the lordship was contested by regional magnates before its secular rights and properties were fully acquired by the Prince-Bishopric of Regensburg in 1379. \n\n Status: Imperial barony; Capital: Hohenburg; Common languages: Middle High German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal lordship; Ruler title: Lord of Hohenburg; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Disestablished: 1379; Succeeded by: Prince-Bishopric of Regensburg

name: Marquisate of Podenzana
label: holy roman empire
description: The Marquisate of Podenzana was an autonomous feudal estate of the Holy Roman Empire nestled in the Lunigiana region of northern Tuscany. Ruled by a cadet branch of the Malaspina dynasty from their hillside castle overlooking the Magra valley, the marquisate exercised judicial sovereignty over a compact cluster of rural villages. The state navigated neighbouring Italian powers and imperial politics for centuries until dynastic transfers and subsequent regional reorganisation incorporated it into neighbouring Malaspina domains in 1711. \n\n Status: Imperial marquisate; Capital: Podenzana; Common languages: Italian and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Malaspina; Ruler title: Marquis; Historical era: Middle Ages to Early modern; Disestablished: 1711

name: Metsepole
label: latgalian elderships
description: Metsepole was an indigenous Livonian county situated along the north-eastern coast of the Gulf of Riga in modern Latvia. Inhabited by Finnic Livonians and led by district elders, the territory relied on wooden ringforts including Skulte and Limbaži for communal defence and market exchange. Metsepole was among the earliest regions targeted by Bishop Albert of Riga during the Northern Crusades, falling under German crusader dominion by 1207 and subsequently becoming incorporated into the ecclesiastical territories of the Bishopric of Riga. \n\n Status: Autonomous tribal county; Administrative seat: Turaida; Common languages: Livonian; Religion: Livonian paganism; Government: Eldership; Ruler title: Elder; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Disestablished: 1207; Succeeded by: Bishopric of Riga

name: Mitla
label: mesoamerican polities
description: Mitla was an important Zapotec and Mixtec city-state located in the upper Tlacolula Valley of Oaxaca in southern Mexico. Serving as the primary religious and funerary centre of the Zapotec culture following the decline of Monte Albán, the city was renowned for its palatial architecture decorated with intricate geometric stone mosaics. The ecclesiastical and civil authorities exercised regional sway throughout the Postclassic era until Spanish conquistadors conquered the valley in 1522, bringing the city under the authority of New Spain. \n\n Status: Sovereign city-state; Capital: Mitla; Common languages: Zapotec and Mixtec; Religion: Mesoamerican polytheism; Government: Theocratic monarchy; Historical era: Postclassic Mesoamerica; Disestablished: 1522; Succeeded by: New Spain

name: Mõhu
label: ancient estonian counties
description: Mõhu was a small landlocked county of ancient Estonia located in the interior plains between Lake Võrtsjärv and the Pedja River basin. Administered by an assembly of local elders with its main stronghold at Kursi, the county relied on subsistence agriculture and collective defence pacts with adjacent Estonian territories. The independent existence of Mõhu was terminated in the 1220s when German crusaders subdued the inland districts, annexing its lands into the monastic state established by the Livonian Brothers of the Sword. \n\n Status: Autonomous county; Administrative seat: Kursi; Common languages: Old Estonian; Religion: Estonian paganism; Government: Tribal eldership; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Historical region: Ancient Estonia; Disestablished: 1225; Succeeded by: Monastic state of the Teutonic Knights

name: Mzab
description: Mzab was an autonomous confederation of fortified oasis cities established in the northern Sahara Desert of Algeria by Ibadi Muslim Berbers. Following the destruction of the Rustamid dynasty at Tahert, Mozabite refugees constructed five pentapolis towns along the Mzab Valley, including Ghardaïa and Melika, protected by strict civic councils and compact stone architecture. The confederacy managed lucrative trans-Saharan trading routes and sustained extensive palm groves through sophisticated hydraulic systems, maintaining internal self-rule throughout the medieval and early modern eras. \n\n Status: Sovereign tribal confederation; Capital: Ghardaïa; Common languages: Mozabite Berber and Arabic; Religion: Ibadi Islam; Government: Theocratic council of elders; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 1001; Historical region: Maghreb

name: Nurmekund
label: ancient estonian counties
description: Nurmekund was a sovereign Finnic county situated on the northern approaches to Lake Võrtsjärv in central Estonia. Structured around roughly six hundred agrarian hides, the territory was governed by regional chieftains and elders operating out of regional administrative centres, notably Põltsamaa and Pilistvere. The county preserved its traditional animist customs and local autonomy until the Livonian Crusade overwhelmed its defences in the early 1220s, resulting in its direct annexation by the Livonian Brothers of the Sword. \n\n Status: Autonomous county; Administrative seat: Põltsamaa; Common languages: Old Estonian; Religion: Estonian paganism; Government: Tribal eldership; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Historical region: Ancient Estonia; Disestablished: 1225; Succeeded by: Livonian Brothers of the Sword

name: Piemare
label: latgalian elderships
description: Piemare was an independent Baltic Curonian coastal territory situated along the eastern littoral of the Baltic Sea in modern western Latvia. Centred on the fortified maritime stronghold of Seeburg near modern Grobiņa and Liepāja, the realm was governed by noble elders and chieftains such as King Lammekinus. The county prospered from coastal fishing, amber collection and maritime commerce until the 1253 partition treaties between the Bishopric of Courland and the Livonian Order extinguished its native political autonomy. \n\n Status: Autonomous tribal principality; Capital: Liepāja; Common languages: Curonian; Religion: Baltic paganism; Government: Tribal eldership; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Disestablished: 1254; Succeeded by: Bishopric of Courland and Livonian Order

name: Prince-Bishopric of Metz
label: holy roman empire
description: The Prince-Bishopric of Metz was an ecclesiastical state of the Holy Roman Empire centred in the fertile Moselle Valley of Lorraine. Granted imperial immediacy by German monarchs, the bishops exercised temporal authority across extensive rural domains while contending with the rising municipal autonomy of the city of Metz. After townspeople asserted self-rule in the thirteenth century, the bishops relocated their residence to Vic-sur-Seille. French royal forces occupied the prince-bishopric in 1552, formalising direct administration under the crown by 1633. \n\n Status: Prince-bishopric of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Metz and Vic-sur-Seille; Common languages: Old French, Middle High German and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Ecclesiastical principality; Ruler title: Prince-Bishop; Historical era: Middle Ages to Early modern; Disestablished: 1633; Succeeded by: Three Bishoprics

name: Principality of Jersika
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Jersika was an early medieval Latgalian and East Slavic state centred on a fortified hillfort overlooking the Daugava River in eastern Latvia. Governed by Prince Visvaldis as a tributary vassal under the Rurikid rulers of Polotsk, the realm controlled vital riverine commerce linking the Baltic Sea with Russian river routes. Its strategic importance and adherence to Eastern Orthodoxy drew the hostility of crusading German knights, who sacked the citadel in 1209 and forced the prince to cede sovereignty to the Bishopric of Riga. \n\n Status: Vassal principality; Capital: Jersika; Common languages: Latgalian and Old East Slavic; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy and Baltic paganism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Prince; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Disestablished: 1210; Succeeded by: Bishopric of Riga

name: Principality of Polotsk
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Polotsk was a powerful East Slavic realm established along the Western Dvina River in what is today northern Belarus. Governed by a distinct branch of the Rurikid dynasty founded by Iziaslav of Polotsk, the principality flourished as a major riverine trade nexus, defended by a prominent urban citadel and the Cathedral of Saint Sophia. Although frequently embroiled in dynastic clashes with Kiev and Novgorod, Polotsk maintained broad sovereign autonomy until thirteenth-century external pressures brought the territory under the expanding Grand Duchy of Lithuania. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Polatsk; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Princely monarchy; Ruler title: Prince of Polotsk; Legislature: Veche; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Disestablished: 1241; Succeeded by: Grand Duchy of Lithuania

name: Republic of Ancona
label: maritime republics;holy roman empire
description: The Republic of Ancona was a sovereign maritime commune situated on the Adriatic coast of central Italy. Governed by a council of six elders representing its three historic urban quarters, the merchant republic maintained profitable diplomatic and commercial ties with the Byzantine Empire, the Republic of Ragusa and the Levant. Despite chronic commercial rivalry with the Republic of Venice and nominal papal claims, Ancona preserved its republican constitution and maritime laws until Pope Clement VII dispatched papal forces to annex the city in 1532. \n\n Status: Sovereign maritime republic; Capital: Ancona; Common languages: Italian, Marchigiano and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Oligarchic republic; Historical era: Middle Ages to Renaissance; Currency: Agontano; Disestablished: 1533; Succeeded by: Papal States

name: Republic of Pisa
label: maritime republics;holy roman empire
description: The Republic of Pisa was a premier Italian maritime power that commanded vital commercial sealanes across the western Mediterranean from the mouth of the Arno River. Governed initially by consular officials and later by an elected podestà, Pisa established lucrative trading outposts across the Levant, Sardinia and the Balearic Islands during the Crusades. Exhausting conflicts with Genoa, culminating in the naval catastrophe at Meloria, weakened the republic, which ultimately succumbed to military conquest and annexation by the Republic of Florence in 1406. \n\n Status: Sovereign maritime republic; Capital: Pisa; Common languages: Tuscan Italian and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Commercial republic; Ruler title: Podestà; Currency: Grosso pisano; Historical era: Middle Ages; Disestablished: 1406; Succeeded by: Republic of Florence

name: Republic of San Marino
label: holy roman empire
description: The Republic of San Marino is an enduring mountainous microstate enclaved within north-central Italy, founded around the slopes of Monte Titano. Established in antiquity as a monastic refuge, the commonwealth secured imperial recognition and evolved a communal constitution governed by the Grand and General Council and two co-equal Captains Regent chosen bi-annually. The republic consistently preserved its sovereign independence through skilled diplomacy amidst peninsula-wide conflicts, except for brief foreign occupations in the eighteenth and twentieth centuries. \n\n Status: Sovereign constitutional republic; Capital: San Marino; Official languages: Italian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Diarchic directorial republic; Head of state: Captains Regent; Legislature: Grand and General Council; Historical era: Middle Ages to Modern

name: Revala
label: ancient estonian counties
description: Revala was an ancient Finnic coastal county in northern Estonia, bordering the Gulf of Finland around the prominent natural harbour of Lindanise. Governed by a council of elders and parish assemblies, the county controlled crucial maritime trading corridors between the Baltic archipelagoes and Novgorod. In 1219, Danish crusaders led by King Valdemar II landed at Lindanise and constructed Toompea Castle on the bluff overlooking the bay, subjugating the county in 1220 and establishing the Duchy of Estonia. \n\n Status: Autonomous tribal county; Administrative seat: Tallinn; Common languages: Old Estonian; Religion: Estonian paganism; Government: Council of elders; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Historical region: Ancient Estonia; Disestablished: 1220; Succeeded by: Danish Estonia

name: Saaremaa
label: ancient estonian counties
description: Saaremaa, historically known as Ösel, was an independent island county encompassing the largest island of the West Estonian archipelago in the Baltic Sea. Governed by warlike elders and maritime assemblies, the Osilians built formidable naval fleets that carried out daring seafaring raids across Scandinavian and Livonian coasts. The islanders defended their independence from hillforts across the island until German crusaders crossed the frozen sea in 1227, compelling their final surrender and integrating the island into the Bishopric of Ösel-Wiek in 1228. \n\n Status: Autonomous maritime county; Administrative seat: Kuressaare; Common languages: Old Estonian; Religion: Estonian paganism; Government: Tribal eldership; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Historical region: Ancient Estonia; Disestablished: 1228; Succeeded by: Bishopric of Ösel-Wiek

name: Sakala
label: ancient estonian counties
description: Sakala was a prominent ancient Estonian county situated across the rolling forested hills of south-central Estonia. Administered by parish chieftains and elder assemblies, the county coordinated regional defence from heavily fortified ringforts, chief among them the stronghold at Viljandi. Sakala emerged as the core of anti-crusader resistance during the Northern Crusades under the leadership of Elder Lembitu, before relentless military expeditions by the Livonian Brothers of the Sword subjugated the territory in the early thirteenth century. \n\n Status: Autonomous county; Administrative seat: Viljandi; Common languages: Old Estonian; Religion: Estonian paganism; Government: Tribal eldership; Ruler title: Elder; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Historical region: Ancient Estonia; Disestablished: 1208; Succeeded by: Livonian Brothers of the Sword

name: Sultanate of Dawaro
description: The Sultanate of Dawaro was a medieval Muslim state located in the eastern highlands of the Horn of Africa, situated east of Hadiya and south of the Awash River. Founded by eastern Cushitic and Somali clans, the sultanate commanded crucial inland caravan routes that linked the interior plateau with coastal Red Sea and Gulf of Aden ports. Dawaro defended its autonomy against neighbouring Christian rulers until Emperor Amda Seyon I launched a successful punitive campaign around 1330, subjugating the realm to imperial Ethiopian hegemony. \n\n Status: Sovereign sultanate; Capital: Dawaro; Common languages: Harari, Somali and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Islamic sultanate; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Middle Ages; Disestablished: 1330; Succeeded by: Ethiopian Empire

name: Talava
label: latgalian elderships
description: Talava was a major Latgalian territory situated in northern Vidzeme and Latgale, bordering the Estonian lands of Ugandi and Sakala. Governed by noble elders, notably Elder Tālivaldis from the fortified residence at Beverīna and administrative seat at Trikāta, the county practised Baltic animism alongside growing Eastern Orthodox influences from neighbouring Rus'. Confronted by Estonian raiders and German crusader pressure, its leaders accepted baptism from the Bishopric of Riga in 1208, leading to full partition between the bishop and the Sword Brothers by 1215. \n\n Status: Autonomous eldership; Administrative seat: Trikāta; Common languages: Latgalian; Religion: Baltic paganism and Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Eldership; Ruler title: Elder; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Disestablished: 1215; Succeeded by: Bishopric of Riga and Livonian Brothers of the Sword

name: Virumaa
label: ancient estonian counties
description: Virumaa was an ancient Finnic county situated in north-eastern Estonia, fronting the Gulf of Finland and extending east toward the Narva River. Divided into five distinct clan districts known as kilikunda, the territory was defended by robust timber and stone fortifications, notably the hillfort of Tarwanpe at modern Rakvere. The county engaged in continuous maritime and overland skirmishes with Novgorod and Scandinavian fleets until Danish and German crusaders subdued its elder-led confederacy, formally dividing its lands by 1228 into Danish Estonia. \n\n Status: Autonomous county; Administrative seat: Tarwanpe; Common languages: Old Estonian; Religion: Estonian paganism; Government: Tribal eldership; Ruler title: Elder; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Historical region: Ancient Estonia; Disestablished: 1228; Succeeded by: Danish Estonia

name: Wildgraviate
label: holy roman empire
description: The Wildgraviate was an imperial comital lordship situated in the forested Nahegau region of the Rhineland within the Holy Roman Empire. Originating from the ancient comital house of the Emichones and Salm dynasties, the counts adopted the title of Wildgraves, or forest counts, establishing their primary residence at the fortified hilltop castle of Kyrburg near Kirn. The rulers maintained extensive woodland fiefs, hunting rights and feudal jurisdictions across the Hunsrück hills until subsequent dynastic partitions in 1149 divided their ancestral holdings among rival heirs. \n\n Status: Imperial comital lordship; Capital: Kyrburg; Common languages: Middle High German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal county; Ruler title: Wildgrave; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Disestablished: 1149; Preceded by: Nahegau

name: Zanzibar
label: polities of the swahili coast
description: Zanzibar was an independent Swahili mercantile city-state centred on the island of Unguja off the eastern coast of Africa. Administered from ancient port settlements including Unguja Ukuu and later Shangani, the island served as an indispensable transshipment hub connecting Indian Ocean dhow traffic with coastal mainland trade in ivory, timber and mangrove poles. Blending indigenous Bantu traditions with Persian and Arab cultural elements, the autonomous island realm flourished through maritime trade until Portuguese naval expeditions subjugated the Swahili archipelago during the late fifteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign city-state; Capital: Unguja Ukuu; Common languages: Swahili and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Mercantile monarchy; Historical era: Middle Ages; Historical region: Swahili Coast; Disestablished: 1451; Succeeded by: Portuguese Empire

name: Rajahnate of Butuan
label: barangay states
description: The Rajahnate of Butuan was an ancient maritime and metallurgical state located along the Agusan River delta on north-eastern Mindanao in the Philippines. Governed by a Hindu-Buddhist royal dynasty, the realm attained international renown for its exquisite gold metallurgy, seafaring outrigger balangay vessels and extensive diplomatic missions dispatched to the Song imperial court in China. Butuan maintained thriving trading partnerships across Maritime Southeast Asia before inland shifts in river channels and regional political realignments reduced its trade dominance prior to Spanish colonisation. \n\n Status: Sovereign rajahnate; Capital: Butuan; Common languages: Butuanon, Old Malay and Visayan; Religion: Hinduism, Buddhism and Animism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Rajah; Currency: Piloncitos and gold rings; Historical era: Classical Southeast Asia; Disestablished: 1522

name: County of Savoy
label: holy roman empire
description: The County of Savoy was a prominent feudal state of the Holy Roman Empire that emerged from the dissolution of the Kingdom of Burgundy in the western Alps. Founded by Count Humbert the White-Handed, the comital dynasty secured control over vital transalpine trade routes across the Mont Cenis and Great Saint Bernard passes. The counts transferred their administrative capital to Chambéry in 1295, consolidating an extensive territory spanning both slopes of the Alps until Emperor Sigismund elevated the realm into the Duchy of Savoy in 1416. \n\n Status: County of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Chambéry; Common languages: Arpitan, Old French, Piedmontese and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Savoy; Ruler title: Count of Savoy; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Disestablished: 1417; Succeeded by: Duchy of Savoy

name: Lohara Dynasty
description: The Lohara Dynasty was a Hindu royal lineage of Khasa extraction that ruled the Kashmir Valley and adjacent mountainous regions in the northern Indian subcontinent. Established by King Sangramaraja with its royal seat at Srinagar, the dynasty defended the valley against external Ghaznavid invasions and patronised literary culture, most famously documented in Kalhana's chronicle Rajatarangini. The realm gradually weakened during the fourteenth century due to factional court feuds and regional uprisings, paving the way for the establishment of the Kashmir Sultanate in 1339. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Srinagar; Common languages: Sanskrit and Old Kashmiri; Religion: Shaivite Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Medieval India; Established: 1004; Disestablished: 1340; Succeeded by: Kashmir Sultanate

name: Lordship of Deutz
label: holy roman empire
description: The Lordship of Deutz was an imperial territory situated directly opposite the city of Cologne on the eastern bank of the Rhine River. Centred on the ancient Roman fortification and the prominent Benedictine Abbey of Deutz, founded by Archbishop Heribert of Cologne, the settlement held independent market privileges and defensive rights within the Holy Roman Empire. The lordship retained local autonomy through complex feudal arrangements until the Archbishopric of Cologne and the Duchy of Berg consolidated their territorial authority over the eastern bank in the early fourteenth century. \n\n Status: Imperial lordship; Capital: Deutz; Common languages: Middle Low German and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal lordship; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Disestablished: 1312; Succeeded by: Electorate of Cologne and Duchy of Berg

name: Banu Kanz
description: Banu Kanz was a semi-nomadic Arab-Beja dynasty that governed the frontier borderland between Upper Egypt and northern Nubia along the First Cataract of the Nile. Originating from the intermarriage of Banu Hanifa tribesmen with indigenous Hadariba nobility, the rulers established their political centre at Aswan and exercised control over lucrative gold mining in the Wadi Allaqi. After earning the hereditary title of Kanz al-Dawla from the Fatimid caliphs, the dynasty ruled autonomously until military pressure from Saladin's Ayyubid forces in 1174 forced their migration south into Christian Nubia. \n\n Status: Autonomous emirate; Capital: Aswan; Common languages: Arabic and Beja; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Tribal principality; Ruler title: Kanz al-Dawla; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Disestablished: 1175; Succeeded by: Ayyubid Sultanate

name: Prince-Bishopric of Merseburg
label: holy roman empire
description: The Prince-Bishopric of Merseburg was an ecclesiastical territory of the Holy Roman Empire situated along the Saale River in the eastern marches of the Duchy of Saxony. Re-founded in 1004 by King Henry II following earlier Slavic rebellions, the episcopal see governed a compact domain stretching toward the Mulde River while integrating Christian institutions into surrounding Sorbian communities. The prince-bishops exercised temporal immediacy from Merseburg Cathedral until the Protestant Reformation undermined Catholic ecclesiastical authority, culminating in the annexation of its secular administration by the Electorate of Saxony in the 1560s. \n\n Status: Prince-bishopric of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Merseburg; Common languages: Upper Saxon and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Ecclesiastical principality; Ruler title: Prince-Bishop; Historical era: High Middle Ages to Early modern; Disestablished: 1566; Succeeded by: Electorate of Saxony

name: Kalahandi State
description: Kalahandi State was an ancient and medieval kingdom situated across the densely forested and mineral-rich hill tracts of southwestern Odisha. Founded by the Nagavamsi royal dynasty, the realm maintained independent rule from administrative strongholds around Bhawanipatna, extracting wealth from agricultural river basins and highland trade passes. The rulers skilfully balanced relations with surrounding Ganga and Gajapati monarchs, preserving their local sovereignty and distinctive tribal customs through centuries of regional warfare until the arrival of Maratha and British overlordship. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Bhawanipatna; Common languages: Odia and Kui; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Nagavamsi; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 1006

name: Burgraviate of Meissen
label: holy roman empire
description: The Burgraviate of Meissen was an imperial military and judicial domain centred on the fortified Albrechtsburg heights above the Elbe River in Saxony. Distinct from the neighbouring margraviate, the office of burgrave was established by German emperors to garrison the citadel and oversee regional imperial estates in the eastern borderlands. name: Prince-Bishopric of Bamberg
label: holy roman empire
description: The Prince-Bishopric of Bamberg was an ecclesiastical principality of the Holy Roman Empire established in Upper Franconia along the Regnitz River. Founded in 1007 by King Henry II to accelerate Christian missionary efforts among neighbouring Slavic settlements, the bishopric obtained imperial immediacy and expanded through extensive territorial acquisitions across Franconia and Carinthia. name: Kingdom of Georgia
description: The Kingdom of Georgia was a unified medieval Christian monarchy that arose in the South Caucasus through the dynastic integration of Abkhazia and Caucasian Iberia by King Bagrat III. label: holy roman empire

name: Taifa of Alpuente

description: The Taifa of Alpuente was a small independent Muslim principality established in the rugged mountainous highlands northwest of Valencia following the collapse of the Caliphate of Córdoba. name: Taifa of Badajoz
label: spanish taifas
description: The Taifa of Badajoz was a major Islamic kingdom of western al-Andalus that emerged during the disintegration of the Umayyad Caliphate. Ruled initially by the Aftasid dynasty, the taifa governed a vast expanse encompassing modern Extremadura and central Portugal, controlling critical crossings of the Guadiana River and the Atlantic littoral. The kingdom engaged in recurring territorial warfare with Seville and the Kingdom of León, flourishing culturally until internal crises and the Almoravid military advance extinguished Aftasid rule in 1094, prior to fleeting resurgences in subsequent centuries. \n\n Status: Sovereign taifa; Capital: Badajoz; Common languages: Andalusi Arabic and Mozarabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Aftasid dynasty; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1010; Disestablished: 1231; Currency: Dirham and Dinar

name: Taifa of Denia
label: spanish taifas
description: The Taifa of Denia was an influential maritime Islamic kingdom situated along the eastern coast of Spain and across the Balearic Islands. Founded by the Slavic freedman and military commander Mujahid al-Amiri, the realm constructed a powerful corsair navy from its port at Dénia, launching naval expeditions against Sardinia and dominating Mediterranean sealanes. Denia prospered through international sea trade and intellectual patronage until the Hudids of Zaragoza annexed the mainland territory in 1076, followed by a brief separate resurgence prior to Christian conquest. \n\n Status: Sovereign taifa; Capital: Dénia; Common languages: Andalusi Arabic and Mozarabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Maritime monarchy; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1011; Disestablished: 1228; Succeeded by: Taifa of Zaragoza and Crown of Aragon

name: Taifa of Morón
label: spanish taifas
description: The Taifa of Morón was an independent Berber principality centred on the fortified hillside settlement of Morón de la Frontera in southern al-Andalus. Established by the Banu Dammar, a clan belonging to the Zenata Berber confederation, the micro-state maintained defensive sovereignty over the agricultural plains south of Seville. name: Taifa of Toledo
label: spanish taifas
description: The Taifa of Toledo was a prominent and wealthy Muslim state that controlled the central plateau of the Iberian Peninsula along the Tagus River valley. Ruled by the Dhunnunid dynasty of Hawwara Berber origins, the taifa expanded across New Castile and briefly annexed Valencia, patronising scientific learning, astronomy and monumental garden architecture. Internal dynastic instability and heavy Christian tribute demands culminated in May 1085 when King Alfonso VI of León and Castile negotiated the peaceful surrender of Toledo, incorporating the ancient Visigothic capital into his realm. \n\n Status: Sovereign taifa; Capital: Toledo; Common languages: Andalusi Arabic, Mozarabic and Ladino; Religion: Sunni Islam, Christianity and Judaism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Dhunnunid dynasty; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Disestablished: 6 May 1085; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Toledo

name: Taifa of Tortosa
label: spanish taifas
description: The Taifa of Tortosa was a coastal Islamic principality situated around the fertile estuary of the Ebro River in north-eastern al-Andalus. Founded by Slavic commanders known as the Saqaliba who had served the Cordoban caliphs, the kingdom controlled vital riverine commerce and maintained an active seafaring port at Tortosa. name: Taifa of Valencia
label: spanish taifas
description: The Taifa of Valencia was an important Islamic kingdom centred on the prosperous agricultural plain of the Huerta and the Mediterranean port of Balansiyya. Initially governed by Slavic commanders and later the Amirid dynasty, descendants of Almanzor, the taifa flourished as a vibrant hub of silk manufacturing, paper production and irrigated horticulture. The state survived successive interventions from Toledo, the famous military lordship of El Cid and Almoravid occupation, before its final independent period under Zayyan ibn Mardanish ended with the Aragonese conquest of Valencia in 1238. \n\n Status: Sovereign taifa; Capital: València; Common languages: Andalusi Arabic and Mozarabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1011; Disestablished: 1239; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Valencia

name: Taifa of Arcos
label: spanish taifas
description: The Taifa of Arcos was an independent Berber principality centred on the precipitous sandstone cliffs of Arcos de la Frontera above the Guadalete River. Established by the Banu Jizrun, a clan of the Zenata Berber confederation who had ousted the Cordoban governor, the kingdom asserted dominion over the ancient cora of Sidonia. name: Taifa of Murcia
label: spanish taifas
description: The Taifa of Murcia was an Andalusian Islamic state situated along the fertile Segura River basin in south-eastern Iberia. Achieving its greatest prominence during the twelfth century under the charismatic warrior-king Muhammad ibn Mardanish, known as the Wolf King, Murcia served as the bastion of Andalusi resistance against the puritanical Almohad Caliphate. name: Sharifate of Mecca
description: The Sharifate of Mecca was an autonomous Arabian principality governed by the Hasanid Sharifs, patrilineal descendants of the Islamic Prophet Muhammad through his grandson Hasan. Centred on the holy sanctuaries of Mecca and the Tihamah coastal strip, the emirate derived religious authority and diplomatic leverage from its guardianship of the Kaaba and the annual Hajj pilgrimage. Although repeatedly forced to acknowledge nominal suzerainty from Fatimid, Ayyubid or Seljuk overlords, the Sharifs exercised autonomous local governance, levying transit dues and organising Bedouin tribal alliances across the western Hejaz. \n\n Status: Sovereign sharifate; Capital: Mecca; Official languages: Arabic; Religion: Zaydi Islam and Sunni Islam; Government: Islamic emirate; Ruling dynasty: Hasanid dynasty; Ruler title: Sharif of Mecca; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 1013

name: Taifa of Albarracín

description: The Taifa of Albarracín was a mountainous Islamic buffer kingdom located in the rugged Sierra de Albarracín along the upper Guadalaviar River. Founded and governed by the Banu Razin, a Berber dynasty that had settled in central Iberia during the early Muslim conquest, the polity defended its independence from a formidable rocky promontory. The rulers skilfully balanced diplomatic relations between Christian Aragon, Navarre and the rival Muslim taifas of Toledo and Zaragoza until the Almoravid military advance extinguished the independent emirate in May 1104. \n\n Status: Sovereign taifa; Capital: Albarracín; Common languages: Andalusi Arabic, Berber and Mozarabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Hereditary emirate; Ruling dynasty: Banu Razin; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1013; Disestablished: 1 May 1104; Succeeded by: Almoravid Empire

name: Taifa of Almería
label: spanish taifas
description: The Taifa of Almería was a prosperous maritime Islamic kingdom located along the arid Mediterranean coast of south-eastern Spain. Flourishing under the rule of Slavic emirs such as Khayran and later the Banu Sumadih dynasty, Almería developed into one of the wealthiest ports in al-Andalus, famed for its five thousand silk looms, shipbuilding docks and international commerce. The state defended its lucrative coastline against incursions from Granada and Seville until expanding Almoravid armies incorporated the territory into their North African empire in the late eleventh century. \n\n Status: Sovereign taifa; Capital: Almería; Common languages: Andalusi Arabic and Mozarabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Emir; Currency: Dirham and Dinar; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1013; Disestablished: 1148; Succeeded by: Almoravid Empire

name: Taifa of Saltés and Huelva
label: spanish taifas
description: The Taifa of Saltés and Huelva was a compact maritime kingdom situated around the estuary of the Odiel and Tinto rivers in south-western Iberia. Governed by the Banu Bakr, a lineage belonging to the Arab Hawazin tribe, the taifa was centred on the island fortress of Saltés and the neighbouring port town of Huelva. The principality drew its livelihood from coastal fisheries, salt panning and coastal trade, fostering notable scholars such as the geographer al-Bakri before the expansionist Abbadid ruler of Seville annexed the realm in 1052. \n\n Status: Sovereign taifa; Capital: Huelva; Common languages: Andalusi Arabic and Mozarabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Hereditary emirate; Ruling dynasty: Banu Bakr; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1013; Disestablished: 1052; Succeeded by: Taifa of Seville

name: North Sea Empire
label: norse/viking polities
description: The North Sea Empire was an extensive maritime personal union that temporarily united the kingdoms of England, Denmark and Norway under Norse dynastic authority. name: Taifa of Algeciras

description: The Taifa of Algeciras was a fortified maritime kingdom situated on the Bay of Gibraltar at the southern tip of the Iberian Peninsula. Originally established under the Hammudid dynasty, who also claimed the caliphate in Córdoba and Málaga, the taifa commanded essential naval crossings linking al-Andalus with North Africa. The emirs operated from the well-defended coastal port of Al-Jazira al-Khadra, controlling maritime traffic and regional customs until the ascendant Abbadid monarchs of Seville annexed the strategic territory into their expanding kingdom in 1056. \n\n Status: Sovereign taifa; Capital: Algeciras; Common languages: Andalusi Arabic and Mozarabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Hereditary emirate; Ruling dynasty: Hammudid dynasty; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1014; Disestablished: 1056; Succeeded by: Taifa of Seville

name: Taifa of Carmona

Despite enduring several protracted sieges, the small emirate was finally overwhelmed and absorbed by the rival Taifa of Seville under Abbad II al-Mu'tadid in 1068, before a brief revival in the twelfth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign taifa; Capital: Carmona; Common languages: Andalusi Arabic, Berber and Mozarabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Hereditary emirate; Ruling dynasty: Banu Birzal; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1014; Disestablished: 1068; Succeeded by: Taifa of Seville

name: Taifa of Granada

description: The Taifa of Granada was a powerful Muslim kingdom established in the foothills of the Sierra Nevada by the Zirids, a Sanhaja Berber dynasty originating from North Africa. The Zirid emirs maintained an influential court that employed notable Jewish viziers like Samuel ibn Naghrela, until growing Christian military pressure and religious orthodox revival culminated in conquest by the Almoravid Empire in 1091. \n\n Status: Sovereign taifa; Capital: Granada; Common languages: Andalusi Arabic, Berber, Mozarabic and Hebrew; Religion: Sunni Islam, Judaism and Christianity; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Zirid dynasty; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1014; Disestablished: 1091; Succeeded by: Almoravid Empire

name: County of Beichlingen
label: holy roman empire
description: The County of Beichlingen was a noble feudal domain within the Holy Roman Empire, located in the Thuringian Basin north of Weimar and Erfurt. Founded by comital descendants of the Saxon noble House of Weimar, the counts ruled from the fortified hilltop castle of Beichlingen on the southern edge of the Schmücke ridge. The comital house exercised judicial authority, forest regalia and market patronages across adjacent settlements until mounting financial debts and line divisions compelled the cession of their ancestral properties to the House of Werthern in 1519. \n\n Status: County of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Beichlingen; Common languages: Middle High German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal county; Ruler title: Count of Beichlingen; Historical era: High to Late Middle Ages; Established: 1015; Disestablished: 1520; Succeeded by: Electorate of Saxony

name: County of Bobbio
label: holy roman empire
description: The County of Bobbio was a historic feudal territory of the Holy Roman Empire situated in the Trebbia River valley of northern Emilia. Established in 1014 when Emperor Henry II elevated the renowned monastic settlement around the Abbey of Saint Columbanus into an episcopal see and imperial comital jurisdiction, Bobbio guarded strategic mountain passes between Piacenza and Genoa. The counts and prince-bishops defended their autonomy against encroachment by neighbouring communes, maintaining distinct feudal privileges until subsequent integration into the territorial domains of the Duchy of Milan. \n\n Status: Imperial county; Capital: Bobbio; Common languages: Italian, Ligurian and Emilian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal county; Ruler title: Count of Bobbio; Historical era: High Middle Ages to Renaissance; Disestablished: 1517; Succeeded by: Duchy of Milan

name: Hammadid Sultanate
label: berber kingdoms
description: The Hammadid Sultanate was a powerful Sanhaja Berber dynasty that ruled the central Maghreb across modern northern Algeria. Founded when Hammad ibn Buluggin broke away from the parent Zirid dynasty, the realm was governed initially from the mountain fortress of Qal'at Bani Hammad and subsequently from the coastal port of Béjaïa. The state flourished through Mediterranean maritime trade, architectural patronage and scholarship, dominating coastal cities from Algiers to Constantine before the relentless eastward expansion of the Almohad Caliphate brought the sultanate to an end in 1152. \n\n Status: Sovereign sultanate; Capital: Béjaïa; Common languages: Berber and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Hammadid dynasty; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1015; Disestablished: 1153; Succeeded by: Almohad Caliphate

name: Kingdom of Kakheti-Hereti

Formed in 1014 when the energetic ruler Kvirike III the Great united the principalities of Kakheti and Hereti, the state established its royal capital at Telavi. The realm resisted repeated attempts at unification by the Bagrationi monarchs of western Georgia, defending its frontiers against regional nomadic incursions until King David IV the Builder decisively defeated its noble faction and annexed the territory into unified Georgia in 1104. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Telavi; Common languages: Georgian; Religion: Georgian Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1015; Disestablished: 1105; Preceded by: Principality of Kakheti; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Georgia

name: County of Loon
label: holy roman empire
description: The County of Loon was a feudal state of the Holy Roman Empire encompassing the Dutch-speaking region that corresponds to modern Belgian Limburg. Governed initially from the ancestral motte-and-bailey castle at Borgloon before relocating its administrative court to Kuringen near Hasselt, the county developed ten fortified Good Cities along the Meuse and Demer rivers. The counts maintained an autonomous policy while navigating feudal subjection to the Prince-Bishopric of Liège, which formally and permanently incorporated Loon directly into the episcopal domain upon the extinction of the comital line in 1366. \n\n Status: County of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Borgloon; Common languages: Limburgish, Middle Dutch and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal county; Ruler title: Count of Loon; Historical era: High to Late Middle Ages; Disestablished: 1367; Succeeded by: Prince-Bishopric of Liège

name: Burgraviate of Döben
label: holy roman empire
description: The Burgraviate of Döben was an imperial defensive and territorial lordship situated along the Mulde River near Grimma in Saxony. Centred on the fortified castle of Döben, historically recorded as Dewin, the burgraves were imperial officials appointed by Salian and Staufen monarchs to protect regional trade crossings and control colonised Slavic districts. The burgraviate exercised judicial and military rights over nearby villages within the Holy Roman Empire until expanding Wettin influence during the late thirteenth century absorbed the castle into the Margraviate of Meissen. \n\n Status: Imperial burgraviate; Capital: Dewin; Common languages: Middle High German and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal burgraviate; Ruler title: Burgrave; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Disestablished: 1292; Succeeded by: Margraviate of Meissen

name: Kingdom of Croatia
description: The Kingdom of Croatia during this early eleventh-century phase was a South Slavic monarchy that temporarily accepted tributary vassalage under the Eastern Roman Empire. Following Emperor Basil II's total conquest of the First Bulgarian Empire, the Byzantine court asserted direct suzerainty over the Dalmatian coastline, compelling the Croatian king Krešimir III to acknowledge imperial overlordship. Governed from inland administrative residences including Knin, the realm preserved its native royal administration, feudal nobility and Latin Christian ecclesiastical institutions until imperial authority waned in the Adriatic, restoring sovereign Croatian independence. \n\n Status: Vassal kingdom under the Byzantine Empire; Capital: Knin; Common languages: Old Croatian, Latin and Old Church Slavonic; Religion: Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Trpimirović dynasty; Ruler title: King; Historical era: High Middle Ages

name: North Sea Empire
label: norse/viking polities
description: The North Sea Empire during this dual-monarchy phase was a personal union uniting the crowns of England and Denmark under Anglo-Scandinavian rulers. Governed from the royal seat at Winchester and Danish regional centres, the realm coordinated trans-maritime trade and naval security across the North Sea basin under Cnut the Great and later his son Harthacnut. Following periods when Norway broke away, this Danish-English union maintained common legal charters, defensive fleets and ecclesiastical links until Harthacnut's sudden demise in June 1042 terminated Scandinavian dominion over England. \n\n Status: Sovereign personal union; Capital: Winchester; Common languages: Old English, Old Norse and Latin; Religion: Christianity; Government: Monarchy in personal union; Ruler title: King; First ruler: Cnut the Great; Subsequent ruler: Harthacnut; Historical era: Viking Age; Disestablished: 8 June 1042; Succeeded by: Kingdom of England and Kingdom of Denmark

name: Taifa of Santa Maria do Algarve
label: spanish taifas
description: The Taifa of Santa Maria do Algarve was a small Islamic kingdom located at the southernmost tip of modern Portugal along the Atlantic ocean. Founded by the Banu Harun, a family of Muladi and Arab origins, the principality was centred on the ancient port city of Shantamariyya al-Gharb, present-day Faro. The taifa prospered through maritime trade, coastal fishing and agricultural orchards until 1051, when the aggressive expansion of the Taifa of Seville under Abbad II al-Mu'tadid forcibly subdued and annexed the realm. \n\n Status: Sovereign taifa; Capital: Faro; Common languages: Andalusi Arabic and Mozarabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Hereditary emirate; Ruling dynasty: Banu Harun; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1019; Disestablished: 1052; Succeeded by: Taifa of Seville

name: Taifa of Zaragoza
label: spanish taifas
description: The Taifa of Zaragoza was an influential Islamic state that dominated the Upper March of al-Andalus along the fertile Ebro River basin. Governed successively by the Tujibid and Hudid dynasties from their fortified capital of Saraqusta, the taifa was renowned for its splendid Aljafería palace, mathematical scholarship and sophisticated diplomacy. The emirs guarded the northern frontier against the expanding Christian kingdoms of Aragon, Navarre and Castile through tributary diplomacy, surviving until advancing Almoravid forces annexed the city in 1110 just before Aragonese reconquest. \n\n Status: Sovereign taifa; Capital: Zaragoza; Common languages: Andalusi Arabic, Mozarabic and Hebrew; Religion: Sunni Islam, Christianity and Judaism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Banu Hud; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1019; Disestablished: 1111; Succeeded by: Almoravid Empire

name: Almoravid Emirate
label: berber kingdoms
description: The Almoravid Emirate was a powerful Saharan Berber empire founded by a reformist religious coalition of the Lamtuna, Gudala and Massufa nomadic tribes. Establishing their imperial capital at Marrakesh around 1070, the leaders Yusuf ibn Tashfin and his successors crossed the Strait of Gibraltar, halting the Christian Reconquista at the Battle of Sagrajas and unifying the fractured taifas of al-Andalus with the Maghreb. Strict Maliki jurisprudence and gold-backed currency underpinned imperial cohesion until the rise of the rival Almohad movement dismantled Almoravid power by 1147. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Marrakesh; Common languages: Berber languages, Arabic and Mozarabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Theocratic monarchy; Ruler title: Amir al-Muslimin; Currency: Almoravid dinar; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1020; Disestablished: 1148; Succeeded by: Almohad Caliphate

name: Kahuripan Kingdom
description: The Kahuripan Kingdom was an eleventh-century Hindu-Buddhist monarchy that reunited eastern Java following the catastrophic collapse of the Mataram Kingdom. Established by King Airlangga in the fertile Brantas River valley, the realm reconstructed extensive irrigation canals, rebuilt maritime river ports and sponsored classical Javanese court literature, notably the Kakawin Arjunawiwaha. Prior to his retirement into an ascetic hermitage in 1045, Airlangga partitioned the kingdom between his two sons, establishing the successor states of Janggala and Panjalu, later known as Kediri. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Kahuripan; Common languages: Old Javanese and Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism, Buddhism and Kejawen; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Maharaja; First ruler: Airlangga; Historical era: Classical Indonesia; Established: 1020; Disestablished: 1046; Succeeded by: Janggala and Kediri

name: Judicate of Gallura
label: sardinian judicates
description: The Judicate of Gallura was an autonomous medieval realm encompassing the granite mountains and northeastern coastline of Sardinia. name: Kachchhapaghata Dynasty
description: The Kachchhapaghata Dynasty was a prominent Rajput royal family that asserted sovereignty over north-western Madhya Pradesh following the disintegration of the Gurjara-Pratihara Empire. Centred on the formidable rock fortress of Gopagiri, modern Gwalior, the dynasty ruled across the Chambal River valley, defending their kingdom through shifting alliances with the Chandelas and Paramaras. The Kachchhapaghatas were distinguished patrons of monumental Hindu architecture, commissioning the ornate Sasbahu Temple complex inside Gwalior Fort, before expanding Ghurid armies led by Qutb ud-Din Aibak captured the fortress and extinguished their kingdom in the late twelfth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Gwalior; Common languages: Sanskrit and Prakrit; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Kachchhapaghata dynasty; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical era: Medieval India; Established: 1036; Disestablished: 1197; Succeeded by: Ghurid dynasty

name: Kingdom of Castile
description: The Kingdom of Castile was an influential Christian monarchy that emerged from a frontier county of the Kingdom of León to become the dominant military power of the Iberian Reconquista. Elevated to royal status under Ferdinand I and Sancho II with historic capitals at Burgos and Toledo, Castile spearheaded major territorial expansions southwards across the Meseta Central and Andalusia. Guided by legal codifications such as the Siete Partidas and supported by the Cortes of Castile, the kingdom maintained independent sovereignty across multiple historical phases until the Catholic Monarchs unified Castile and Aragon in 1479. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Burgos, Toledo and Valladolid; Common languages: Castilian Spanish and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: King of Castile; Legislature: Cortes of Castile; Currency: Spanish real; Historical era: High to Late Middle Ages; Disestablished: 20 January 1479; Succeeded by: Crown of Spain

name: Kingdom of Navarre
description: The Kingdom of Navarre was a historic Basque monarchy encompassing fertile valleys and rugged mountain passes on both slopes of the western Pyrenees. Known originally as the Kingdom of Pamplona, the realm established its royal court at Pamplona, playing a central role in early Iberian resistance against the Caliphate of Córdoba. The kingdom maintained its distinct legal charters known as the fueros, navigating complex marital alliances with French noble houses across successive centuries of independence until King Henry III of Navarre acceded to the French throne as Henry IV in 1589. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Pamplona; Common languages: Basque, Gascon, Romance and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: King of Navarre; Historical era: High Middle Ages to Early modern; Established: 1036; Disestablished: 2 August 1589; Succeeded by: Kingdom of France and Kingdom of Spain

name: Seljuk Empire
description: The Seljuk Empire was a vast Turco-Persian Muslim empire founded by the Qïnïq branch of Oghuz Turks under the brothers Tughril Beg and Chaghri Beg. Spanning from Anatolia and the Levant eastwards to the Hindu Kush, the empire operated from imperial capitals including Nishapur, Rayy and Isfahan, governing in close collaboration with the Abbasid Caliph in Baghdad. Guided by the famed vizier Nizam al-Mulk, the Seljuks established institutional madrasas, championed Sunni Islam and reshaped Middle Eastern geopolitics following the Battle of Manzikert until internal dynastic partitions fractured the imperial domain in the mid-twelfth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Nishapur, Rayy and Isfahan; Common languages: Persian, Oghuz Turkic and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Imperial monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Seljuk dynasty; Ruler title: Great Sultan; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1036; Disestablished: 1158; Succeeded by: Sultanate of Rûm and Khwarazmian Empire

name: Chudasama Dynasty
description: The Chudasama Dynasty was an enduring Rajput royal lineage that exercised sovereign dominion over the Saurashtra peninsula in modern Gujarat. Governed from the ancient citadel of Uparkot in Junagadh and their earlier seat at Vamanasthali, the kings defended their western maritime realm against neighbouring Chaulukya monarchs and maritime invaders. The dynasty patronised extensive stepwell engineering, rock-cut architecture and classical bardic traditions across Kathiawar until Sultan Mahmud Begada of the Gujarat Sultanate besieged Junagadh in 1472, capturing the last king Mandalika III and annexing Saurashtra into his sultanate. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Junagadh; Common languages: Old Gujarati and Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism and Jainism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Chudasama dynasty; Ruler title: Ra; Historical era: Medieval India; Established: 1037; Disestablished: 1473; Succeeded by: Gujarat Sultanate

name: Kingdom of Mewar
description: The Kingdom of Mewar was a renowned Rajput state situated across the south-central plains and Aravalli ranges of Rajasthan. Governed initially by the Guhila dynasty and later by their Sisodia descendants from historic strongholds including Nagda, Ahar and Chittorgarh, the kingdom defended its political independence against consecutive Delhi Sultanate and Mughal invasions. Under legendary maharanas such as Kumbha and Sanga, Mewar became the premier bastion of Rajput martial resistance, maintaining its sovereign status and indigenous administrative traditions until British paramountcy treaties were concluded in the early nineteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Chittorgarh and Udaipur; Common languages: Mewari and Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Guhila and Sisodia dynasties; Ruler title: Maharana; Historical era: Medieval to Early modern India; Established: 1037; Disestablished: 1807; Succeeded by: Udaipur Princely State

name: County of Babenburg
label: holy roman empire
description: The County of Babenburg was an early comital domain of the Holy Roman Empire located in the Franconian hills along the upper Main River. Rooted in the ancestral estates of the Popponid House of Babenberg centred on the fortress of Babenberch near Bamberg, the counts exercised regional judicial prerogatives and imperial immediacy. The family maintained significant political influence during Ottonian and Salian rule until dynastic successions and territorial redistributions in the late eleventh century incorporated their comital holdings into the emerging House of Henneberg and the Prince-Bishopric of Bamberg. \n\n Status: County of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Bamberg; Common languages: East Franconian and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal county; Ruling dynasty: Popponids; Ruler title: Count; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1038; Disestablished: 1097; Succeeded by: House of Henneberg and Prince-Bishopric of Bamberg

name: Miecław's State
description: Miecław's State was an autonomous eleventh-century pagan and Slavic polity that broke away from the Piast monarchy in Mazovia during the Polish realm's internal collapse. Seated at the riverine stronghold of Płock along the Vistula River, the former royal cupbearer Miecław established an independent principality supported by pagan traditionalists and neighbouring Prussian and Yatvingian tribes. Miecław successfully defended his breakaway realm against Bohemian incursions until Duke Casimir I the Restorer, aided by Yaroslav the Wise of Kiev, defeated Miecław's army in battle in 1047, reuniting Mazovia with the Duchy of Poland. \n\n Status: Sovereign breakaway principality; Capital: Płock; Common languages: Old Polish; Religion: Slavic paganism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Prince; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1038; Disestablished: 1048; Preceded by: Duchy of Poland; Succeeded by: Duchy of Poland

name: Numayrid Dynasty
description: The Numayrid Dynasty during this mid-eleventh-century period was an Arab Bedouin emirate based in Diyar Mudar in western Upper Mesopotamia, ruling as a tributary vassal under the Fatimid Caliphate. Operating from their principal urban capital at Harran and riverine fortresses along the Euphrates, the emirs of the Banu Numayr tribe acknowledged Fatimid spiritual suzerainty to counter Byzantine and Abbasid pressures. Under Emir Mani' ibn Shabib, the dynasty controlled lucrative caravan routes connecting Syria to Iraq, maintaining an influential court in Harran until expanding Seljuk armies and local Uqaylid rivals extinguished their regional hegemony. \n\n Status: Vassal emirate under the Fatimid Caliphate; Capital: Harran; Common languages: Arabic; Religion: Shia Islam; Government: Bedouin emirate; Ruling dynasty: Banu Numayr; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Disestablished: 1061; Succeeded by: Seljuk Empire and Uqaylid dynasty

name: County of Ventimiglia
label: holy roman empire
description: The County of Ventimiglia was an autonomous feudal state of the Holy Roman Empire situated along the Ligurian coastline where the Roia River meets the Mediterranean Sea. Governed by the comital House of Ventimiglia, descendants of the Arduinici and Obertenghi dynasties, the counts controlled crucial alpine passes linking the coastal Riviera with Piedmont. The county fiercely resisted the naval and territorial expansion of the Republic of Genoa for more than two centuries, engaging in repeated armed conflicts until military defeat and financial exhaustion forced the comital line to cede their coastal holdings to Genoa in 1258. \n\n Status: County of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Ventimiglia; Common languages: Ligurian, Occitan and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal county; Ruling dynasty: House of Ventimiglia; Ruler title: Count of Ventimiglia; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1040; Disestablished: 1259; Succeeded by: Republic of Genoa

name: Taifa of Ronda
label: spanish taifas
description: The Taifa of Ronda was an independent Berber principality centred on the precipitous clifftop city of Irunda, modern Ronda, in the rugged Serranía mountains of southern al-Andalus. Established by the Banu Ifran, a warrior clan of the Zenata Berber confederation, the micro-state maintained formidable natural defences along the deep El Tajo gorge. The emirs held sway over surrounding mountain villages and defended their mountain stronghold against surrounding Arab rulers until the aggressive Abbadid dynasty of Seville conquered and annexed the taifa under Abbad II al-Mu'tadid in 1065. \n\n Status: Sovereign taifa; Capital: Ronda; Common languages: Andalusi Arabic, Berber and Mozarabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Hereditary emirate; Ruling dynasty: Banu Ifran; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1040; Disestablished: 1066; Succeeded by: Taifa of Seville

name: Habsburg Domains
label: holy roman empire
description: The Habsburg Domains constituted an extensive composite monarchy centred in Central Europe that grew from a Swabian comital castle into one of Europe's foremost imperial powers. Anchored at the imperial residence of the Hofburg in Vienna following the 1278 victory on the Marchfeld, the dynasty accumulated hereditary duchies, the Kingdom of Bohemia and the Kingdom of Hungary through strategic dynastic marriages. The monarchs held the imperial crown of the Holy Roman Empire almost continuously from 1438 until Francis II proclaimed the unified Austrian Empire in August 1804 in response to Napoleonic expansion. \n\n Status: Composite imperial monarchy; Capital: Vienna; Common languages: German, Hungarian, Latin and Czech; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Composite monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Habsburg; Ruler title: Archduke and Holy Roman Emperor; Historical era: High Middle Ages to Early modern; Disestablished: 11 August 1804; Succeeded by: Austrian Empire

name: Lordship of Tarasp

description: The Lordship of Tarasp was an imperial baronial enclave of the Holy Roman Empire located in the Lower Engadin valley along the Inn River in modern Graubünden. Commanded by the imposing hilltop fortress of Tarasp Castle, the lordship was held by local noble dynasts and later by the Counts of Matsch, maintaining immediate imperial rights independent of surrounding Rhaetian leagues. The Catholic barony controlled vital alpine passes linking Tyrol with the Engadin, repeatedly resisting annexation by the Bishopric of Chur until the House of Habsburg acquired the strategic enclave in 1464. \n\n Status: Imperial lordship; Capital: Tarasp; Common languages: Romansh, Alemannic German and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal lordship; Ruler title: Lord of Tarasp; Historical era: High to Late Middle Ages; Disestablished: 1466; Succeeded by: Habsburg Hereditary Lands

name: March of Carniola

description: The March of Carniola was an imperial frontier margraviate of the Holy Roman Empire established in the upper Sava River basin of modern Slovenia. Separated from the Duchy of Carinthia to bolster southeastern alpine defences against the Kingdom of Hungary, the march was administered from administrative centres including Kranj, Kamnik and Ljubljana. Ruled by imperial margraves from the Houses of Weimar-Orlamünde and Andechs, Carniola fostered German and Slavic agrarian settlement until the extinction of the Babenbergs and subsequent territorial consolidation led to its elevation as the Duchy of Carniola in 1364. \n\n Status: Imperial margraviate; Capital: Ljubljana; Common languages: Slovene, Middle High German and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal margraviate; Ruler title: Margrave of Carniola; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Disestablished: 1246; Preceded by: Duchy of Carinthia; Succeeded by: Duchy of Carniola
